frq.title: Rhetorical analysis: a hardware store owner on who pays for a tax break
frq.stem:
In 2025, the town council of a small river town considered granting a ten-year property-tax exemption to a national home-improvement chain that planned to build a store on the highway at the edge of town. At the council's public hearing, the owner of a hardware store her family has run downtown for sixty years spoke. The passage below is her statement. (The owner, the town, the chain, the neighboring town, and every figure are invented for practice; an exam passage runs 600 to 800 words.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the owner makes to persuade the council to deny the tax exemption.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

My father opened Hollis Hardware in 1965 with one counter, two aisles, and a sign he painted himself. I was eight. My job on Saturdays was to sort loose screws into their bins, and my father's job, as far as I could tell, was to listen. A man would come in holding a dripping length of pipe, my father would ask what it was attached to, and twenty minutes later the man would leave with a two-dollar part and a plan.

I do not tell you this to ask for your pity. I know what a store like mine costs to run, and I know what the store you are considering can offer. It will stock forty thousand items; I stock nine thousand. It will sell a box of deck screws for a dollar less than I can. If I had a pickup truck and a free Saturday, I might drive out to Route 6 myself.

But price is one line on the receipt. Consider what else each store gives this town. Last year my store paid eleven thousand dollars in property tax, about what the town spends to plow Main Street for a winter. Under the exemption before you, the new store would pay nothing for ten years. My six employees live within three miles of the counter; the chain will hire, and I hope it hires well, but its profits will be counted in another state. When Carver Falls gave the same chain the same exemption in 2014, two hardware stores, a lumberyard, and a paint shop closed within four years, and the town raised its property tax twice to cover the empty storefronts.

So what, exactly, would the exemption buy? Not the store. The chain's own filing says it chose this site for the highway access and the thirty-five thousand people who live within twenty miles. It is coming either way. The exemption does not bring the store here; it decides who pays for the roads, the plowing, and the police the store will use. Under this plan, that is every downtown business and every homeowner in this room.

I am not asking you to keep anyone out. Let the chain come, and let it compete with me on price, on selection, on service. I will lose some of those contests and win others. My father would have liked the fight. I am asking only that you not make me pay its taxes while we have it. Deny the exemption.

rows.earns: A defensible thesis that analyzes the owner's rhetorical choices in light of her purpose and audience, for example: 'Knowing the council may hear a rival's plea as self-interest, the owner concedes everything the chain does better, then compares the two stores on what each gives the town and reframes the vote from whether the store should come to who should pay for it, so that her demand, held until the last line, arrives as the only fair conclusion.' The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the owner uses rhetorical choices to persuade the council'); naming appeals with no purpose ('she uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); summarizing the statement; or arguing about big-box stores or tax breaks instead of analyzing her choices.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how multiple choices serve her purpose: the opening narration (her father 'was to listen,' 'a two-dollar part and a plan') defines what a local store gives before any argument begins; the concession ('forty thousand items; I stock nine thousand,' 'I might drive out to Route 6 myself') disarms the charge that she fears competition; the turn 'But price is one line on the receipt' moves the comparison to like categories the council governs (eleven thousand dollars in tax against nothing for ten years, employees within three miles against profits 'in another state'); the Carver Falls precedent traces cause and effect to closings and two tax increases; and the question 'So what, exactly, would the exemption buy?' uses the chain's own filing to show the store 'is coming either way,' so the thesis 'Deny the exemption' lands last as the conclusion her reasoning has reached.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for every claim, but commentary explains only some choices, or explains one choice well and lists the rest. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it, or no line of reasoning joins the paragraphs. 1: mostly general evidence and a summary of the statement. 0: restates the thesis, repeats the passage, or is irrelevant. Labeling the father story 'pathos' without saying what it establishes for the later comparison stays at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A consistently complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, for example explaining the tension she must manage (a competitor asking a council to act against her competitor) and how her structure resolves it: she separates the store, which she welcomes, from the exemption, which she opposes, and withholds her demand until the council has accepted that the store will come regardless; or explaining the significance of the frame, the father who listened returning as the father who 'would have liked the fight,' which recasts her position as a call for fair competition rather than protection; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: A sentence praising the statement as 'very effective'; a general claim about small businesses in America; a tension named once in the conclusion and dropped; or elevated vocabulary that carries no insight. The point rewards the essay's thinking throughout, not a closing flourish.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'Speaking to a council that could easily dismiss her as a rival protecting her own business, the owner grants the chain its advantages, compares the two stores on what each returns to the town, and redefines the exemption as a transfer of costs to residents, so that her one-line demand at the end reads as fairness rather than fear.' It names the audience's likely suspicion, her main moves in the order she makes them, and the purpose they serve.
parts.n: 'The owner uses a story, statistics, and a rhetorical question to persuade the council' lists devices with no function and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with evidence and the commentary that earns the points.
parts.a:
¶1 Conceding to earn a hearing: 'I do not tell you this to ask for your pity,' forty thousand items against nine thousand, the dollar-cheaper deck screws, 'I might drive out to Route 6 myself.' Commentary: by stating the chain's advantages before the council can, she shows she is not blind to them, so the council cannot dismiss what follows as a competitor's fear; the father story has already shown what her store offers that a price tag cannot.
¶2 Changing the categories of comparison: 'But price is one line on the receipt'; eleven thousand dollars in property tax, 'about what the town spends to plow Main Street for a winter,' against nothing for ten years; local employees against profits 'counted in another state'; then Carver Falls, where four businesses closed and taxes rose twice. Commentary: she compares the stores on what the council is responsible for, the town's revenue and services, and the precedent turns that comparison into a predicted chain of effects, so the exemption's cost becomes concrete and local.
¶3 Reframing the vote and arriving at the claim: 'So what, exactly, would the exemption buy? Not the store,' the chain's own filing, 'It is coming either way,' 'every downtown business and every homeowner in this room,' and the final 'Deny the exemption.' Commentary: using the chain's own document removes the council's reason to offer the break, and naming the people in the room makes them the ones who would pay; because the demand comes only after this reasoning, it reads as the conclusion the evidence forces.
parts.n: Paragraphs organized by appeal ('the ethos paragraph, the logos paragraph') tend to list; organize by what she does to the council, in the order she does it, and explain each step.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Develop the central tension throughout: as a rival asking the council to rule against a rival, the owner risks sounding self-serving, and every major choice manages that risk. Show that her line of reasoning separates the store from the tax break, concedes the first so she can oppose the second, and saves the demand for last, when the council has already accepted that the chain is coming; then explain how the closing return to her father, who 'would have liked the fight,' turns the argument into a defense of fair competition.
parts.n: A final sentence saying 'this speech shows the struggles of small businesses everywhere' is a broad claim, not sophistication; the complexity has to shape the analysis from the thesis on.

frq.title: Argument: does showing your reasoning matter more than being right?
frq.stem:
In a column for a magazine read by teachers, a veteran mathematics teacher wrote: 'A right answer without its reasoning is only a rumor. I would rather grade a wrong answer that shows its work than a right one that does not.' (The teacher and the column are invented for practice.)

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which showing the reasoning behind a conclusion matters more than reaching the right conclusion.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

rows.earns: A defensible position on the extent to which reasoning matters more than the right conclusion, for example: 'Wherever other people must trust, check, or build on a conclusion, as in a classroom, a laboratory, or a courtroom, the reasoning matters more than the answer, because a right answer no one can check cannot be relied on twice; only when a decision must be right at once, as in an emergency, does the answer come first.' Agreeing with the teacher, disagreeing, or qualifying the claim by context can all earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt; 'both reasoning and answers are important' with no position on which matters more or when; an obvious fact ('teachers want students to show their work'); or a summary of the teacher's column.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how it does. Evidence may come from school (a proof graded on its steps, a lab report's methods section), public life (a judge who writes an opinion explaining a ruling, a city that publishes the study behind a decision), work, or personal experience (a group project, a coach who explains a play), each followed by commentary on why seeing the reasoning let someone trust, check, correct, or repeat the conclusion, or why, in a counterexample such as an emergency diagnosis, the answer had to come first. The paragraphs are ordered so each builds on the last.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence for each claim, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it, or the paragraphs could be reordered with no loss because no line of reasoning joins them. 1: mostly general evidence ('in life, people need to explain themselves') and summary. 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. Three examples that each say only 'reasoning is important' repeat the thesis rather than advance it.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently explores a tension, for example that shown reasoning can also dress up a wrong conclusion (a confident, well-organized argument for a false claim) so the value of showing work lies in letting others test it, not in the display itself; or articulating the implication of the position in a broader context, such as why public trust in experts depends on seeing their reasoning; or effective rhetorical choices, such as a concession that consistently strengthens the argument; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: 'Of course, some people disagree' added to the conclusion; a counterexample named once and never answered; or a sweeping closing claim about society. The complexity must shape the position throughout.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'The teacher is right for any conclusion that others must rely on: a right answer whose reasoning is hidden can be neither checked nor repeated, while a wrong answer that shows its steps can be corrected; but when there is no time to check, as when a paramedic must act in seconds, the right answer matters first and the reasoning can be explained afterward.' It takes a position and limits it by a stated condition, which previews a line of reasoning.
parts.n: 'Reasoning and correct answers are both important in different ways' names two values without choosing between them and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with evidence and the commentary that earns the points.
parts.a:
¶1 Shown reasoning makes errors fixable: a geometry proof with one wrong step. Commentary: a teacher can find the step and the student can fix it, so the wrong answer teaches more than a right answer copied from a friend, which teaches nothing and cannot be repeated on the test.
¶2 Shown reasoning makes conclusions trustworthy to others: a court's written opinion, or a city council that publishes the traffic study behind a new stop sign. Commentary: people who lose a decision can still accept it when they can see how it was reached, and they can challenge the step they doubt instead of the whole outcome; the reasoning, not the verdict alone, is what earns public trust. This builds on ¶1: what lets a student fix an error is what lets a community check a decision.
¶3 Concession and limit: a paramedic treating a patient who cannot breathe. Commentary: here a right action now outweighs an explanation, but even here the reasoning returns afterward in the report other medics learn from, so the exception confirms that reasoning is what makes a right answer repeatable.
parts.n: Three paragraphs each saying 'this shows reasoning is important' earn at most 2; each paragraph needs its own reason, placed so it builds on the one before.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Work the tension throughout between reasoning as a tool for checking and reasoning as performance: a polished argument can make a wrong conclusion look sound, so the essay can argue that the value of showing work lies in exposing each step to someone who might test it. Carry that idea through each paragraph (the teacher who checks the proof, the public that checks the council, the medics who check the report) rather than raising it once at the end.
parts.n: Ending with 'this debate will continue as technology changes how we find answers' gestures at a broader context without explaining its implications, and earns nothing.

frq.title: Synthesis: should school districts move to a four-day week?
frq.stem:
A growing number of school districts, many of them rural, have moved from a five-day to a four-day school week, lengthening each remaining day. Supporters point to savings and to teacher recruitment; critics point to child care, school meals, and learning, especially for young students.

Carefully read the following six sources, including the introductory information for each source. Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether school districts should adopt a four-day school week.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning. Indicate clearly the sources used through direct quotation, paraphrase, or summary. Sources may be cited as Source A, Source B, etc., or by using the description in parentheses.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

(All six sources, their authors, and their figures are invented for practice and summarized here; on the exam each text source runs about 500 words and two sources are visual.)

Source A (Brandt, district statement)
Lena Brandt, superintendent of a rural district of 1,100 students, 'Why We Went to Four Days,' a statement posted on the district's website, 2024. Before the switch, each posted teaching job drew an average of 3 applicants; in the two years since, it has drawn 11. Brandt reports savings on buses, heating, and substitutes of about 2 percent of the budget and says the real gain is keeping teachers who would otherwise leave for larger districts nearby. School days now run from 7:55 a.m. to 3:50 p.m., Monday through Thursday.

Source B (reading growth chart)
A bar chart from a state education department report, 2024, titled 'Average yearly growth on the state reading test (scale points), districts of similar size and income.' Each grade band has two bars. The data:
Grade band · Five-day districts · Four-day districts
Grades 3–5 · 14 · 12
Grades 6–8 · 9 · 8.5
Grades 9–11 · 6 · 6
A note under the chart states that the grades 6–8 difference is within the report's margin of error and the grades 3–5 difference is not, and that districts chose their own schedules.

Source C (Okafor, op-ed)
Ruth Okafor, director of a nonprofit child-care center, 'Who Pays for Friday?', an op-ed in a county newspaper, 2023. After the local district moved to four days, the center's Friday enrollment of school-age children tripled and it now keeps a waiting list of 40. A full Friday of care costs families about 45 dollars per child. Okafor argues that the district's savings were moved onto working parents, most of all those with young children who cannot stay home alone.

Source D (Delgado, policy brief)
Mateo Delgado, an education economist, from a policy brief for a state legislative committee, 2024. Across the districts he studied, four-day weeks saved between 1 and 3 percent of operating budgets, far less than supporters predicted, because salaries, the largest cost, did not change. He notes the schedule's appeal to job applicants and concludes that the decision 'is about people, not pennies.'

Source E (Park, student editorial)
Joon Park, a high school senior in a four-day district, an editorial in his school newspaper, 2024. Park uses Fridays for a paid job and for a class at the community college, and reports that attendance at his school rose because families now schedule appointments on Fridays. He adds that in a day ending near 4 p.m. the last period is 'a blur,' and that athletes often miss it for away games.

Source F (food bank fact sheet)
A fact sheet from a regional food bank, 2024. In the four-day districts it serves, 38 percent of students qualify for free or reduced-price school meals, so a three-day weekend means an extra day without those meals. The food bank began sending take-home bags of food on Thursdays, and demand for them has risen by about a third since the districts switched.

rows.earns: A defensible position on whether districts should adopt a four-day week, for example: 'Districts that cannot fill teaching jobs should adopt a four-day week only if they also pay for the fifth day, with Friday care and meals for the families who would otherwise absorb the district's small savings.' Arguing for the schedule, against it, or for it only under stated conditions can all earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt; 'the four-day week has pros and cons'; 'schools are important to communities' (an obvious fact, not a position on the schedule); or a summary of the sources with no position.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from at least three sources, clearly cited (Source A or 'Brandt'), supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how: Delgado's 1 to 3 percent and Brandt's 2 percent show the savings are small, so the case must rest on people, as Delgado says; Brandt's rise from 3 to 11 applicants per job shows the recruiting gain; the chart shows almost no difference for older students but a 2-point gap in grades 3–5 that the report calls real; Okafor's tripled Friday enrollment at 45 dollars a day and the food bank's one-third rise in weekend bags show where the costs land; Park shows what older students gain from a free Friday.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence from three sources, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: evidence from three sources, but explanation is limited or there is no line of reasoning. 1: evidence from at least two sources, summarized rather than explained. 0: restates the thesis, repeats provided information, or references fewer than two sources. Reading the chart as 'four-day students learn much less' misreports it: the older grades show little or no difference.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently works the tensions among the sources, for example the pattern by age (older students such as Park gain a working Friday, while the chart's grades 3–5 gap, Okafor's young children, and the food bank's meals all point to costs for the youngest), or the tension between what the schedule does for staff (Brandt, Delgado) and what it does to families (Okafor, the food bank); or explaining the limits of the evidence (Brandt reports on her own decision, the chart compares districts that chose their schedules, so it shows a difference, not its cause); or situating the question in a broader context, such as the unstated jobs schools do beyond teaching; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: One sentence granting that 'some parents may have trouble with child care'; a counterargument named once and dropped; or a list of the sources' disagreements that never shapes the position.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'A four-day week is worth adopting only where it solves a problem money cannot, keeping teachers in hard-to-staff districts, and only if the district spends part of what it saves on Friday care and meals; otherwise its small savings are bought with young children's learning and poorer families' budgets.' It takes a position, limits it with conditions the sources support, and previews the line of reasoning.
parts.n: 'Districts should carefully consider the four-day week' takes no position and does not earn the point.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs, naming the sources each uses and the commentary that ties them to the line of reasoning.
parts.a:
¶1 The real benefit is people, not money (Sources D, A): Delgado's 1 to 3 percent savings and Brandt's 2 percent; Brandt's 3 applicants per job rising to 11. Commentary: since the savings are too small to justify the change alone, the schedule is worth considering only as a recruiting tool, which is exactly where Brandt's evidence is strongest.
¶2 The costs fall on the youngest and poorest (Sources B, C, F): the grades 3–5 gap of 2 points, which the report says is real, against almost none in older grades; Okafor's tripled Friday enrollment and 45 dollars a day; the food bank's one-third rise in weekend bags for the 38 percent who rely on school meals. Commentary: together they show the district's savings move onto families who can least absorb them, which a transition such as 'But those savings are not free' should signal as the essay's turn.
¶3 A conditional yes (Sources E, C, A): Park's working Friday shows the schedule suits older students; Okafor's center shows the care Fridays require. Commentary: a district that uses part of its savings for Friday programs keeps Brandt's recruiting gain without shifting its costs, which is the condition the thesis sets.
parts.n: A paragraph per source ('Source A says... Source B says...') is the classic Row B score of 1 or 2; organize by claim and let two or three sources meet in each paragraph.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Build the essay on the age pattern the sources reveal together: Park, a senior, gains the most from a free Friday, while the chart's grades 3–5 gap, Okafor's young children, and the food bank's weekend bags show the youngest paying the most. Let that tension shape the position (a schedule for high schools but not elementary schools, or a four-day week with a supervised fifth day) and note that the chart shows a difference between self-selected districts, not proof that the schedule caused it.
parts.n: Adding 'however, every district is different' to the conclusion is not complexity; the tension has to shape the claim throughout.

frq.title: Reading set: a planner on the paths people wear across lawns
frq.stem:
The following passage is from an essay by a campus planner, published in a magazine for architects and landscape designers. (The essay, the writer, and the two campuses are invented for practice.)

(1) Every campus has them: the brown stripes worn across a lawn where people refuse to use the sidewalk. (2) Planners call them desire paths, and for decades the usual response has been a fence, a hedge, or a sign asking walkers to keep off the grass. (3) The stripes almost always come back.

(4) They come back because a desire path is not vandalism; it is information. (5) Each one records thousands of small decisions by people who know exactly where they need to go and how little time they have to get there. (6) A sidewalk that bends around a flower bed may look graceful on the designer's drawing, but it costs every walker twenty extra steps, and walkers are counting.

(7) Consider two campuses built in the same year. (8) At the first, designers laid out a grid of paths on paper, and within five years the groundskeepers were reseeding the same worn lawns every spring. (9) At the second, designers planted grass everywhere, waited a year, and then paved the paths that walkers had already worn. (10) The second campus paved fewer feet of sidewalk, and its lawns needed almost no repair.

(11) None of this means that every shortcut deserves concrete. (12) A path through a wetland or across a loading dock should be redirected, and sometimes the longer route is the safer one. (13) But a planner who treats every worn stripe as a problem to be fenced is fighting the very people the plan exists to serve. (14) Before we draw another sidewalk, we should find out where people are already walking.

parts.q:
The writer's thesis is stated most directly in
(A) sentence 2
(B) sentence 4
(C) sentence 10
(D) sentence 14
parts.a: (D). Sentence 14 states the overarching claim the passage leads to: planners should learn where people already walk before drawing sidewalks. Sentence 4 is a subclaim that redefines desire paths as information, a step toward that recommendation; sentence 2 reports the usual response the writer opposes; sentence 10 reports evidence from the comparison.
parts.n: REO-1.A, skill 5.A. The passage arrives at its thesis; the strongest distractor is the early claim (sentence 4), which supports the thesis rather than stating it.

parts.q:
Sentence 4 functions primarily to
(A) redefine desire paths in a way that sets up the argument of the rest of the passage
(B) concede that desire paths damage campus lawns
(C) introduce the comparison of two campuses
(D) summarize the evidence presented in the first paragraph
parts.a: (A). 'Not vandalism; it is information' replaces the view behind fences and signs with a new definition, and every later step depends on it: sentences 5 and 6 explain it, the comparison tests it, and the recommendation acts on it. It concedes nothing (B), the comparison begins in sentence 7 (C), and the first paragraph offers a situation, not evidence to summarize (D).
parts.n: REO-1.E and REO-1.L, skill 5.A. Ask what the sentence makes possible for the paragraphs that follow; that is its function in the line of reasoning.

parts.q:
In sentences 7 through 10, the writer develops the argument primarily by
(A) narrating the writer's own experience as a campus planner
(B) comparing two campuses on the same categories of planning and upkeep
(C) defining the term 'desire path'
(D) describing the appearance of worn lawns in sensory detail
parts.a: (B). The writer presents two campuses built the same year and measures both on like categories: how the paths were planned (drawn in advance or paved where walkers went) and what followed (yearly reseeding or almost no repair, and how much was paved). The comparison-contrast lets the difference in method carry the argument. The writer does not narrate personal experience (A), and the definition (C) and description (D) come earlier.
parts.n: REO-1.K, skill 5.C. Comparison-contrast needs like categories on both sides; spotting the shared categories confirms the method.

parts.q:
The word 'But' at the beginning of sentence 13 primarily signals
(A) a return from acknowledged exceptions to the writer's main claim
(B) a contradiction of the evidence presented in sentences 8 through 10
(C) the introduction of a new counterargument
(D) a shift from the writer's view to the view of groundskeepers
parts.a: (A). Sentences 11 and 12 grant exceptions (wetlands, loading docks, safer long routes); 'But' turns back to the writer's position that fencing every path fights the people the plan serves, which leads into the recommendation in sentence 14. It does not dispute the comparison (B), no new objection follows (C), and the view remains the writer's (D).
parts.n: REO-1.P, skill 5.B. A contrast transition after a concession usually marks the turn back to the writer's claim, not a new opposing point.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the line of reasoning of the passage as a whole?
(A) It states a recommendation and then offers three equal reasons in support of it.
(B) It moves from a familiar problem, to a new explanation of it, to a comparison that tests that explanation, to a qualified recommendation.
(C) It traces the history of campus design from its beginnings to the present.
(D) It presents a series of objections to desire paths and refutes each one in turn.
parts.a: (B). Paragraph 1 presents the problem (paths return despite fences), paragraph 2 explains why (paths are information), paragraph 3 tests the explanation with two campuses, and paragraph 4 limits the claim before recommending action. The recommendation comes last, not first (A); there is no history (C); and the only objections are the exceptions the writer grants in paragraph 4 (D).
parts.n: REO-1.A and REO-1.E, skill 5.A. Describe each paragraph's job and how it prepares the next; the sequence of paragraphs is the line of reasoning.

frq.title: Writing set: a student's draft on cafeteria composting
frq.stem:
The following passage is a draft of an editorial that a high school student is writing for the school newspaper, whose readers include students, teachers, and members of the school board. The blank in sentence 13 marks a word or phrase the writer has not yet chosen. (The draft, the schools, and the figures are invented for practice.)

(1) Every school day, our cafeteria throws away about ninety pounds of food. (2) Most of it is fruit peels, bread crusts, and half-eaten vegetables, all of which could become compost instead of landfill. (3) Our school should start a composting program for cafeteria waste.

(4) Composting would cut the school's trash costs. (5) The district pays for trash hauling by weight, and food scraps are the heaviest thing in the cafeteria bins. (6) Lincoln Middle School, across town, began composting two years ago. (7) Its hauling bill fell by about 30 percent in the first year. (8) The cafeteria at Lincoln also serves breakfast.

(9) Composting would also give our science classes something they lack. (10) For three years, our biology teacher has asked for a garden where students can study soil. (11) The finished compost could enrich that garden, so students would see the whole cycle, from lunch tray to soil to plant.

(12) Some people worry that compost bins would smell and attract pests. (13) ______ sealed bins emptied twice a week, like the ones Lincoln uses, have caused neither problem there. (14) The school board should approve a one-year trial of composting beginning in the spring and compare the hauling bills at the end of the year.

parts.q:
Which sentence should the writer delete because it does not support the claim of its paragraph?
(A) sentence 5
(B) sentence 7
(C) sentence 8
(D) sentence 10
parts.a: (C). Paragraph 2 claims that composting would cut trash costs; sentence 5 explains why (hauling is paid by weight), and sentence 7 gives the result at Lincoln. That Lincoln also serves breakfast neither supports the claim nor links to the sentences around it, so it breaks the paragraph's unity. Sentence 10 belongs to paragraph 3 and supports its claim about science classes.
parts.n: REO-1.M and REO-1.N, skill 6.A. A sentence can be true and on the general topic and still belong nowhere in the reasoning; test it against the paragraph's claim.

parts.q:
The writer wants to fill the blank at the beginning of sentence 13 (reproduced below) with a transition that shows how the sentence relates to sentence 12.
'______ sealed bins emptied twice a week, like the ones Lincoln uses, have caused neither problem there.'
Which of the following choices best accomplishes this goal?
(A) Therefore,
(B) For example,
(C) However,
(D) Similarly,
parts.a: (C). Sentence 12 states an objection (smell and pests) and sentence 13 answers it with evidence that the problem has not occurred, a relationship of contrast. 'Therefore' (A) would make the answer a result of the worry, 'For example' (B) would make it an instance of the worry, and 'Similarly' (D) would make the two sentences agree.
parts.n: REO-1.P and REO-1.Q, skill 6.B. Name the relationship between the two sentences first (here, objection and reply), then choose the transition that states it.

parts.q:
The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the evidence about Lincoln Middle School supports the claim in sentence 4. Which of the following choices best accomplishes this goal?
(A) Lincoln Middle School has more students than our school does.
(B) Because food scraps are what make the bins heavy, taking them out of the trash is what cut Lincoln's bill, and the same change would cut ours.
(C) Many other schools around the country have also started composting programs.
(D) Composting is one of the best things a school can do for the environment.
parts.a: (B). It connects the evidence to the claim through the paragraph's own mechanism (hauling is billed by weight, and scraps are the heaviest waste), explaining why Lincoln's result would apply here. (A) adds a detail that, if anything, weakens the comparison; (C) adds unsupported evidence; (D) shifts to a different claim, the environment.
parts.n: REO-1.C and REO-1.D, skill 6.A. Commentary explains why the evidence proves this claim; a new fact or a different claim is not commentary.

parts.q:
The writer wants to revise sentence 9 (reproduced below) so that it better guides the reader from paragraph 2 to paragraph 3.
'Composting would also give our science classes something they lack.'
Which of the following versions best accomplishes this goal?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) Saving money is not composting's only benefit: it would also give our science classes something they lack.
(C) Next, I will discuss science classes.
(D) In conclusion, composting would give our science classes something they lack.
parts.a: (B). It names the idea of paragraph 2 (saving money) and states its relationship to the new claim (another benefit), so the reader sees how the two paragraphs work together toward the thesis. The current version's 'also' (A) adds without naming what it adds to; (C) announces a topic instead of relating ideas; and 'In conclusion' (D) misstates the relationship, since the argument is not ending.
parts.n: REO-1.N and REO-1.P, skill 6.B. A strong transition between paragraphs carries the last idea forward and names how the next one relates to it.

parts.q:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 10.
'Last spring, her class planned to grow tomatoes to study how soil nutrients affect plants, but the project was canceled because the school had no place to plant them.'
Should the writer make this addition?
(A) Yes, because the brief account gives a concrete instance of the need described in sentence 10, which the compost would help meet.
(B) Yes, because it shows that the biology teacher planned poorly.
(C) No, because a narrative has no place in an argument.
(D) No, because it shifts the paragraph's focus from the science classes to the cafeteria.
parts.a: (A). The added sentence develops paragraph 3 by narration: a real, recent experience (a canceled project) makes the teacher's request concrete and shows what students lose without a garden, strengthening the claim in sentence 9. It does not fault the teacher (B); narration can serve an argument when it supports a claim (C); and it stays on the science classes (D).
parts.n: REO-1.I, skill 6.C. Narration earns its place when the experience it relates supports the paragraph's claim; answers that reject narration outright misread the method.

units.title: Style
units.blurb: Schemes and tropes by name, from anaphora and antithesis to metonymy and litotes, plus periodic and cumulative sentences, irony, punctuation for effect, passive voice and the usage rules the writing questions test.
keys: Schemes of repetition are named by position, with anaphora at clause openings, epistrophe at closings, and anadiplosis chaining end to start.
Antithesis sets contrasts in parallel form, antimetabole repeats the same words reversed, and chiasmus reverses only the grammatical shape.
Asyndeton speeds a list and polysyndeton slows it, while a rhetorical question recruits the audience and hypophora answers its own question.
Metaphor asserts, simile compares with like or as, metonymy swaps an associated thing, synecdoche swaps a part, and litotes affirms by negating.
Verbal irony builds complicity with readers who catch the gap, and Juvenalian satire like A Modest Proposal condemns where Horatian amuses.
Periodic sentences delay the main clause for suspense, cumulative ones lead with it, and subordination ranks ideas that coordination equalizes.
A colon promises a payoff and a dash breaks in for emphasis, while passive voice can erase the actor on purpose, as in mistakes were made.
That marks a restrictive clause and which a nonrestrictive one, and comma splices, dangling modifiers and broken parallelism are revision targets.

topics.t: What punctuation does for a purpose
Style as a mix of choices

frq.title: Rhetorical analysis: a shop teacher asks the board to keep her woodshop
frq.stem:
In 2025, a middle school shop teacher who had taught at her school for twenty-six years spoke at a public meeting of her district's school board. The board was considering a committee's proposal, delivered to staff in a memo, to convert the school's woodshop into a computer design lab. The passage below is her speech. (The teacher, the school, and the meeting are invented for practice; an exam passage runs 600 to 800 words.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the teacher makes to persuade the school board to keep the woodshop.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

I have been told that my classroom is obsolete. The word came in a memo, which is fitting; a memo is how you tell someone something you would rather not say to their face.

So let me say a few things to your faces.

For twenty-six years I have taught twelve-year-olds to use a handsaw. Not a laser cutter. Not a design app. A saw, which cuts exactly as straight as the hand that pushes it. On the first day, every one of them cuts crooked. They blame the saw. They blame the wood. They blame me. And then, some Tuesday in October, a boy who has not finished a worksheet all year holds up a board with an edge so true you could check a door frame by it, and he does not say a word, because he does not have to.

The proposal before you calls my room a "legacy space." I looked the phrase up. It means a room you are planning to empty.

I understand the argument for the computer lab. I am not a fool, and neither is the committee that wrote the memo. Our students will live in a world of screens, and they should learn to build things there, too. I would sign up for that class myself. But a screen forgives. It offers undo. It lets you try forty versions in an afternoon and throw away thirty-nine without a splinter or a scrap. That is its gift, and it is a real one.

The shop does not forgive, and that is its gift. Wood that is cut stays cut. A student who measures once and cuts twice learns something about attention that no lecture can teach, and she learns it with her own hands, on her own board, in front of her own classmates. She learns that the mistake was hers, and so was the fix.

You have been told that the choice is between the past and the future. It is not. It is between a room that teaches students how to start over and a room that teaches them how to get it right the first time. They will need both. Every carpenter I know uses a computer. I have never met an engineer who was sorry she learned to use a saw.

Keep the lab on your list. Keep my room, too. Find the money for both, and then come visit in October. Bring a door frame.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'Facing a board that has been told her woodshop is obsolete, the teacher answers the memo's evasive language with blunt, concrete speech, concedes the real value of the computer lab, and then recasts the choice as one between two kinds of learning, so that keeping the shop sounds like finishing the district's plan rather than resisting it.' It names her situation, her main stylistic moves in order, and the purpose they serve.
parts.n: 'The teacher uses diction, syntax, and tone to persuade the board' restates the prompt with a list of devices and earns nothing.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs in a line of reasoning, each with evidence and the commentary that earns the points.
parts.a:
¶1 Plain speech against official language: 'a memo is how you tell someone something you would rather not say to their face,' the one-line paragraph 'So let me say a few things to your faces,' and the quoted 'legacy space' translated as 'a room you are planning to empty.' Commentary: the irony about memos and the plain translation expose the committee's euphemism, so the board hears the proposal as a loss, and her directness makes her the more honest voice in the room.
¶2 Concrete detail and syntax that enact the lesson: the fragments 'Not a laser cutter. Not a design app.,' the repeated 'They blame the saw. They blame the wood. They blame me.,' and the long sentence that ends with a board 'so true you could check a door frame by it' and a boy who 'does not say a word.' Commentary: the short, repetitive sentences mimic the students' frustration and the long one builds to their quiet success; a boy who 'has not finished a worksheet all year' shows the board a learner a screen might never reach.
¶3 Concession and balance that reframe the choice: 'I am not a fool, and neither is the committee'; the matched sentences 'a screen forgives... That is its gift' and 'The shop does not forgive, and that is its gift'; 'They will need both'; and the closing 'Bring a door frame.' Commentary: granting the lab's value keeps the committee's supporters listening, the parallel 'gift' sentences set the two rooms side by side as equals, so the either-or choice looks false, and the closing invitation returns to the opening image, turning a protest into a request the board can grant.
parts.n: Paragraphs organized by device ('the diction paragraph,' 'the syntax paragraph') tend to list; organize by what she does to the board, in the order of the speech.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Develop the central tension throughout: the teacher must defend an old-fashioned class without sounding like an enemy of the future the board wants to fund. Show that her style resolves it: she is blunt about the memo but generous to the committee, and her reversal 'Every carpenter I know uses a computer' makes her, not the committee, the one who wants both kinds of learning. Explain the significance of the shifts in tone from wry to conciliatory to warm.
parts.n: Adding 'this speech shows that hands-on learning matters everywhere' to the conclusion is not sophistication; the complexity has to shape the argument throughout.

rows.earns: A defensible thesis that analyzes the teacher's rhetorical choices in light of her purpose and audience, for example: 'By exposing the memo's euphemisms in plain language, conceding what the computer lab offers, and balancing the two rooms as equal gifts, the teacher makes the board see the vote as a false choice it can refuse.' The thesis may be more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt ('the teacher uses rhetorical choices to persuade the board'); naming devices with no purpose ('she uses anaphora, fragments, and irony'); summarizing the speech; or arguing about shop classes instead of analyzing her choices.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning (the memo line, 'So let me say a few things to your faces,' 'legacy space,' the fragments and the repeated 'They blame,' the boy with the true board, 'I am not a fool,' the two 'gift' sentences, 'They will need both,' the carpenter and engineer sentences, 'Bring a door frame') and commentary consistently explains how the style choices work together: plain speech exposes the proposal's evasions, concrete narrative shows what the shop teaches, and balanced sentences recast an either-or vote as a choice to fund both.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence throughout, but commentary explains only some choices or ties them loosely to the board. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it or no line of reasoning connects the paragraphs. 1: mostly general evidence and summary. 0: restates the thesis, repeats the passage, or is irrelevant. Labeling 'They blame the saw. They blame the wood.' as anaphora without saying what the repetition shows the board stays at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A consistently complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, for example explaining the tension she must manage (defending an old class without seeming to resist the future) and how her generosity toward the committee and her 'both' framing resolve it; or tracing the significance of her shifts in tone from wry to conciliatory to warm; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: One sentence praising the speech as 'very effective'; a general claim about technology in schools; a tension named once and dropped; or elevated vocabulary that carries no insight. The point rewards the whole essay's thinking.

frq.title: Argument: are plain words the most persuasive words?
frq.stem:
In an essay on writing, a veteran newspaper editor argued: 'Plain words are the most persuasive words. The moment a writer reaches for an ornament, the reader starts to suspect a sales pitch.' (The editor and the essay are invented for practice.)

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which plain language is more persuasive than figurative or elaborate language.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'The editor is right that ornament breeds suspicion when it replaces evidence, but wrong that plain words always persuade best: a well-chosen figure of speech can make an abstract problem concrete for readers whom plain statistics leave unmoved, as long as it clarifies the claim rather than decorating it.'
parts.n: 'Plain and figurative language both have their place' takes no position and earns nothing.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs with specific evidence and commentary.
parts.a:
¶1 Concede where plain words win: a product recall notice that says 'Stop using this heater. It can catch fire.' protects more buyers than one that promises 'proactive safety enhancements.' Commentary: when stakes are high and trust is low, ornament reads as evasion, so the editor describes these moments accurately.
¶2 Show where a figure persuades better: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 image of America handing Black citizens 'a bad check' marked 'insufficient funds' turned an abstract injustice into a debt every listener understood and expected to be paid. Commentary: the metaphor carried the argument's logic (a promise owed and unpaid) in a form plain statements of inequality had not.
¶3 Draw the line: a school newsletter that calls a tutoring program 'a synergistic learning ecosystem' loses parents, while a teacher who calls it 'a second chance at algebra, every Tuesday' wins them. Commentary: both are figurative or elaborate to a degree; what fails is language that hides the claim, and what persuades is language that makes the claim easier to see.
parts.n: Evidence need not be famous, but it must be specific and explained; three examples with no commentary score as 1 or 2.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Build the essay on the distinction between ornament that clarifies and ornament that conceals, then complicate it: plain language can conceal too ('mistakes were made' is plain and evasive), so the real test is whether the words expose or hide the claim. Close by explaining why the distinction matters when readers are primed to distrust any polished phrase.
parts.n: A closing sentence saying 'it depends on the situation' is equivocation, not nuance.

rows.earns: A defensible position on the extent to which plain language persuades better, for example: 'Plain language persuades best when an audience doubts the speaker, but figurative language persuades best when an audience needs to see an unfamiliar problem, so the editor's rule holds only for the first case.' Agreeing, disagreeing, or qualifying the editor's claim can all earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the editor's claim; 'there are advantages to both plain and elaborate language'; 'it depends on the writer' with no position; or an obvious fact ('some writers use metaphors').

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from reading, history, current events, or experience supports every claim in a line of reasoning (for instance, a blunt safety notice, King's 'bad check,' a jargon-filled school newsletter, a coach's plain halftime speech, an advertisement that oversold its product) and commentary consistently explains how each example shows when plain or figurative language persuades and why.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: some specific evidence, but commentary mostly restates it or no clear line of reasoning. 1: general or hypothetical evidence with little explanation ('for example, if someone uses a metaphor...'). 0: restates the thesis or is irrelevant. Examples listed without saying what each proves stay at 2 or below.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently explores the tension, for example distinguishing ornament that clarifies from ornament that conceals and showing that plain language can also conceal; or situating the question in a broader context such as public distrust of polished political and corporate speech; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: 'This is a complex issue' with no development; a counterargument named in one sentence and dropped; or an essay that praises plain language in ornate prose without noticing the irony.

frq.title: Synthesis: should governments require plain language in public documents?
frq.stem:
Government documents such as tax instructions, benefit applications, court notices, and utility bills are often written in dense legal and technical language. Some governments now require agencies to write documents meant for the public in plain language: common words, short sentences, and clear organization. Critics argue that such rules can sacrifice the precision that legal documents depend on.

Carefully read the following six sources, including the introductory information for each source. Write an essay that synthesizes material from at least three of the sources and develops your position on whether governments should require that documents written for the public be in plain language.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
• Select and use evidence from at least three of the provided sources to support your line of reasoning. Indicate clearly the sources used through direct quotation, paraphrase, or summary. Sources may be cited as Source A, Source B, etc., or by using the description in parentheses.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

(All six sources, their authors, and their figures are invented for practice and summarized here; on the exam each text source runs about 500 words and two sources are visual.)

Source A (Whitcomb, public policy journal)
Dana Whitcomb, a professor of public administration, 'Words the Public Can Use,' an article in a journal of public policy, 2023. Whitcomb reports that in one state benefits office, 38 percent of denied applications were denied for missing documents that the agency's notice had requested in a single 94-word sentence. She argues that plain language is a matter of fairness, not style: 'A rule that no one can read is a rule that only lawyers can follow.'

Source B (city chart)
Adapted from a city office of civic innovation, 'Testing Our Notices,' 2024. A bar chart titled 'Comprehension of three city notices, original and plain-language versions.' The horizontal axis lists three notices; the vertical axis shows the percent of five questions about each notice answered correctly, from 0 to 100. Values:
Notice · Original version · Plain-language version
Water shutoff notice · 48 · 81
Jury summons · 55 · 79
Property tax appeal instructions · 41 · 64
A note below the chart says that 600 adult residents were randomly assigned one version of each notice and that the plain versions averaged 40 percent fewer words.

Source C (Aldana, legal magazine)
Martin Aldana, an attorney who drafts state legislation, 'In Defense of Hard Words,' an essay in a magazine for lawyers, 2022. Aldana argues that legal terms such as 'shall' and 'indemnify' carry meanings settled by decades of court decisions, so replacing them with everyday words can create new ambiguity and new lawsuits. He supports attaching a plain-language summary to legal documents but opposes rewriting the binding text itself.

Source D (county utilities report)
'Clearer Bills, Fewer Calls,' a report by a county utilities department, 2024. After the department rewrote its late-payment notice (from 410 words to 190), calls to its help line about the notice fell from about 2,100 a month to about 1,300, and the share of customers who paid within 30 days of receiving a notice rose from 61 to 70 percent. Rewriting and testing the notice cost about 18,000 dollars in staff time. The department cautions that it tested only one notice over six months.

Source E (Raman, research blog)
Priya Raman, a linguist, 'Plain to Whom?,' a post on the blog of a language-research group, 2023. Raman warns that readability formulas measure syllables and sentence length, not understanding, so a notice can score as 'plain' and still fail readers with limited English or limited literacy. She recommends testing documents with the people who will use them and translating the most important notices, not just shortening them.

Source F (Ferreira, newspaper interview)
Luis Ferreira, director of a community legal aid clinic, interviewed in a local newspaper, 2024. Ferreira says his staff spends about a third of each appointment explaining government letters. He describes a client who nearly lost her apartment because the deadline to respond appeared in the sixth paragraph of her notice. He supports plain-language rules but adds that 'a clear letter still needs a phone number that someone answers.'

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
parts.a: Model: 'Governments should require plain language in the documents the public must act on, because residents cannot follow rules they cannot understand, clearer notices measurably improve both comprehension and compliance, and the precision critics fear can be protected by keeping the binding legal text while requiring a tested plain version alongside it.'
parts.n: 'Governments should think carefully about how they write documents' takes no position and earns nothing.

parts.q: Row B plan: outline three body paragraphs, naming the sources each uses and the commentary that ties them to the line of reasoning.
parts.a:
¶1 Unreadable notices cost people what they are owed (Sources A, F): Whitcomb's 38 percent of denials traced to one 94-word sentence and Ferreira's client whose deadline sat in paragraph six. Commentary: together they show the harm falls on the people least able to hire help, which makes clarity a question of fairness, as Whitcomb argues, not taste.
¶2 Plain language works, and pays for itself (Sources B, D): comprehension rose from 48 to 81 percent on the water shutoff notice and from 41 to 64 on the tax appeal; the county's calls fell from about 2,100 to 1,300 a month and on-time payment rose from 61 to 70 percent for about 18,000 dollars. Commentary: the gains appear in two different settings, though D tested one notice for six months, so the claim is strong but should be monitored rather than assumed.
¶3 Require plain versions, keep precise law, and test with real readers (Sources C, E, F): Aldana's case for settled legal terms, his support for plain summaries, Raman's warning that formulas measure length rather than understanding, and Ferreira's point about a phone number someone answers. Commentary: a requirement that pairs the binding text with a plain version tested on actual readers answers Aldana's precision concern and Raman's caution at once.
parts.n: Summarizing each source in turn ('Source A says... Source B says...') without tying it to the thesis is the classic Row B score of 1 or 2.

parts.q: Row C plan: name one way this essay could earn the sophistication point.
parts.a: Make the shared value the engine of the essay: Whitcomb and Aldana both want people to be bound only by rules they can know; they disagree about whether everyday words or settled legal terms make rules knowable. Build the position from that tension, and acknowledge the evidence's limits (one county notice over six months in D, formulas that mislead in E) while explaining why the requirement still holds.
parts.n: Adding 'however, some people disagree' in the conclusion is not complexity; the tension has to shape the position throughout.

rows.earns: A defensible position on whether governments should require plain language, for example: 'Governments should require plain-language versions of public documents, because the public cannot follow rules it cannot read, and a tested plain version can sit alongside the precise legal text rather than replace it.' Arguing against a requirement, or for a limited one such as Aldana's summaries, can equally earn the point.
rows.loses: Restating the prompt; 'there are good arguments on both sides about plain language'; 'clear writing is important' (an obvious fact, not a position on a requirement); or a summary of the sources with no position.

rows.earns: 4: specific evidence from at least three sources, clearly cited (Source B or 'the city chart'), supports every claim in a line of reasoning, and commentary consistently explains how each supports it: the chart's gains (48 to 81, 55 to 79, 41 to 64) show comprehension improves; the county's drop in calls and rise in on-time payments show compliance improves at a modest cost; Aldana's concern is answered by pairing binding text with a plain version; Raman's warning shapes how documents should be tested.
rows.loses: 3: specific evidence from three sources, but commentary explains only some of it. 2: evidence from three sources, but explanation is limited or there is no line of reasoning. 1: evidence from at least two sources, summarized rather than explained. 0: restates the thesis, repeats provided information, or references fewer than two sources. Citing the chart as 'Source B proves plain language always works' overstates three notices tested once.

rows.earns: A nuanced argument that consistently works the tensions among sources, for example showing that Whitcomb and Aldana share a value (rules people can know) but disagree about which words make rules knowable; or explaining the limits of the evidence (one county notice over six months, readability formulas that mislead); or situating the question within the broader problem of public trust in government; or a consistently vivid, persuasive style.
rows.loses: One sentence acknowledging that 'lawyers might not like this'; a counterargument named once and dropped; or listing the sources' disagreements without using them to shape the position.

frq.title: Reading set: a columnist on Main Street's new signs
frq.stem:
The following passage is from a column published in a small town's weekly newspaper in 2025. Its writer, a longtime resident, was responding to the village board's decision to replace the hand-painted signs on the town's main street. (The column, the town, and the writer are invented for practice.)

(1) Last spring the village board voted, unanimously and with a slideshow, to replace the hand-painted signs on Main Street with matching backlit panels. (2) The panels are handsome. (3) They are also identical: the same white letters, the same blue field, the same polite glow from the pharmacy to the pawnshop. (4) The old signs were not identical. (5) Tony's Barbershop leaned a little to the left, as Tony did; the bakery's sign had been repainted so many times that its painted loaves had grown, over forty years, into something like small canoes. (6) Nobody would have called them professional. (7) Everybody could have told you whose they were. (8) I am told the new panels will improve the street's "visual coherence," a phrase that sounds like something a doctor would check for after a fall. (9) I do not doubt that the improvement is real. (10) A street where every sign can be read at forty miles per hour is a safer street, and I have been, on occasion, a driver going forty miles per hour. (11) But a town is not only a thing we drive through. (12) It is also a thing we recognize, the way we recognize a friend's handwriting before we read a word of the letter. (13) The panels will be easy to read. (14) I am less sure they will say anything.

parts.q:
In sentence 1, the phrase 'unanimously and with a slideshow' primarily serves to
(A) gently mock the board's confidence and the formality of its process
(B) praise the board for researching the decision carefully
(C) suggest that the board's vote broke the village's rules
(D) show that residents strongly supported the new signs
parts.a: (A). Pairing 'unanimously' with the trivial detail 'with a slideshow' deflates the vote's solemnity, conveying the writer's wry view of the board's certainty and its presentation. Nothing suggests praise for research (B) or illegality (C), and the phrase describes the board, not residents (D).
parts.n: STL-1.B and STL-1.R, skill 7.A. Descriptive phrases convey a perspective; the mismatch between a formal word and a trivial detail is the tell for wry irony.

parts.q:
The details in sentence 5 ('leaned a little to the left, as Tony did'; loaves grown 'into something like small canoes') chiefly convey the writer's
(A) affection for the old signs' imperfections as marks of the people who made them
(B) criticism of the shop owners' lack of skill
(C) belief that the old signs were a danger to drivers
(D) wish that the bakery had repainted its sign correctly
parts.a: (A). The comic, fond comparisons tie each sign's flaws to its owner ('as Tony did') and to its history ('over forty years'), and sentences 6 and 7 confirm that the imperfections are what made the signs recognizable. The tone is affectionate, not critical (B, D), and safety (C) enters only later, as the board's argument.
parts.n: STL-1.E, skill 7.A. Tone is inferred from connotation; 'leaned... as Tony did' is gentle teasing, not complaint.

parts.q:
In sentence 8, the writer places 'visual coherence' in quotation marks primarily to
(A) signal skepticism toward the official language used to justify the change
(B) cite the title of a published study
(C) define a technical term for readers
(D) emphasize that the writer agrees with the phrase
parts.a: (A). The quotation marks mark the phrase as someone else's term, and the comparison to 'something a doctor would check for after a fall' mocks its clinical sound. No study is named (B), nothing is defined (C), and the joke shows distance, not agreement (D).
parts.n: STL-1.O, skill 7.C. Scare quotes contribute to tone by distancing the writer from a word; they do not emphasize it.

parts.q:
Sentences 9 and 10 primarily serve to
(A) qualify the writer's position by conceding a genuine benefit of the new panels
(B) reverse the writer's earlier view of the old signs
(C) criticize drivers who speed through the town
(D) introduce a subject unrelated to the signs
parts.a: (A). The tone shifts from mocking to candid as the writer grants that readable signs make a safer street, even admitting to being one of the drivers. The concession limits the argument without abandoning it, since 'But' in sentence 11 turns back to what the panels cost. The writer never reverses (B), the self-inclusion is not an attack (C), and safety is tied to the signs (D).
parts.n: STL-1.F, skill 7.A. A shift in tone can signal qualification; a concession that keeps the position is not a reversal.

parts.q:
The final two sentences (13 and 14) are most notable for
(A) their pairing of two short sentences, which sets the panels' readability against their lack of meaning
(B) their technical vocabulary, which proves the panels are poorly designed
(C) their shift to open anger at the village board
(D) their summary of the evidence presented in sentences 1 through 12
parts.a: (A). Two short sentences placed side by side ('The panels will be easy to read. / I am less sure they will say anything.') set a conceded strength against the writer's doubt, with a play on signs that 'say' something, and their placement at the end, after longer sentences, makes the doubt land as the column's final judgment. The words are plain (B), the tone stays wry rather than angry (C), and nothing is summarized (D).
parts.n: STL-1.H, skill 7.B. The arrangement of sentences emphasizes ideas; a short closing pair after long sentences carries the weight.

frq.title: Writing set: a student's email about unsold bread
frq.stem:
The following passage is a draft of an email that a high school junior who works evenings at a grocery store plans to send to the store's manager, asking the store to donate its unsold bread to the school's food pantry. (The draft is invented for practice.)

(1) Every night at closing, your store throws away bread that is still good to eat. (2) I know this because I have worked the evening shift in the bakery department since June, and part of my job is clearing the day-old shelves after the doors are locked. (3) Last Tuesday I threw forty-two loaves into the dumpster still wrapped in plastic. (4) Meanwhile, our school's food pantry, which serves about sixty families, has not had fresh bread since September. (5) The pantry is run by the student council. (6) We have a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van. (7) What we do not have is bread. (8) I am asking you to let us pick up the day's unsold bread three evenings a week. (9) Our volunteers would arrive at 9:00 p.m., after closing, and use the loading door, so the pickups would not interfere with customers or with the closing staff. (10) We would also keep a record of every donation for the store's files. (11) Some stores worry that donated food could make them legally responsible if someone gets sick, however, a federal law protects businesses that donate food in good faith. (12) Wasting the bread is honestly kind of a crime. (13) I hope you will consider this, and I would be glad to meet with you any afternoon to answer questions or to show you the pantry.

parts.q:
In sentence 12 (reproduced below), the writer wants to convey concern in language suited to a manager she hopes to persuade.
Wasting the bread is honestly kind of a crime.
Which version of the sentence best achieves this purpose?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) Every loaf we collect could feed a family instead of filling a dumpster.
(C) Throwing away good bread is disgusting and selfish.
(D) Wasting bread is, like, not a great look for the store.
parts.a: (B). Its concrete contrast (feeding a family versus filling a dumpster) conveys concern through precise, respectful wording and points the manager toward what the donation would achieve. (A) and (D) are vague and too casual for a request to a manager, and (C) insults the person whose permission she needs.
parts.n: STL-1.A and STL-1.C, skill 8.A. Choose the wording whose connotations fit the audience and purpose; an accusation costs the request.

parts.q:
The writer wants to combine sentences 5 and 6 (reproduced below) to emphasize that the pantry is ready to handle donations.
The pantry is run by the student council. We have a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van.
Which of the following best achieves this purpose?
(A) The pantry is run by the student council, and we have a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van.
(B) Run by the student council, the pantry already has a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van.
(C) The pantry is run by the student council, a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van.
(D) Although the pantry is run by the student council, we have a refrigerator, volunteers, and a van.
parts.a: (B). The opening phrase correctly modifies 'the pantry,' which follows it, and the pantry's resources take the main clause, where the emphasis falls; 'already' underlines its readiness. (A) gives the two facts equal weight and shifts from 'the pantry' to 'we'; (C) lists the council alongside the equipment; (D)'s 'Although' signals a concession that makes no sense here.
parts.n: STL-1.K, STL-1.I and STL-1.S, skill 8.B. Put the idea you want stressed in the independent clause, and make sure an opening modifier names the right subject.

parts.q:
Which of the following is the best version of the portion of sentence 11 reproduced below?
...if someone gets sick, however, a federal law protects...
(A) (as it is now)
(B) if someone gets sick; however, a federal law protects
(C) if someone gets sick however a federal law protects
(D) if someone gets sick, however a federal law, protects
parts.a: (B). 'However' begins a new independent clause, so the two clauses must be joined by a semicolon (or split into two sentences), with a comma after 'however.' (A) is a comma splice, (C) runs the clauses together, and (D) puts a comma between the subject and its verb.
parts.n: STL-1.M and STL-1.N, skill 8.C. 'However' is not a conjunction, so a comma before it cannot join two independent clauses.

parts.q:
In sentence 3 (reproduced below), the writer wants to make clear that the loaves, not the dumpster, were still wrapped in plastic.
Last Tuesday I threw forty-two loaves into the dumpster still wrapped in plastic.
Which version of the sentence best achieves this purpose?
(A) (as it is now)
(B) Last Tuesday I threw forty-two loaves, still wrapped in plastic, into the dumpster.
(C) Still wrapped in plastic, last Tuesday I threw forty-two loaves into the dumpster.
(D) Last Tuesday, still wrapped in plastic, I threw forty-two loaves into the dumpster.
parts.a: (B). The modifier now sits directly after 'loaves,' the word it describes, and the commas set it off as a parenthetical detail that sharpens the waste. In (A) it seems to describe the dumpster; in (C) and (D) it seems to describe the writer, 'I.'
parts.n: STL-1.S, skill 8.B. Place a modifier closest to the word it modifies; an opening modifier attaches to the subject that follows it.

parts.q:
The writer is considering deleting the clause 'which serves about sixty families' from sentence 4. Should the writer keep or delete it?
(A) Keep it, because it gives the manager a concrete sense of how many people the donations would help.
(B) Keep it, because it explains how the pantry is funded.
(C) Delete it, because it repeats information given in sentence 2.
(D) Delete it, because it shifts the focus from the bread to the student council.
parts.a: (A). The nonrestrictive clause is not needed to identify the pantry, but it supplies the fact a manager weighing the request most needs, how many people would benefit, which advances the writer's purpose. It says nothing about funding (B), sentence 2 is about the writer's job (C), and the clause keeps the focus on who needs the bread (D).
parts.n: STL-1.T, skill 8.B. A parenthetical element is not essential to meaning, but it can meet an audience's need; judge it by what it does for the purpose.

units.title: Connections
units.blurb: Carries ideas across the four Big Ideas: how one choice serves audience, claim, reasoning and style at once, which look-alike tool a task calls for, and what weak analysis and commentary get wrong.

topics.t: Appeals are built from evidence, structure and style
Purpose, thesis and line of reasoning
Qualifying a claim: logic, syntax and tone
Relationships between ideas, clause to paragraph
Methods of development double as evidence
Sources inside your own line of reasoning

excl.s: The CED names no required texts and no required literary or grammatical terminology; the exam assesses the skills and essential knowledge, not term recall.

units.check: Across units · no CED progress check

frq.title: Rhetorical analysis: a 911 dispatcher asks for a second night shift
frq.stem:
In 2026, a county commission held a public hearing on its budget for the coming year. Among those who spoke was a dispatcher at the county's 911 center, who asked the commissioners to fund a second dispatcher for the overnight shift. The passage below is her statement. (The dispatcher, the county, and the hearing are invented for practice; an exam passage runs 600 to 800 words. This question draws on all four Big Ideas: the rhetorical situation of a budget hearing, a concession and cost evidence, narration and an analogy in the line of reasoning, and syntax and tone.)

Read the passage carefully. Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices the dispatcher makes to persuade the commissioners to fund a second overnight dispatcher.

In your response you should do the following:
• Respond to the prompt with a thesis that analyzes the writer's rhetorical choices.
• Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning.
• Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning.
• Demonstrate an understanding of the rhetorical situation.
• Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.

At 2:40 on a Sunday morning last March, my console lit up with three calls in the same minute. A man on Quarry Road said his wife was not breathing. A driver on Route 17 had hit a deer and was pinned behind the wheel. A teenager whispered that someone was trying the back door. I was the only dispatcher on duty for a county of 48,000 people.

I answered them in the order they came. That is the rule, and it is a good rule when someone else is there to take the second call. No one was. The man on Quarry Road waited fifty-one seconds for me to reach him. I know the number because I have listened to that recording more times than I will admit.

I understand the budget in front of you. I have read it, all of it, and I know that every line you add tonight has to come from somewhere. Nobody in this room is careless with public money, and I am not here to suggest that anyone is. A second overnight dispatcher would cost about $68,000 a year, with benefits. That is real money. It is also less than the $74,000 the county paid last year in overtime to cover the nights when one of us was sick.

Most of our calls come between seven in the morning and midnight, and that is how the schedule was built. But emergencies do not keep office hours. Between midnight and six, there are fewer calls, and they are different calls: crashes on empty roads, overdoses, fires, people alone in the dark. One dispatcher on those hours is one lifeguard for the whole lake. Most nights, the water is calm. Some nights it is not, and on those nights everyone is in the water at once.

The woman on Quarry Road lived. Her husband did everything I told him, once I could tell him. I think about those fifty-one seconds, and I think about the next Sunday morning, and the one after that.

I am not asking you for a new program. I am asking you for a second chair, and a person in it, from midnight to six. If you fund it, you will never hear about the calls that person answers. If you do not, you may someday hear about the ones no one could.

parts.q: Row A plan: write a thesis that earns the point.
