cards.a: A concession accepts that an opposing point is correct in whole or in part, or under some circumstances, or admits a limit of the writer's own case; a refutation shows that an opposing point is invalid. Writers often pair them: conceding what is true earns trust, and refuting what is not reclaims the ground.
cards.h: → accept vs invalidate + why they pair
cards.n: Label the pair and explain the sequence's effect on a skeptical reader; naming 'concession' alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast counterargument and rebuttal.
cards.a: The counterargument is the opposing position or objection itself, stated in the writer's text; the rebuttal is the writer's response, offering a contrasting perspective or alternative evidence to show that all or part of it is invalid. One raises the objection, the other answers it.
cards.h: → objection vs answer
cards.n: A counterargument left standing with no rebuttal reads as a concession the writer never meant to make.

cards.q: Identify the move: 'Cutting the budget will save money short term - but it guts the programs that prevent costlier crises later.'
cards.a: Concession followed by rebuttal: the writer accepts a portion of the competing claim as correct (the cut saves money in the short term), then pivots on 'but' to offer a contrasting perspective (long-term costs) showing that the case for cutting is incomplete.
cards.h: → the two moves + the pivot word
cards.n: Quote the pivot: 'but' marks the exact point where the writer takes the ground back, which is what an analysis should point to.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'Senator Cole wants stricter emissions limits, but why listen to someone who just bought a second house?'
cards.a: Ad hominem: it attacks Cole's personal purchase instead of the emissions proposal, so it rebuts nothing. A genuine rebuttal would offer a contrasting perspective or alternative evidence about the emissions limits themselves.
cards.h: → fallacy + what a real rebuttal would do
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Not every personal remark is ad hominem; a real conflict of interest can bear on credibility.

cards.q: Identify the fallacy: 'You say I text too much at dinner, but you're always checking email at the table too.'
cards.a: Tu quoque ('you too'): it deflects the criticism by accusing the critic of the same behavior, which says nothing about whether texting at dinner is a problem. It looks like a rebuttal but offers no contrasting perspective on the claim itself.
cards.h: → fallacy + why it answers nothing
cards.n: Borrows flawed reasoning (REO-1.F). Both people can be wrong at once, so hypocrisy in the critic never settles the criticism.

cards.q: Contrast how concession is used in Rogerian argument versus in classical refutation.
cards.a: In Rogerian argument, concession comes first and is genuine: the writer grants the opposing view's validity to build trust before proposing common ground. In classical arrangement, concession usually comes in the refutation, after the writer's case, granting a minor point so the rebuttal that follows seems fair.
cards.h: → placement + goal, in each
cards.n: The same concession lands differently depending on where it sits; say what its placement does to the audience.

cards.q:
Identify which of the CED's three kinds of concession each sentence makes (accepting all or part of a competing claim; agreeing it is correct under different circumstances; acknowledging a limitation of one's own argument):
1. 'Opponents are right that the market would draw some shoppers away from the grocery store.'
2. 'In a larger city with an existing market district, the mill might well be better used as housing.'
3. 'My survey reached only residents who attend town meetings, so it may overstate enthusiasm.'
4. 'If the repairs truly cost $2 million, I would agree the plan should wait.'
5. 'The critics' figures on repair costs are accurate.'
6. 'No one knows yet whether vendors will stay past the first year, and my case depends on it.'
cards.a:
1 → accepts part of the competing claim
2 → agrees it would be correct under different circumstances
3 → acknowledges a limitation of the writer's own argument
4 → agrees the competing claim is correct under a different set of circumstances (a higher cost)
5 → accepts part of the competing claim (its figures)
6 → acknowledges a limitation of the writer's own argument
cards.h: → one kind of concession per line
cards.n: Item 4 is conditional, not a full surrender; a concession under different circumstances keeps the writer's position for the actual case.

cards.q: Explain where a concession is most effective when placed within a body paragraph.
cards.a: Early, before the writer's own point: granting the opposing point first shows fairness, and the rebuttal or refutation that follows gets the last and most memorable word. A concession placed after the writer's point reads as a retreat and leaves the opposing view echoing.
cards.h: → concede first → fairness shown → rebuttal gets the last word → reader ends on the writer's claim
cards.n: 'It is the rule to concede first' gives no reason; explain what the order does to the reader's final impression.
o: An early concession disarms a skeptical reader, who then hears the rebuttal as reasonable rather than defensive.
Readers weigh what comes last most heavily, so the writer's claim should close the paragraph.

w.a: Concessions should come last so the essay ends on a fair note.
w.why: ending on the opposition's point weakens the writer's claim

w.a: Where the concession goes does not matter as long as it is there.
w.why: placement changes what the reader carries away

cards.q: Explain the risk of placing a concession at the very end of an argument essay.
cards.a: Readers carry away the final paragraph; ending on a point granted to the opposition, with no rebuttal after it, leaves the counterargument as the last word and makes the writer's position seem to weaken at the close. Concede earlier, then rebut, and end on the writer's own claim.
cards.h: → ending weighs most → unanswered concession last → opposition gets the final word → thesis seems to fade
cards.n: 'It is confusing' is vague; say that the final impression favors whatever comes last.
o: A late concession can look like a writer losing confidence, which undermines everything argued before.
Sophistication comes from integrating the concession into the reasoning, not from tacking it onto the conclusion.

w.a: Ending with a concession always shows maturity and earns the sophistication point.
w.why: a concession tacked on at the end is not integrated complexity

w.a: Concessions belong only in the conclusion so they do not interrupt the argument.
w.why: they work best where they can be answered

cards.q: Explain why conceding part of an opposing argument can enhance a writer's credibility.
cards.a: A concession shows the writer has weighed the opposition honestly rather than caricaturing it, so readers trust the writer's judgment where the writer does disagree. It also narrows the dispute to the ground the writer can defend, which makes the rebuttal more convincing.
cards.h: → fair concession → writer seen as honest → trust transfers to the rebuttal → dispute narrowed to defensible ground
cards.n: 'It shows both sides' misses the effect; a concession earns trust for the writer's own position, it is not balance for its own sake.
o: Readers who hold the opposing view are more willing to listen once they see part of it accepted.
Conceding what the evidence clearly supports keeps the writer from defending indefensible ground.

w.a: Conceding a point means the writer's argument is weak.
w.why: a fair concession strengthens trust in what remains

w.a: Writers should concede as many points as possible to seem fair.
w.why: conceding everything leaves no position to defend

cards.q: Define a line of reasoning.
cards.a: A line of reasoning is the sequence of claims and evidence, joined by the writer's commentary, that leads a reader to the thesis or justifies it. Each step prepares the next, so the order carries part of the argument. REO-1.A and REO-1.B name its two basic directions: the reasoning can lead up to the thesis, or the thesis can come first and the reasoning justify it.
cards.h: → definition + the two directions
cards.n: A list of reasons in any order is not a line of reasoning; if the paragraphs could be shuffled with no loss, the reasoning is not building.

cards.q: Explain what an effective conclusion does.
cards.a: It brings the line of reasoning to a unified end by stating what the argument has established and why it matters: implications, stakes in a broader context, a call to act, or a return to the opening. In an argument that arrives at its thesis, the conclusion is where the thesis itself lands, so it must follow from the evidence already given.
cards.h: → unified end + what it may do
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. 'In conclusion, I have shown...' plus a re-list of topic sentences extends nothing; say what the reasoning has earned.

cards.q: Identify conclusion habits to avoid.
cards.a: Four habits: restating the thesis and topic sentences word for word; introducing new evidence that cannot be analyzed; apologizing for or retracting the argument ('but this is just my opinion'); and ending on a question or sweeping claim that undoes the position argued. Each breaks the line of reasoning at the point where it should arrive.
cards.h: → four habits + what each breaks
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. The subtlest trap is the last-line hedge ('of course, both sides have a point'), which reads as abandoning the thesis just defended.

cards.q: Explain the call-to-action technique as a way to end an argument essay.
cards.a: A call to action ends the argument by naming a specific actor, a specific action, and often a time ('the council should vote Thursday to restore the grant'), turning the claim the reasoning established into a next step. It works when the line of reasoning has already made the action seem necessary, so the request reads as the argument's logical end.
cards.h: → actor + action + why it follows from the reasoning
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. 'We must all do better' is a mood, not a call to action: with no named actor or act it gives the reasoning nowhere to land.

cards.q: Explain how an effective AP Lang conclusion differs from a simple restatement of the thesis.
cards.a: A restatement repeats the thesis in new words; an effective conclusion shows what the argument has earned: why the claim matters, what follows from it, or where it leads beyond the essay. It adds a last step to the line of reasoning instead of circling back to the first one.
cards.h: → extend the reasoning vs repeat it
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. Test it: if the conclusion could be swapped with the introduction unchanged, it has not moved the reasoning anywhere.

cards.q: Identify the conclusion habit: an essay's final paragraph introduces a brand-new piece of evidence not discussed anywhere in the body.
cards.a: The new-evidence conclusion. A fresh fact appears when there is no room left to explain it, so it sits without commentary and breaks the line of reasoning at its end. Move it into a body paragraph where it can be explained, or cut it; the conclusion should draw out what the evidence already given proves.
cards.h: → named habit + why it fails + the fix
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. Calling it 'a strong final point' misses the problem: evidence with no commentary earns nothing, and a conclusion has no room for commentary.

cards.q: Contrast a conclusion that broadens the stakes of an argument and one that merely summarizes the body paragraphs.
cards.a: A conclusion that broadens the stakes carries the argued claim into a larger context (who else is affected, what the principle implies next), so the reasoning ends by showing why it matters. A summarizing conclusion re-lists points already made and ends where the reasoning began. The first extends the argument; the second only repeats it.
cards.h: → extends the claim vs re-lists the points
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.J. Broadening fails when it leaps to a vague universal ('this affects all humanity'); the wider stakes must follow from the specific claim argued.

cards.q:
Identify where the thesis arrives in this passage and describe the line of reasoning that leads to it:
'Our district spent 2.1 million dollars on new laptops in 2022. Within a year, a third of them sat in closets because no one had been trained to use them. That same year, the one school that hired a technology coach had its laptops in daily use. Two of our three new reading programs followed the same path: purchased, unexplained, abandoned. Before we buy anything else, we should pay for the people who teach us how to use what we already own.' (an invented school board member's statement; figures invented)
cards.a: The thesis arrives in the last sentence: the district should fund training before buying more. The passage reaches it inductively: a costly failure (a third of the laptops unused), a contrasting success (the school with a coach), then a second instance of the same pattern (the reading programs). Each case narrows toward the lesson, so the claim reads as the conclusion the evidence forces rather than an opinion announced in advance.
cards.h: → thesis sentence + the steps that lead to it
cards.n: Calling the first sentence the thesis mistakes the fact that opens the reasoning for the claim it arrives at; a thesis must require defense.

cards.q: Write the sentence that should end this paragraph so that its line of reasoning arrives at a thesis: 'In 2019 our town replaced the crosswalk signal near the middle school with a push-button light. In 2021, after a student was clipped by a car, it added a crossing guard. In 2023, after two more near misses, it painted the crosswalk bright green. Each fix came after a scare, and each cost more than the last.' (an invented letter to a town council)
cards.a: Model: 'Rather than paying for another fix after the next scare, the council should commission a safety study of the whole school route now.' It states an arguable claim that follows from the pattern the paragraph built (repairs that are reactive and escalating in cost), so the thesis lands as the conclusion of the evidence.
cards.h: → one arguable claim the pattern points to
cards.n: 'These are all examples of the town trying to help' summarizes the evidence; the arriving sentence must be a claim the evidence leads to.

cards.q: Explain the risk of ending an AP Lang essay mid-argument because time ran out.
cards.a: The cost is the reasoning left unwritten, not the missing wrap-up: the rubric has no conclusion row and the thesis may sit anywhere, but Row B scores only the commentary on the page, so a line of reasoning cut off mid-paragraph earns nothing for the step it never took.
cards.h: → rows score what is on the page → no conclusion row → the unfinished reasoning is what loses credit
cards.n: Leans on the rubric (Exam Craft). Rushing a formula conclusion while a body paragraph lacks commentary trades a point you can earn for nothing.
o: Because Row B asks whether the line of reasoning is sustained, an essay that stops mid-argument shows a gap in reasoning whatever its thesis promised.
A paragraph cut off after its evidence leaves that evidence unexplained, and unexplained evidence is what holds Row B at 2 or 3 instead of 4.

w.a: The essay loses a whole point because every AP essay must have a conclusion.
w.why: the rubric has no conclusion row

w.a: Readers fail an unfinished essay because it is incomplete.
w.why: rows are scored on what is written, not failed wholesale

w.a: It does not matter, since only the thesis is really scored.
w.why: Row B, worth 4 of 6 points, scores the reasoning

cards.q: Explain why an argument that withholds its thesis until the end depends heavily on the order of its evidence.
cards.a: With no stated claim to steer by, readers can only follow the evidence in the sequence given, so each step must prepare the next: early cases set up a pattern, later ones narrow it, and the thesis must be what they point to. Evidence out of order leaves the arriving claim unearned.
cards.h: → no claim to steer by → readers follow the sequence → each step sets up the next → thesis must be where they point
cards.n: Saying 'the evidence is in chronological order' names an order without explaining what the order does for a thesis that arrives last.
o: A reader who does not yet know the claim cannot sort relevant from irrelevant evidence, so any detour reads as the argument losing its way.
The persuasive force of an inductive argument is that the claim seems to emerge from the evidence, which only happens if the evidence visibly builds.

w.a: Order does not matter as long as the thesis is stated clearly at the end.
w.why: without a claim up front, order is the only guide the reader has

w.a: Writers delay the thesis to create suspense, so the order just needs to be interesting.
w.why: suspense is not the reasoning the order must carry

cards.q: Explain why withholding the thesis can backfire with a busy audience, such as a council reading dozens of public comments.
cards.a: A reader who must act quickly may stop before the claim arrives, or read every detail without knowing what it is meant to prove. When the audience needs the point at once, withholding it wastes their attention and hides the purpose of the evidence, so a claim-first order serves them better.
cards.h: → busy reader skims → evidence without a known purpose → claim missed or never weighed
cards.n: 'Delayed theses are confusing' is too absolute; the trap is ignoring which audience the order serves.
o: Evidence is easiest to weigh when the reader already knows what it must prove, which a claim-first order supplies.
A reader who never reaches the last paragraph never meets the thesis at all, so the argument fails for exactly the reader who skims.

w.a: A delayed thesis is always weaker because the reader cannot find it.
w.why: ignores audiences an inductive order persuades

w.a: Busy readers do not care about evidence anyway, so order does not matter.
w.why: dismisses the audience instead of explaining the choice

cards.q: Explain what an effective introduction does on an AP Lang essay.
cards.a: It orients the reader to the issue or passage, narrows to the specific question, and, in a claim-first argument, states a defensible thesis that sets up the line of reasoning the body will justify. Two to four sentences usually suffice. The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay, but stating it early lets every paragraph read as justification of a known claim.
cards.h: → orient + narrow + claim the body will justify
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. 'The thesis must end paragraph one' is a myth: the rubric says it may be anywhere; early placement is a choice, not a requirement.

cards.q: Identify introduction moves that waste time or hurt the score.
cards.a: 'Since the beginning of time' openings, dictionary definitions of common words, restating the prompt, announcing the plan ('In this essay I will'), and long summary of the passage or sources before any claim. Each delays the claim the reasoning is meant to justify, and a thesis that only restates the prompt earns no Row A point.
cards.h: → list of moves + what each delays
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. The rubric names 'only restates the prompt' as a 0, so a polished paraphrase of the prompt still loses Row A.

cards.q: Identify four effective ways to open an AP Lang essay besides stating the thesis outright.
cards.a: A brief relevant anecdote, a striking statistic, a short apt quotation, or a concrete scenario tied directly to the issue (the CED also lists questions, intriguing statements, data, and contextualized information). Each should lead within a sentence or two to the claim the essay will justify.
cards.h: → four openers + where each must lead
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. An opener that could introduce any essay on the topic earns nothing; it has to point toward this essay's claim.

cards.q: Identify the introduction habit: an essay opens by defining a dictionary word from the prompt before making any claim.
cards.a: The dictionary-definition opening. It spends the first sentence on a meaning readers already know and delays the claim. Defining belongs in an argument only when the reasoning turns on a contested meaning, and then the writer argues for a definition rather than quoting a dictionary.
cards.h: → named habit + why it delays the claim
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. Contrast definition as a method (REO-1.L), which argues what a term should mean; 'Webster's defines' argues nothing.

cards.q: Contrast a hook that earns its place in an AP Lang introduction and one that only delays the thesis.
cards.a: A hook that earns its place is tied to the claim: a detail from the passage or sources that the thesis then explains. A hook that only delays is generic (an unrelated anecdote, a sweeping question) and could open any essay. The first starts the line of reasoning; the second postpones it.
cards.h: → tied to the claim vs generic
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. Test by deletion: if removing the opener loses nothing the thesis needs, it was a delay, however vivid.

cards.q: Apply an effective opening move: write a one-sentence introduction opener for an essay arguing that social media has weakened, not strengthened, local news.
cards.a: Model: 'As local newspapers close by the hundreds, the platforms that promised to replace them have instead drained the advertising and attention that once kept them alive.' It names the stakes and states the claim in one sentence, so the next sentence can begin justifying it.
cards.h: → one sentence: stakes + claim
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. 'Social media has changed the world in many ways' opens with no claim; the model's claim is already arguable.

cards.q: Explain what it means for a thesis to preview (roadmap) the line of reasoning.
cards.a: A previewing thesis states the claim and signals the reasons or order the body will follow ('because X, Y, and Z'), so the reader knows how the reasoning will justify the claim before it begins. The CED says a thesis may preview the line of reasoning; it does not have to list the points.
cards.h: → claim + signal of the reasons to come
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.O. Believing a thesis must list three points is the trap: Row A goes to a defensible claim whether or not it previews.

cards.q: Explain how a synthesis essay thesis should engage with the range of provided sources without simply agreeing with all of them.
cards.a: It states the writer's own defensible position, then justifies it with the sources, including those that disagree: sources that support become evidence, sources that oppose become positions to answer. The thesis leads; the sources serve its line of reasoning, not the reverse.
cards.h: → own position first + how the sources serve it
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. 'Each source makes valid points' summarizes others' arguments without a position, which the rubric says earns no thesis point.

cards.q: Identify the claim and describe how the rest of this passage justifies it: 'The county should build its new library downtown, not at the highway interchange. Downtown sits on four bus lines; the interchange sits on none. Half of the library's current cardholders live within a mile of Main Street. And a library at the interchange would share a parking lot with a store that closes at 9, while downtown already has the evening foot traffic that makes late hours safe.' (an invented columnist in a county newspaper; figures invented)
cards.a: The claim comes first: the library belongs downtown, not at the interchange. The rest justifies it with three reasons, each comparing the sites on something library users need: access by transit (four bus lines versus none), nearness to current cardholders (half within a mile), and safety for evening hours. Because the claim comes first, readers weigh each reason as support for a position they already know.
cards.h: → claim + each reason that justifies it
cards.n: Listing the facts ('it mentions buses, cardholders, parking') describes content, not reasoning; say how each fact justifies the stated claim.

cards.q: Explain why opening an AP Lang essay with a broad, generic claim about 'society' or 'history' usually hurts more than it helps.
cards.a: A generic opener delays the claim the essay must justify and usually states something no one would dispute, so it earns nothing and spends time the commentary needs. Readers meet the argument a paragraph late, and the vague frame can make the thesis that follows look vague too.
cards.h: → generic frame → no arguable claim + lost time → thesis arrives late and looks vague
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.I. Defending it as 'background' fails when the background is all of history; context must be specific to this issue.
o: The rubric scores a defensible claim, not the essay's opening, so a sentence that cannot be argued is time taken from commentary that can score.
Specific context (the event, the source, the dispute) orients a reader; universal statements orient them to nothing in particular.

w.a: Starting broad is good because it shows the big picture before the thesis.
w.why: a picture of all history is not this issue's context

w.a: A general opening makes the essay sound more sophisticated.
w.why: sophistication is earned by complex reasoning, not by scope

cards.q: Explain why a writer answering a decision-maker who has asked for a recommendation usually states the claim first.
cards.a: A reader who asked for a recommendation wants the answer first. Stating the claim at once lets every paragraph read as justification of a known position, so the reader can weigh each reason as it arrives and stop at any point knowing what is recommended.
cards.h: → reader asked for an answer → claim first → each reason read as support → nothing hidden
cards.n: 'Because the thesis always goes first' is a formula; the reason is this reader's need for the recommendation before the justification.
o: Evidence read without a claim is hard to judge; giving the claim first tells the reader what each piece of evidence must prove.
A claim-first order signals confidence, which suits a writer whose authority to recommend has already been granted.

w.a: Writers put the claim first because that is the rule for essays.
w.why: a formula, not a reason tied to this audience

w.a: Stating the claim first is always the most persuasive order.
w.why: skeptical readers may resist a claim stated first (REO-1.A)

cards.q: Explain why an essay that states its claim first and then drifts into arguing a different claim weakens its line of reasoning.
cards.a: Stating the claim first tells the reader what every paragraph must justify. A paragraph that argues a different claim then reads as a break in the reasoning, and the reader can no longer tell whether the thesis or the drift is the writer's real position.
cards.h: → claim first sets the reader's test → off-claim paragraph fails it → the argument's position blurs
cards.n: Calling the drift 'extra support' misses it: support for another claim is not support for this one.
o: Readers of a claim-first argument check each paragraph against the thesis, so a mismatch is more visible than in an exploratory essay.
A thesis the body abandons makes the writer look unsure, which costs credibility as well as coherence.

w.a: More ideas make an essay stronger, even if they do not match the thesis.
w.why: unrelated claims do not justify the stated one

w.a: As long as the thesis is clear, the paragraphs can discuss anything on the topic.
w.why: the topic is not the claim; each paragraph must justify the claim

cards.q: Define synthesis as the term is used on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Synthesis is building your own argument from several sources: you select material from them as evidence and use your commentary to connect it to your claim, so the sources serve your line of reasoning instead of the essay reporting what each says in turn.
cards.h: → definition + who is in charge
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. A tour of the sources ('Source A says... Source B says...') is summary; without commentary tying them to your claim, nothing is synthesized.

cards.q: Explain what source-dropping is and how to avoid it.
cards.a: Source-dropping is inserting a quotation or citation with no lead-in before it and no commentary after it, so the reader must guess how it connects to the claim. Avoid it by introducing the source, quoting only the words you need, and following with commentary that says how those words support the paragraph's claim.
cards.h: → the problem + the three-step fix
cards.n: A paragraph that ends on a quotation leaves the connection unstated; the commentary after the quotation earns Row B, not the quotation.

cards.q: Identify the mistake: an essay paragraph spends four sentences listing every number on a bar graph before stating any claim about them.
cards.a: Data-dumping: the paragraph recites the chart's figures before (or without) any claim, so nothing tells the reader what the numbers prove. Commentary has to connect chosen evidence to a claim; state the claim, select the one or two figures that matter, and explain what they show.
cards.h: → named flaw + the missing connection
cards.n: Calling it 'thorough use of evidence' is the trap; evidence with no claim to connect to is summary, whatever its volume.

cards.q: Identify what is missing: a paragraph analyzes a photograph's composition in detail but never states what claim the photograph is meant to support.
cards.a: The claim. Commentary connects evidence to a claim, and here there is analysis with nothing to connect it to: the paragraph needs a topic sentence stating what the photograph is evidence for, and each observation about composition should be tied back to that claim.
cards.h: → what is missing + where it goes
cards.n: Adding more detail about the photograph misses the fix; the missing piece is the claim the detail is supposed to support.

cards.q: Explain the evidence-to-commentary ratio a strong AP Lang body paragraph should aim for.
cards.a: Commentary should outweigh evidence: a common rule of thumb is two or more sentences of commentary for each sentence of quoted or cited material. The reason is that Row B credits explaining how evidence supports the line of reasoning, and explanation takes more words than citation.
cards.h: → ratio + why the rubric favors it
cards.n: The ratio is a teacher's rule of thumb, not a rubric rule; three sentences that restate the quotation are still summary, not commentary.

cards.q: Identify the weakness: a synthesis essay cites three sources but never explains how any two of them relate to each other.
cards.a: The sources are listed, not synthesized: each is tied (at best) to the claim on its own, and the commentary never says how they bear on one another. Synthesis needs commentary that relates the sources to each other and to the writer's claim, for example that one confirms, extends, or complicates another.
cards.h: → named weakness + the missing commentary
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. Adding a fourth source repeats the problem; the fix is a sentence of commentary relating two sources to the claim.

cards.q: Define commentary as the CED uses the term in Reasoning and Organization.
cards.a: Commentary is the writer's explanation of their reasoning: it connects chosen evidence to a claim (REO-1.C) and explains the significance and relevance of that evidence in relation to the line of reasoning (REO-1.D). It is the writer's own account of why the evidence proves the point, not the evidence restated.
cards.h: → connects evidence to claim + explains significance
cards.n: Paraphrasing the quotation ('this means she was tired') is summary, not commentary; commentary says how the evidence proves the claim.

cards.q: Identify the sentence that serves as commentary in this paragraph from an invented student essay: '(1) The town's plan to replace the Elm Street oaks with young ornamental trees would waste money. (2) The parks department estimates that the new trees would need watering by truck for their first three summers. (3) Because the oaks already shade the street for free, every dollar spent watering their replacements is money spent to rebuild shade the town already has.'
cards.a: Sentence 3. Sentence 1 states the claim and sentence 2 gives the evidence (three summers of truck watering); sentence 3 connects them by explaining why the watering cost supports 'would waste money': the town would pay to rebuild shade it already has for free.
cards.h: → number + how it links evidence to claim
cards.n: Picking sentence 2 because it holds a fact confuses evidence with commentary; commentary is the sentence that explains what the fact proves.

cards.q: Write two sentences of commentary connecting this evidence to this claim. Claim: The school library should stay open until 6 p.m. instead of closing at 4. Evidence: Last month's sign-in log shows 140 students used the library between 3 p.m., when classes end, and 4 p.m.; 60 percent of them listed 'no internet at home' as their reason. (invented figures)
cards.a: Model: 'Most of these students are not choosing the library over home; they are using the only place where they can finish online work. Closing at 4 leaves them one hour for assignments that classmates with internet can do all evening, so later hours would narrow a gap the school's own log reveals.' It says what the figures mean and ties that meaning to the claim.
cards.h: → what the evidence means + why it proves the claim
cards.n: 'This shows the library is important to students' restates the evidence in general terms; name who is affected and why later hours follow.

cards.q: Contrast paraphrase and direct quotation as ways to use a source.
cards.a: A direct quotation keeps the source's exact words, so use it when the wording itself is the evidence your commentary will analyze (a loaded word, a revealing admission). A paraphrase restates the idea in your own words and sentence structure, so use it when the idea matters but its phrasing does not, such as a finding or background. Either way the source is named and commentary connects it to the claim.
cards.h: → exact words vs restated idea + when each serves
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.E. Quoting a plain finding word for word wastes space; if your commentary will not analyze the wording, paraphrase it.

cards.q: Define plagiarism as it applies to the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Plagiarism is presenting another's words or ideas as your own: quoting or paraphrasing without naming the source, or paraphrasing so closely that the source's wording and structure remain. In a synthesis essay every borrowed idea needs its letter or description, because readers must be able to tell the source's evidence from your commentary on it.
cards.h: → definition + why the line matters in synthesis
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.N. A citation does not rescue a too-close paraphrase: change the wording and the structure, or quote the words and mark them.

cards.q: Explain why quoting an entire long sentence from a source usually weakens Row B more than a short quotation would.
cards.a: Row B credits explaining how evidence supports the reasoning, and a long quotation spends the paragraph's space on words the writer never explains, so commentary thins out. A short quotation of the exact words that prove the claim lets the commentary unpack each one and keeps the link to the claim visible.
cards.h: → long quotation fills the space → commentary thins → the evidence-claim link goes unexplained
cards.n: 'Long quotations show more evidence' is the trap: Row B scores the explanation of evidence, not its volume.
o: The longer the quotation, the more of it is irrelevant to the claim, which blurs which words are doing the work.
Trimming a quotation forces the writer to decide which words matter, and that decision is the first step of commentary.

w.a: Long quotations are better because they give the reader full context.
w.why: context is not commentary; the link to the claim still goes unexplained

w.a: Short quotations are always better because readers get bored.
w.why: names no reasoning or scoring consequence

cards.q: Explain the risk of quoting a caption under a photograph as if it were the photograph's own analysis.
cards.a: A caption is the source's own framing of the image, so quoting it as analysis hands the connection to someone else: the essay supplies no commentary of its own linking the image to its claim. Treat the caption as evidence of how the source wants the image read, then explain what that framing proves.
cards.h: → caption = the source's framing → quoting it is not commentary → the writer's own link is missing
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. Citing the caption as 'what the photo shows' is the trap; the caption is more evidence that still needs your commentary.
o: A caption may steer readers toward a reading the image alone does not support, so relying on it can import the source's bias as fact.
Readers score the writer's reasoning, and a caption quoted without comment contains none of it.

w.a: The caption is the most reliable description of the photo, so quoting it is the best analysis.
w.why: reliability is not commentary

w.a: Captions are not allowed as evidence in a synthesis essay.
w.why: false; a caption is usable evidence if the writer analyzes it

cards.q: Explain why the same piece of evidence can support opposite claims, and what that means for commentary.
cards.a: Evidence does not speak for itself: 'crime fell 10 percent after the curfew' can be read as proof the curfew worked or as part of a decline already under way. Commentary is what ties the evidence to one claim, by explaining why this reading, not the other, follows.
cards.h: → evidence is open to readings → commentary picks and defends one → without it the link is the reader's guess
cards.n: Assuming a quotation 'proves itself' is the trap; if the evidence could support the other side, only your commentary shows why it supports yours.
o: A reader who disagrees will supply the opposing interpretation, so the writer has to state and defend the connection first.
Evidence records what happened, not what it means, so the connection has to live in the writer's reasoning: commentary is where the writer chooses and defends one reading.

w.a: Good evidence is so clear that it needs no explanation.
w.why: evidence can be read more than one way

w.a: If evidence can support both sides, it should not be used at all.
w.why: most evidence can; commentary is what makes it support one side

cards.q: Explain the 'so what' link that ends a body paragraph.
cards.a: The last sentence of a body paragraph should state why the paragraph's claim matters to the thesis: the consequence, stake, or step it adds to the line of reasoning. It explains the paragraph's relevance to the whole argument instead of restating the topic sentence in other words.
cards.h: → what the last sentence must explain
cards.n: 'This shows the author's point is important' is the empty version; name the specific step this paragraph adds to the thesis.

cards.q: Explain the difference between describing a chart and analyzing one in a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Describing restates what the numbers or image show; analyzing explains why that trend or image matters to the writer's claim and what it lets the argument conclude. Only analysis is commentary in the CED's sense, because it explains the evidence's significance and relevance to the line of reasoning.
cards.h: → what it shows vs why it matters to the claim
cards.n: 'The chart shows rates rose from 12 to 47 percent' is description, however precise; the commentary starts where you say what that rise means.

cards.q: Decide which detail from a bar graph is more useful as synthesis evidence: the exact value of one bar, or the overall trend across all the bars.
cards.a: Usually the overall trend: a pattern across the bars bears on a claim about change or comparison, while one bar's value rarely supports an argument alone. Use exact values when they anchor the trend (the first and last bars), and say in commentary why that pattern matters to the line of reasoning.
cards.h: → choice + relevance to the claim
cards.n: Choosing whichever number is most dramatic is the trap; relevance to the claim, not size, decides which detail is evidence.

cards.q: Contrast the kind of commentary a chart's numbers can support versus what a photograph's composition can support.
cards.a: A chart's numbers support claims about scale, trend, or comparison (how much, how fast, which is larger); a photograph's composition supports claims about emphasis, framing, or emotional effect (what the viewer is made to notice or feel). Commentary on each must explain the kind of significance that evidence can actually carry.
cards.h: → what each kind of evidence can prove
cards.n: Treating one photograph as proof of a trend is the trap: an image shows an instance and a framing, not a pattern.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a visual source that seems to contradict the claims in the prose sources.
cards.a: Use the contradiction: acknowledge the tension and explain what it reveals, for instance that the problem is real but narrower than a prose source claims, or that the chart measures something different. Commentary that explains why the sources disagree makes both relevant to a more precise line of reasoning.
cards.h: → acknowledge + explain what the clash reveals
cards.n: Quietly dropping the inconvenient source is the trap; ignoring evidence that clashes with your claim reads as cherry-picking.

cards.q:
Identify the sentence that explains the evidence's significance for the essay's larger line of reasoning, and say how it differs from sentence 3. The paragraph comes from an invented essay arguing that the city should turn the Grove Street parking lot into a park:
'(1) The Grove Street lot is rarely more than a third full. (2) The city's own counts found an average of 38 of its 120 spaces in use on weekdays last year. (3) Those numbers mean the lot could lose most of its spaces without turning away a single regular driver. (4) And once lost parking, the main objection to the park, disappears, the question is no longer whether the city can afford a park there but whether it can afford to keep paving land nobody uses.'
cards.a: Sentence 4. Sentence 3 is commentary tied to this paragraph's claim: it explains what the count means (the lot is underused). Sentence 4 explains why that matters to the whole argument: it removes the chief objection to the park and turns the essay toward its next step, the cost of keeping the lot. That is relevance to the line of reasoning, not just to the paragraph.
cards.h: → number + paragraph-level vs argument-level commentary
cards.n: Choosing sentence 3 is the near miss: it explains the evidence, but only for this paragraph; REO-1.D asks for significance to the line of reasoning.

cards.q: Write a final sentence for this body paragraph that explains the evidence's significance to the essay's thesis. Thesis: The state should require recess in every elementary school. Paragraph claim: Recess improves attention in class. Evidence: In an invented district study, teachers rated students on task 72 percent of the time after recess and 58 percent on days without it.
cards.a: Model: 'If fifteen minutes outside buys back that much focus, recess is not time taken from learning but a condition for it, which is why a state that already mandates minutes of instruction should mandate recess too.' It moves from the paragraph's claim (attention) to the thesis (a statewide requirement) and says why the first supports the second.
cards.h: → one sentence: evidence's meaning → the thesis
cards.n: 'This shows recess is good' restates the paragraph's claim; the last sentence must say why it matters to the thesis, here a requirement.

cards.q: Decide which sentence better explains the significance of this evidence for the writer's line of reasoning, and explain why. Evidence: 'Since the bridge toll began, weekday traffic on the free Route 4 detour has doubled.' The essay's claim: the toll has shifted its costs onto the towns along Route 4. (A) 'This shows that traffic on Route 4 has increased a lot since the toll began.' (B) 'Drivers are dodging the toll by routing through Millbrook and Dover, so the state's toll revenue is being paid for in those towns' congestion and road wear.' (invented)
cards.a: (B). It explains why the doubled traffic matters to the claim: drivers avoid the toll by passing through two towns, so the cost has moved onto their residents. (A) restates the evidence in vaguer words ('a lot') and never connects it to the argument about shifted costs.
cards.h: → letter + what it explains that the other only restates
cards.n: (A) sounds like commentary because it begins 'This shows'; a sentence that only repeats the evidence explains nothing, whatever its opening words.

cards.q: Define what counts as a visual or quantitative source in an AP Lang synthesis set.
cards.a: A source that presents its evidence mainly as an image or as data rather than continuous prose: a chart, graph, table, map, photograph, cartoon, or infographic. The CED says two of the six synthesis sources are visual, at least one of them quantitative (a chart, graph, or table of numbers). Each counts as one source when cited, and its evidence needs commentary like any other.
cards.h: → the forms + how many the exam includes
cards.n: Borrows the exam format. Treating a visual as decoration is the trap: uncited it counts toward nothing, and unexplained it supports no claim.

cards.q: Define an infographic and explain why it can be treated as a single source even though it combines text and images.
cards.a: An infographic combines text, icons, and data displays in one designed piece that makes a single coordinated case, so it is one source with one letter. Its words, images, and numbers are parts of that one argument, and commentary can explain how the design ranks or frames the data, which is part of its significance to your claim.
cards.h: → definition + why one source + what to comment on
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. Counting an infographic's chart and its caption as two sources is the trap; one lettered source is one source, however many parts it has.

cards.q: Explain why a synthesis essay should still explain a chart's axis labels or units in a sentence before analyzing it.
cards.a: Commentary can explain a figure's significance only if the reader knows what it measures: '47' means nothing until the reader knows it is a percentage of teens, per year. One orienting clause (what is measured, in what units) makes the evidence intelligible, so the commentary about why it matters can land.
cards.h: → a number needs its measure and unit → then the reader can follow → then its significance can be explained
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. Three sentences walking through the axes slide into description; one orienting clause is enough before the commentary.
o: Misreading what a chart measures produces specious commentary, so naming the units protects the writer's own reasoning too.
A reader should be able to follow the argument without rereading the source, so evidence has to arrive with enough context to be understood.

w.a: Explaining the axes is unnecessary because the reader already has the sources.
w.why: the essay must still make each figure's meaning clear to support its reasoning

w.a: Describing the axes in detail is the best way to show you understood the chart.
w.why: description is not commentary and costs Row B time

cards.q: Explain why over-relying on the one visual source in a synthesis set can weaken an essay's line of reasoning.
cards.a: One image or chart offers a narrow slice of evidence, so an argument leaning on it alone has little to reason between and drifts into describing it. Pairing it with prose sources lets commentary explain its relevance (what it confirms, complicates, or cannot show), which sustains the line of reasoning.
cards.h: → one visual = narrow evidence → nothing to reason between → description replaces reasoning
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.P. 'Visuals are weaker evidence than text' is the trap; the problem is leaning on any single source, not the format.
o: A chart shows what it measures and nothing else, so a claim broader than its measure needs other sources to carry the rest.
Synthesis is scored on explaining how sources support a line of reasoning, and one source cannot show agreement, tension, or extension.

w.a: Visual sources should be avoided because readers prefer quotations.
w.why: visuals are valid evidence; over-reliance is the problem

w.a: Using the visual for every paragraph shows the essay is consistent.
w.why: repetition of one source is not a sustained line of reasoning

cards.q: Explain why quoting a graph's exact figure can strengthen a synthesis claim more than a rounded summary of it.
cards.a: An exact figure ('rose from 12 to 47 percent') shows the scale of a change, so commentary can explain how much it matters to the claim; 'increased a lot' gives the reader nothing to weigh and the commentary nothing to build on. Precision makes the evidence's significance arguable.
cards.h: → exact figure shows scale → commentary can weigh its significance → a vague summary gives nothing to weigh
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.P. Reciting every figure is the opposite trap; choose the one or two exact numbers the claim needs and explain them.
o: Specific numbers let the writer compare (nearly fourfold), and a comparison is itself commentary about significance.
Vague wording can overstate or understate the evidence, which invites a skeptical reader to distrust the claim built on it.

w.a: Exact numbers are better because they make the essay look more researched.
w.why: appearance is not the reason; precision lets commentary weigh the change

w.a: Rounded summaries are better because readers do not like numbers.
w.why: vagueness leaves the significance unexplained

cards.q: Explain what a political cartoon contributes to a synthesis source set that a prose source usually cannot.
cards.a: A cartoon compresses an argument into one image, so its evidence is the cartoonist's choices (exaggeration, symbol, juxtaposition) and the stance they push. Commentary can explain the significance of those choices to the line of reasoning, such as how an issue is framed for the public, which prose rarely offers.
cards.h: → one image = compressed argument → evidence is the visual choices → commentary explains the stance they push
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.M. Describing what the cartoon depicts ('a man at a desk') is summary; name the exaggeration or symbol and what it argues.
o: A cartoon is evidence of a perspective, so it is most useful for showing how a position is felt or framed, not for proving facts.
Its exaggeration reveals what the cartoonist thinks is absurd, which a writer can use as evidence of a public attitude.

w.a: A political cartoon adds humor to the essay.
w.why: humor is not relevance to a line of reasoning

w.a: A cartoon proves the facts of the issue more clearly than prose.
w.why: a cartoon shows a stance, not proof of facts

cards.q: Explain how to test whether an essay has a line of reasoning.
cards.a: Read only the topic sentences, in order. If they form an argument on their own, each claim building on the last and together justifying or arriving at the thesis, the line of reasoning holds; if they read as a list that could be reshuffled with no loss, it does not.
cards.h: → the test + what passing and failing look like
cards.n: Checking that every paragraph 'relates to the topic' is too weak a test; paragraphs can all be on topic and still not build.

cards.q: Contrast a line of reasoning built on addition and one built on escalation.
cards.a: An additive line of reasoning stacks separate, roughly equal reasons side by side; an escalating one orders reasons so each builds on or intensifies the one before, ending on the strongest. The sequence of paragraphs reveals which: in an escalating essay, moving a paragraph breaks the logic; in an additive one, it barely matters.
cards.h: → two structures + how the sequence reveals each
cards.n: Calling any 'first, second, third' essay escalating is the trap; escalation needs each step to depend on, or raise the stakes of, the last.

cards.q: Define the order of importance organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Order of importance arranges points from least to most significant (or the reverse). Typical use: persuasion, where the strongest point comes last so it is freshest, or first for readers who may stop early. The sequence itself tells readers how the writer ranks the reasons.
cards.h: → pattern + use + what the order signals
cards.n: Putting the strongest point last by habit is the trap; decide by audience, since a skimming reader may never reach it.

cards.q: Define the general-to-specific organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: General-to-specific moves from a broad principle down to particular cases; its reverse, specific-to-general, gathers cases into a principle. Typical use: an argument that states its claim and applies it to instances (REO-1.B), versus one that leads through cases to its thesis (REO-1.A).
cards.h: → pattern + its reverse + which EK each serves
cards.n: Mixing up the directions is the trap: general-to-specific states the principle first; specific-to-general makes the reader arrive at it.

cards.q: Explain how to signal an essay's organizational pattern to a reader.
cards.a: Use topic sentences that name each paragraph's relationship to the last ('A second cost, larger than the first...'), transitions matched to that relationship, and repeated key terms from the thesis. The sequence then shows itself without being announced.
cards.h: → three tools that make the sequence visible
cards.n: 'My second point is' announces a position in a list, not a relationship; it signals order without signaling reasoning.

cards.q: Decide the better organizational pattern for an essay arguing a city's transit failures caused a specific 2019 accident: chronological, or order of importance.
cards.a: Chronological. The essay argues that one failure led to the next and so to the accident, and a time sequence lets readers watch the causal chain form; ranking the failures by importance would break the chain the claim depends on.
cards.h: → choice + why the claim needs that order
cards.n: Let the claim choose the order: an argument about causation needs sequence; an argument about which failure was worst needs ranking.

cards.q:
Describe the line of reasoning revealed by this sequence of topic sentences from an invented op-ed arguing that the town should build a skate park:
(1) Teenagers are already skating downtown, and business owners want them gone.
(2) Fines and signs have not stopped them; the skating has only moved from block to block.
(3) Towns of similar size that built skate parks report fewer downtown complaints within a year.
(4) A park would cost less than two years of the police overtime now spent answering skating complaints.
cards.a: Problem, failed remedy, working remedy, cost: paragraph 1 sets out a problem both sides recognize; paragraph 2 rules out the current response (enforcement has failed); paragraph 3 shows the proposed solution works elsewhere; paragraph 4 answers the likely objection, cost, by comparing it with the price of the status quo. Each paragraph removes an obstacle the next depends on, so the order itself argues.
cards.h: → each paragraph's job + how the order builds
cards.n: Summarizing each paragraph's content misses the task; describe the job each does and why it must come where it does.

cards.q: Decide where this paragraph should go in an invented op-ed: 'Some residents worry that a skate park would bring noise to the streets around Lincoln Field, the proposed site.' The op-ed's other paragraphs, in order, argue: (1) teenagers already skate downtown and business owners want them gone; (2) fines have not stopped them; (3) towns that built parks saw complaints fall; (4) a park costs less than the police overtime now spent. Options: (A) before paragraph 1 (B) between paragraphs 1 and 2 (C) after paragraph 4.
cards.a: (C). The noise objection is about the proposed park and its site, so it makes sense only once the park has been proposed and justified; answered after paragraph 4, it meets a case already made. Before paragraph 1 or 2, it raises a doubt about a plan the reader has not yet heard, breaking the sequence the argument depends on.
cards.h: → letter + why the sequence needs it there
cards.n: Opening with the objection 'to be fair' is the trap here: an objection to a plan must follow the plan, or the reader meets a rebuttal before a proposal.

cards.q: Explain why a line of reasoning matters more to an AP Lang score than the number of body paragraphs.
cards.a: Row B rewards evidence and commentary that support a line of reasoning, not a paragraph count. Three paragraphs whose sequence builds (each claim preparing the next) outscore five that could be shuffled, because the added paragraphs repeat rather than advance the reasoning.
cards.h: → Row B scores reasoning → a sequence that builds → added paragraphs that repeat add nothing
cards.n: The five-paragraph habit is the trap; a fourth paragraph added for symmetry usually restates the third.
o: The top Row B score asks for commentary that consistently explains how evidence supports a line of reasoning, which length alone cannot supply.
Readers follow an argument by its steps, and paragraphs that take no new step dilute the ones that do.

w.a: Five paragraphs are required for a high score on AP Lang.
w.why: the rubric sets no paragraph count

w.a: More body paragraphs always mean more evidence and a higher score.
w.why: Row B scores explanation, not volume

cards.q: Explain why signaling an essay's organizational pattern early helps a reader follow the argument.
cards.a: When the introduction or first topic sentence names the pattern (from the smallest cost to the largest, from past to present), readers can predict the sequence and see each paragraph's role as it arrives, so the order reveals the reasoning instead of leaving readers to reconstruct it.
cards.h: → pattern named → reader predicts the sequence → each paragraph's role is visible on arrival
cards.n: Announcing a list ('I will discuss three reasons') is not signaling a pattern; name the relationship that orders the paragraphs.
o: A reader who knows the plan spends attention on the evidence rather than on working out why a paragraph is where it is.
Naming the pattern commits the writer to it, which keeps later paragraphs from drifting out of sequence.

w.a: Signaling the pattern early is just a way to make the introduction longer.
w.why: it guides the reader through the sequence; it does not pad

w.a: Readers can always work out the organization themselves, so signaling adds nothing.
w.why: reconstructing the order costs the reader attention

cards.q: Explain where to place the counterargument paragraph and why.
cards.a: A common choice is after the main supporting paragraphs and before the conclusion: readers already have the case, so the objection meets a strong argument and the writer answers it last. With a hostile audience, answering its chief objection early can work better, since that objection blocks everything after it.
cards.h: → case built first → objection meets a strong argument → writer answers last (unless it blocks everything)
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.AA to AC. 'Always put the counterargument last' is a formula; placement depends on how strongly this audience holds the objection.
o: Answering the objection late shows the argument survived scrutiny and leaves readers with the writer's reply, not the opposition's case.
Answering it early clears the reader's main doubt before the evidence, so the evidence is read without resistance.

w.a: The counterargument should go in the first paragraph so the reader knows both sides.
w.why: a survey of both sides is not a placement tied to audience

w.a: Counterarguments should be left out so the essay does not weaken its own case.
w.why: answering objections builds credibility (CLE-1.AA)

cards.q: Explain how topic sentences reveal whether an essay has a genuine line of reasoning.
cards.a: Topic sentences state each paragraph's claim, so read in sequence they expose the essay's skeleton: if each claim builds on the last and together they reach the thesis, the reasoning is genuine; if they could be reordered with no loss, or repeat one another, the essay has a list, not a line of reasoning.
cards.h: → topic sentences = paragraph claims → read in order they show the skeleton → build or merely list
cards.n: Topic sentences that only name a subject ('Another example is the park') cannot pass the test; each must state a claim.
o: Commentary inside a paragraph can hide weak sequencing, so isolating the topic sentences strips the detail and shows the order bare.
An essay whose topic sentences announce sources or devices instead of claims fails the test even if its paragraphs are rich.

w.a: If every topic sentence mentions the thesis, the essay has a line of reasoning.
w.why: repeating the thesis is not building on it

w.a: Topic sentences matter for organization, not for reasoning.
w.why: the sequence of paragraph claims is the line of reasoning (REO-1.E)

cards.q: Identify what breaks a line of reasoning even when each paragraph is individually well written.
cards.a: Three signs: paragraphs that could be reordered with no change in meaning (no sequence), subclaims that repeat instead of building on each other, and paragraphs whose claims do not bear on the same thesis. Each is a flaw in the line of reasoning rather than in any paragraph, so the argument can be illogical even when every paragraph is polished.
cards.h: → three failure signs + where the flaw sits
cards.n: Polishing sentences is the wrong repair; the flaw is in the connections between claims, so fix the order and the links.

cards.q: Identify the problem: an essay's three body paragraphs each restate the thesis in different words instead of advancing a distinct reason.
cards.a: The paragraphs are redundant, not progressive: they circle the thesis instead of advancing distinct reasons, so the argument asserts the claim three times without justifying it. The reasoning looks longer but goes nowhere; each paragraph needs its own reason on which the thesis depends.
cards.h: → named flaw + what each paragraph lacks
cards.n: Giving each restatement a new example is the trap; different examples for the same point still add no new step.

cards.q: Apply a qualifier while citing a graph: rewrite 'The chart proves teen screen time causes anxiety' to match what a correlational graph can actually support.
cards.a: Model: 'The chart shows teen screen time and reported anxiety rising together, which suggests a link worth studying, though it cannot show that one causes the other.' A graph of two trends supports correlation, not causation; claiming proof would make the argument specious, plausible on the surface but unsupported by its evidence.
cards.h: → revised sentence + what the graph can support
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.X (qualifiers). Swapping 'proves' for 'shows' keeps the flaw; the fix is changing the claimed relationship from cause to correlation.

cards.q: Define a specious argument, in the sense of REO-1.F, and explain how it differs from a plainly illogical one.
cards.a: A specious argument seems sound on the surface (its evidence is real and its steps sound plausible), but a flaw in its line of reasoning means the conclusion does not actually follow. A plainly illogical argument's steps visibly fail to connect. REO-1.F says flaws in a line of reasoning can make an argument either one.
cards.h: → definition + the difference
cards.n: Treating 'specious' as 'false' is the trap: a specious argument can rest on true facts; what fails is the reasoning that connects them.

cards.q:
Identify the flaw in each line of reasoning and state what the argument would need to repair it (all invented):
1. Our team's grades rose the year we moved practice to the evening, so evening practice raises grades.
2. Three parents at Tuesday's meeting opposed the new schedule, so the community rejects it.
3. The policy is fair because it treats everyone justly.
4. We can either cut the arts budget or raise property taxes.
5. Reject the senator's bike-lane plan; she cannot even balance her own campaign budget.
6. If we allow food in the library, the books will be ruined and the library will have to close.
7. Most students surveyed want a longer lunch, so the school should add 20 minutes to lunch.
8. Running a city is like running a household, so the city should never borrow money.
cards.a:
1 → treats a sequence as a cause; needs evidence that the practice change, not something else that year, raised grades
2 → generalizes from three self-selected people; needs broader evidence, such as a survey of families
3 → circular: the reason restates the claim; needs an independent reason (who is affected, how)
4 → false choice; needs to show other options were weighed and rejected
5 → attacks the person, not the plan; needs reasons about the plan's cost or effect
6 → predicts a chain of steps with no evidence for each; needs evidence that each step is likely
7 → skips a step from wanting to should; needs a reason the change serves the school's aims, weighed against lost class time
8 → the comparison fails where it matters: cities borrow for long-lived projects such as bridges; needs to show the two are alike in that respect
cards.h: → the gap + the repair, one per line
cards.n: Naming a fallacy without saying where the reasoning breaks earns little; the exam asks what the flaw does to the argument, and names are optional.

cards.q: Identify the flaw in this line of reasoning and explain why it makes the argument specious: 'Last spring, Ms. Tran's ninth-grade class used tablets instead of textbooks, and its final exam average rose by eight points. Clearly, tablets improve learning. That is why, starting in the fall, every class in the district will switch from textbooks to tablets.' (an invented principal's newsletter)
cards.a: The reasoning leaps from one class to every class: a single teacher's results (one class, one year, one subject) are treated as proof that tablets improve learning everywhere. The gain might come from Ms. Tran's teaching, the students, or novelty, and the evidence cannot rule those out. The argument is specious: real evidence and plausible steps, but a conclusion the evidence cannot carry.
cards.h: → where it breaks + why the evidence cannot carry it
cards.n: Objecting that tablets are distracting argues against the conclusion, not the reasoning; the task is the gap between evidence and claim.

cards.q: Write a revision of this claim that removes the flaw in its reasoning while keeping the writer's position: 'Either the city raises downtown parking fees or the garage on Fourth Street will have to close.' (an invented council member's newsletter)
cards.a: Model: 'Of the ways to keep the Fourth Street garage open (raising fees, cutting its hours, or applying for a state grant), raising fees is the most dependable, because a grant is uncertain and shorter hours would push drivers onto residential streets.' It admits the other options and argues for the preferred one instead of pretending none exist; the reasons are invented for the model.
cards.h: → admit the alternatives + argue for the chosen one
cards.n: Softening to 'the city should probably raise fees' keeps the flaw hidden; the repair is to acknowledge and answer the other options.

cards.q: Decide which sentence avoids the flaw in reasoning, and explain why. (A) 'Since the new crosswalk was installed, two pedestrians have been hit there, so the crosswalk has made the intersection more dangerous.' (B) 'Two pedestrians have been hit at the new crosswalk since it was installed, which is reason to study whether drivers can see it, though two cases are too few to show it has made the intersection more dangerous.' (invented)
cards.a: (B). It uses the same evidence but claims only what the evidence can support: two accidents raise a question worth studying, not a proven cause. (A) treats a sequence (accidents after installation) as proof of causation from a sample too small to show a trend, which makes the argument specious.
cards.h: → letter + what the evidence can and cannot carry
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it is 'more decisive' is the trap; a confident claim the evidence cannot support is a flaw, not a strength.

cards.q: Explain why a specious argument can mislead an audience more than an obviously illogical one.
cards.a: An obviously illogical argument alerts readers, who reject it. A specious one rests on real evidence and plausible steps, so readers accept its conclusion without noticing the gap, and it can shape a decision before anyone tests the reasoning. Its persuasiveness is what makes it misleading.
cards.h: → illogical = visible gap → readers reject; specious = hidden gap → readers accept → the flawed conclusion wins
cards.n: 'Specious arguments are lies' is the trap; a specious argument can use only true facts, and the flaw is in the reasoning.
o: Because each step of a specious argument sounds reasonable alone, readers check the steps but not the connections between them.
A specious argument borrows credibility from its accurate evidence, so the flaw inherits that trust.

w.a: Specious arguments are more misleading because they use false statistics.
w.why: specious arguments can rest on true evidence

w.a: Illogical arguments are more dangerous because they confuse people.
w.why: confusion prompts rejection; a hidden flaw prompts acceptance

cards.q: Explain why an argument built entirely from accurate evidence can still be specious.
cards.a: Accuracy belongs to the evidence; soundness belongs to the reasoning. Each fact can be true while the step from facts to conclusion fails: a trend treated as a cause, one case treated as a rule. REO-1.F places the flaw in the line of reasoning, so checking the facts alone cannot catch it.
cards.h: → true facts ≠ sound reasoning → the flaw sits in the step between them → fact-checking misses it
cards.n: 'If the facts check out, the argument is valid' is the trap: test the connection, not only the evidence.
o: Selection can mislead too: a writer who cites only the accurate facts that favor the claim leaves out those that complicate it.
The conclusion can claim more than the evidence covers, as when one school's results become a rule for every school.

w.a: An argument with accurate evidence cannot be flawed.
w.why: the flaw can be in the reasoning, not the facts

w.a: An argument is specious only when the writer is trying to deceive.
w.why: specious describes the reasoning, not the writer's intent

cards.q: Explain why a line of reasoning that skips a step may persuade readers who already agree but fail with skeptical readers.
cards.a: Readers who share the conclusion fill the missing step with their own assumptions, so the gap goes unnoticed. Skeptical readers do not supply it; they see a claim that does not follow from the evidence given. An argument meant to persuade must state every step its opponents would question.
cards.h: → sympathetic readers supply the missing step → skeptics do not → the gap shows exactly where persuasion is needed
cards.n: Blaming skeptics as 'closed-minded' misses the point: the flaw is the unstated step, and the writer can repair it.
o: An unstated assumption works as a hidden premise, and the audience that most needs persuading is the one least likely to grant it.
Writing for the skeptical reader forces the writer to find and defend every link, which strengthens the argument for everyone.

w.a: Skeptical readers reject every argument, so the missing step does not matter.
w.why: stating the step is what gives skeptics a reason to move

w.a: If most readers agree, the reasoning must be sound.
w.why: agreement does not repair a missing step

cards.q: Define a method of development, in the CED's terms, and state what it gives an audience.
cards.a: Methods of development are common approaches writers use to develop and organize the reasoning of their arguments, such as narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, and description. A method gives the audience the means to trace the writer's reasoning: once readers recognize the method, they know how each part relates to the next.
cards.h: → definition + what it gives readers
cards.n: Calling a method 'a rhetorical device' confuses scale: a method organizes a passage's reasoning, not a single sentence.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called exemplification and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Exemplification supports a generalization with several specific instances, so readers can trace the reasoning from cases to the pattern they share. A writer chooses it to show that a pattern is real and widespread rather than isolated: three towns, not one, where the change occurred.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Not on the CED's list of typical methods (REO-1.L mentions examples). The trap: one vivid instance is an anecdote, not a pattern.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called process analysis and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Process analysis explains, step by step, how something happens or is done, so readers can trace the reasoning through the sequence. A writer chooses it to show that a plan is feasible, or to pinpoint the step where a system breaks down, such as where a benefits application stalls between two offices.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Not on the CED's list of typical methods. The trap: steps listed without saying which one matters to the claim describe a process but argue nothing.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called classification and division and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Classification sorts many items into categories; division breaks one subject into its parts. A writer chooses it to bring order to a sprawling issue so each category or part can be judged in turn, and the categories give readers a map for tracing the reasoning.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Not on the CED's list of typical methods. Overlapping or incomplete categories are the trap: the argument leaks wherever an item fits two groups or none.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called problem-solution and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Problem-solution establishes a problem, then proposes and defends a remedy, so readers trace the reasoning from need to answer. A writer chooses it for policy arguments, and the solution must be shown to address the problem's cause and to be feasible.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use
cards.n: Not on the CED's list of typical methods. A remedy with no plan to fund or carry it out is the gap an opponent names first.

cards.q: Contrast classification and division as methods of development.
cards.a: Classification sorts many separate items into shared categories (kinds of study habits); division breaks one subject into its parts (the parts of a school budget). Classification groups outward from many things; division splits inward from one.
cards.h: → two-part contrast
cards.n: Count the starting subjects: many things sorted is classification, one thing cut up is division. Neither term is on the CED's list, so function matters more than label.

cards.q: Define the categorical (topical) organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Categorical order arranges material by types or categories rather than by time, space, or importance. Typical use: essays that survey several kinds of causes, groups, or examples side by side. Because categories carry no built-in progression, the writer must give a reason for their order.
cards.h: → pattern + use case
cards.n: Leaving categories in the order they came to mind is the trap: with no reason for the sequence, the essay reads as a list, not a line of reasoning.

cards.q: Explain why identifying a passage's method of development matters in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The method is itself a rhetorical choice: defining a term, narrating a case, or tracing causes decides what the audience sees as the issue and how it follows the reasoning. Naming the method lets an essay analyze how the whole argument is built, a level of analysis that spotting sentence-level devices misses.
cards.h: → method = a choice about how readers see the issue → naming it reveals the structure → analysis above the sentence
cards.n: Naming the method and stopping ('the author uses narration') is device-spotting at a larger scale; say what the method does for the purpose.
o: Because a method tells readers how to trace the reasoning, identifying it shows how the writer guides the audience toward the claim.
Methods explain why a passage is arranged as it is, which lets an essay discuss how parts relate rather than isolated quotations.

w.a: Identifying the method matters because the prompt asks you to list the techniques.
w.why: the prompt asks for analysis of choices, not a list

w.a: The method does not matter as long as you find the devices.
w.why: the method organizes the reasoning the devices serve

cards.q: Explain why a recognizable method of development helps readers follow an argument on an unfamiliar subject.
cards.a: Readers new to a subject cannot yet judge which details matter. A familiar method (a story told in sequence, a comparison on shared categories, a chain of causes) tells them how the parts relate, so they can trace the reasoning even before they understand the subject.
cards.h: → unfamiliar subject → readers can't weigh details → a known method shows how parts relate → reasoning is traceable
cards.n: 'Methods make writing more organized' is too vague; say what the method lets this reader do: trace how each part leads to the next.
o: A method sets expectations (a cause will be followed by its effect, one side of a comparison by the other), and met expectations make reasoning easier to follow.
A shape the audience already knows, such as a before-and-after story, gives them a way to make sense of new content.

w.a: Methods of development are mainly a way to make an essay longer.
w.why: they organize the reasoning, not its length

w.a: Readers who do not know the subject will be confused whatever method is used.
w.why: the CED says a method gives the audience the means to trace the reasoning

cards.q: State the five typical methods of development the CED names.
cards.a: Narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, and description. The CED introduces them as 'some typical methods,' so the list is not closed; writers also use others, such as exemplification or problem-solution.
cards.h: → five names
cards.n: Adding 'persuasion' or 'argument' is the trap: those are purposes or modes, not methods of development.

cards.q: Contrast narration and description as methods of development.
cards.a: Narration relates real-life experiences as a sequence of events and reflects on their significance; description relates the characteristics, features, or sensory details of an object or idea. Narration moves through time; description dwells on what something is like.
cards.h: → two-part contrast
cards.n: Most passages mix them, so ask which dominates and what it accomplishes; a narrative with no reflection is only a story (REO-1.I).

cards.q:
