Identify the dominant method of development (narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, or description) in each invented excerpt:
1. When the mill closed, the town lost its largest taxpayer and then its music program.
2. The first time I voted, my name was found in a binder by hand; I still think of the trust that binder held.
3. A 'food desert' is not a place without food; it is one where fresh food costs more than residents can pay.
4. Unlike the old library, which closed at 5, the new one stays open until 9 and lends laptops.
5. In August the river is the color of weak tea and loud with cicadas.
6. Higher fares drove riders away, and fewer riders brought the next fare increase.
7. Resilience, as I use the word, is not toughness; it is the habit of asking for help early.
8. At 6 a.m. my mother began packing lunches; by the time the bus came she had packed forty.
cards.a:
1 → cause-effect (one cause, a series of effects)
2 → narration (an experience plus a reflection on its meaning)
3 → definition (what the term is and is not)
4 → comparison-contrast (old and new library on hours and lending)
5 → description (sensory details: color and sound)
6 → cause-effect (a chain in which each effect becomes the next cause)
7 → definition (a stated meaning set against a common one)
8 → narration (events moving through time, from experience)
cards.h: → method + the clue, one per line
cards.n: Item 8 has concrete details but moves through time, so it is narration; ask whether an excerpt moves (narration) or dwells (description).

cards.q: Decide which method of development best serves this purpose, and explain why: a columnist wants readers to accept that 'affordable housing' in their city should mean an apartment a first-year teacher can rent on one salary. (A) narration (B) cause-effect (C) comparison-contrast (D) definition
cards.a: (D) definition. The argument turns on what a contested term should mean, and definition lets the writer set out the term's features (rent one starting salary can cover) and exclude rival meanings (housing that is merely below market rate). The other methods could support it, but only definition fixes the meaning the rest of the argument depends on.
cards.h: → letter + why the purpose calls for it
cards.n: Picking narration because a teacher's story would be moving is the trap: a story could illustrate, but the claim itself is about a meaning.

cards.q: Identify the two methods of development in this passage and explain how the first serves the second: 'When my grandmother arrived in this city in 1971, a neighbor she had never met left a pot of soup on her step with a note giving the bus schedule. That, to me, is what a neighborhood is: not a set of streets, but a set of strangers who act as if you already belong.' (an invented essay)
cards.a: Narration and definition. The short narrative (a stranger's soup and bus schedule) supplies a real experience, and the reflection turns it into a definition: a neighborhood is strangers acting as if you belong. The narration serves the definition by providing the example it is drawn from, so the definition reads as earned rather than asserted.
cards.h: → two methods + how one supplies the other
cards.n: Naming only 'an anecdote' misses the task; the question is how the story becomes evidence for the definition the argument needs.

cards.q: Write two sentences developing the claim 'Our school should start at 8:30 instead of 7:30,' one by cause-effect and one by comparison-contrast.
cards.a: Model, cause-effect: 'A 7:30 bell puts most of us on buses before 7, so we arrive short on sleep, and first-period grades show it.' Comparison-contrast: 'East High, which starts at 8:30 and shares our bus company, logs half as many first-period tardies as we do.' (figures invented) The first traces a consequence; the second weighs two schools on one shared category.
cards.h: → one sentence per method, each clearly shaped
cards.n: A comparison with no shared category ('East High is nicer') is not comparison-contrast; both schools must be measured on the same thing.

cards.q: Explain why writers often combine several methods of development within one argument.
cards.a: Each method does one kind of work: narration makes a problem concrete, cause-effect shows why it happens, comparison weighs options, definition fixes terms. Most arguments need several of these jobs, so writers combine methods, one supplying what the next depends on, as a story becomes evidence for a causal claim.
cards.h: → each method does one job → arguments need several jobs → methods combine, each feeding the next
cards.n: 'To keep the reader interested' is the trap; name the job each method does for the argument.
o: An audience that includes both the moved and the skeptical is reached by pairing a story with data.
One method can leave a gap, as a narrative alone can seem anecdotal, which a second method such as cause-effect can close.

w.a: Writers combine methods because using only one is not allowed.
w.why: no rule forbids it; the reason is what each method does

w.a: Using many methods shows the writer knows many techniques.
w.why: display is not a purpose; each method must serve the argument

cards.q: Explain why the same subject can be developed by different methods depending on the writer's purpose.
cards.a: A method follows from what the writer needs the audience to see. A school's closing could be narrated to make readers feel the loss, traced by cause-effect to assign responsibility, or compared with another school's survival to argue for a remedy. The subject stays the same; the purpose selects the method.
cards.h: → purpose decides what readers must see → each method shows something different → subject alone doesn't pick it
cards.n: 'Some subjects are narrative subjects' is the trap: no subject requires a method; purpose and audience choose it.
o: The method follows from what the audience needs: readers who doubt a problem exists need a story or a description of it, while readers who accept it need cause-effect or comparison to choose a remedy.
Choosing a method is a rhetorical choice, and the choice shows what the writer thinks the audience most needs to see.

w.a: Every topic has one correct method of development.
w.why: purpose, not topic, decides the method

w.a: Writers choose whichever method they are most comfortable with.
w.why: that ignores purpose and audience

cards.q: Explain the method of development called narration and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Narration develops an idea through details about real-life experiences plus reflection on their significance: the story supplies concrete evidence, and the reflection says what it shows. A writer chooses it to make an abstract problem concrete and connect the audience to the stakes, especially when statistics alone would feel distant.
cards.h: → experience + reflection + when to choose it
cards.n: A story with no reflection is the trap: the CED's narration includes insight into the experience's significance, which is what links it to the claim.

cards.q: Define the chronological organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Chronological order arranges material in time order. Typical uses: narratives, accounts of how a problem developed, and process explanations. In narration it lets readers live through events in sequence before the writer reflects on what they mean.
cards.h: → pattern + use case
cards.n: Telling events in order is not yet arguing: a sequence needs reflection or causal commentary before it becomes reasoning.

cards.q: Identify the details and the reflection in this narrative passage, and explain what the reflection adds: 'The summer I was fifteen I worked the register at my uncle's hardware store. A man came in every Saturday for one screw, paid in coins, and asked my name each time. By August I understood he was not there for the screws. I have thought of him every time someone tells me a store is just a business.' (an invented essay on small-town shops)
cards.a: Details: the register job, the weekly single screw, the coins, the man asking her name each time. Reflection: 'By August I understood he was not there for the screws' and the final sentence. The reflection turns the story into a claim about significance (a local shop serves loneliness as well as commerce), which is what lets the narration argue against 'just a business.'
cards.h: → details + reflection + what the reflection claims
cards.n: Summarizing the story ('a man buys screws') misses the task; the reflection is where narration turns experience into argument.

cards.q: Identify what this narrative paragraph lacks as a method of development, according to REO-1.I: 'My grandfather worked on the same assembly line for 31 years. He took the 6:10 bus every morning. He retired in 1998 with a watch and a pension. He died in 2016.' (from an invented essay arguing that pensions built the middle class)
cards.a: Reflection. The paragraph gives details of a real life but no insight into their significance, so it never connects to the claim about pensions. One sentence of reflection (what the pension let him do, or what it meant that he could retire at all) would turn the chronology into evidence.
cards.h: → what is missing + what it would supply
cards.n: Adding more details (his wages, the plant's name) is the trap; the gap is significance, not information.

cards.q: Write a sentence of reflection that turns this anecdote into support for the claim that the city should keep its branch post offices open: 'Every month my neighbor, who is 84 and does not drive, walks three blocks to the Elm Street post office to mail her rent check and buy one book of stamps.' (invented)
cards.a: Model: 'For her, the branch is not a convenience but the last errand she can still run on her own, and closing it would turn an independent woman into one who must ask for help to pay her rent.' It reflects on what the experience means, which ties the story to the claim about keeping branches open.
cards.h: → one sentence: what the experience means → the claim
cards.n: 'This story shows post offices are important' names a conclusion with no insight; reflection explains what the experience reveals.

cards.q: Decide which closing sentence makes this narrative serve the writer's argument that high schools should teach students to cook, and explain why: 'In ninth grade, my friend Ana could name every element on the periodic table but could not boil an egg. Her first month in her own apartment, she spent more on takeout than on groceries.' (A) 'Ana is a great friend and a very smart person.' (B) 'School had prepared Ana for a chemistry test but not for her own kitchen, and the gap cost her.' (invented)
cards.a: (B). It reflects on the significance of the experience, the gap between what school taught and what Ana needed, and its cost, which is exactly the claim about teaching cooking. (A) adds a detail about Ana but no insight, so the narration stays a story instead of becoming evidence.
cards.h: → letter + which one reflects on significance
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it is kind to Ana misreads the task; the right close turns the story into insight about the claim.

cards.q: Explain why a personal narrative can persuade an audience that statistics alone leave unmoved.
cards.a: Statistics describe many people at a distance; a narrative gives one real experience readers can picture. When the writer reflects on its significance, the story shows what the numbers mean for a person, so the audience grasps the stakes the statistics only measure.
cards.h: → numbers are abstract → a story makes one case concrete → reflection links it to the stakes
cards.n: 'Stories use pathos' is not enough on its own; say what the narrative lets this audience see that the numbers do not.
o: A narrative gives the writer firsthand standing, so it can build credibility as well as feeling.
Pairing the story with the statistic lets the narrative show the human cost and the number show the case is not isolated.

w.a: Narratives are more persuasive than statistics in every argument.
w.why: some audiences need data; the story's value depends on the audience

w.a: Stories persuade because readers enjoy them.
w.why: enjoyment is not the reasoning the reflection supplies

cards.q: Explain why reflection, not just detail, is what makes narration a method of argument.
cards.a: Details alone record what happened; readers may take any lesson from them, or none. REO-1.I describes narration as experience plus reflection on its significance, and the reflection is where the writer states the insight that connects the experience to the claim, turning a story into reasoning.
cards.h: → details = what happened → reflection = what it means → meaning is the link to the claim
cards.n: Treating a vivid story as self-explanatory is the trap; without the writer's insight, the reader decides what it proves.
o: Reflection is narration's form of commentary: it explains the significance of the evidence the story supplies.
Without reflection a narrative can support opposite claims, so the insight fixes which one it supports.

w.a: The more details a story has, the more persuasive it is.
w.why: details without insight do not connect to the claim

w.a: Reflection is optional because readers can work out the lesson.
w.why: readers may draw a different lesson, or none

cards.q: Explain the method of development called cause-effect and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Cause-effect develops an idea by presenting a cause and asserting its effects or consequences, or by presenting a series of causes and the effect they produce. A writer chooses it for arguments about responsibility or consequence (what a policy will do, why a problem arose) and must show the mechanism linking cause to effect.
cards.h: → the CED's patterns + when to choose it
cards.n: Sequence is not causation: 'it happened after' is the post hoc trap, so the writer must explain how the cause produces the effect.

cards.q:
Identify the cause-effect structure of each excerpt: one cause with several effects, several causes with one effect, or a chain (all invented):
1. The factory's closing cost the town 400 jobs, a quarter of its tax base, and its only bus route.
2. A dry spring, a late freeze, and a new pest together cut the apple harvest in half.
3. Once the bridge was tolled, traffic moved to Route 4, repair costs there tripled, and the county raised its gas tax to pay them.
4. Low pay, long commutes, and a housing shortage have left the district forty teachers short.
5. The later start time gave students more sleep, fewer tardies, and better first-period grades.
cards.a:
1 → one cause, several effects (closing → jobs, tax base, bus route)
2 → several causes, one effect (drought, freeze, pest → half the harvest)
3 → a chain: each effect causes the next (toll → traffic shift → repair costs → gas tax)
4 → several causes, one effect (pay, commute, housing → teacher shortage)
5 → one cause, several effects (start time → sleep, tardies, grades)
cards.h: → structure + causes → effects, one per line
cards.n: Item 3 looks like one cause with several effects, but each step causes the next; a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

cards.q: Identify the cause and the asserted effects in this passage, and describe what the writer must show for the reasoning to hold: 'If the county closes the Oak Street clinic, the 2,000 patients who walk there will not simply drive to the hospital; many have no car. They will wait until a cough becomes pneumonia, and the emergency room, the most expensive care the county pays for, will absorb them.' (an invented public comment; figures invented)
cards.a: Cause: closing the Oak Street clinic. Asserted effects, as a chain: patients without cars delay care, minor illnesses become serious, and the county's emergency room absorbs costlier cases. For the reasoning to hold, the writer must support each link: that many patients lack cars, that delayed care leads to worse illness, and that these patients would end up in the emergency room.
cards.h: → cause + chain of effects + the links to support
cards.n: Calling it 'fear-mongering' dodges the task; judge whether each link in the chain is supported, not whether the prediction is alarming.

cards.q: Explain how a writer can use cause-effect to argue about a proposal that has not yet happened.
cards.a: By asserting the effects or consequences the proposal would have: 'If the council adds a toll, drivers will shift to Route 4.' Because the effects have not occurred, the reasoning must rest on evidence that the mechanism operates, such as what happened when a similar toll was added elsewhere, or on the known behavior of the people affected.
cards.h: → asserted consequences + the evidence they need
cards.n: A prediction with no evidence for its mechanism is the slippery-slope trap: each asserted step needs its own support.

cards.q: Write a sentence that develops this claim through cause-effect by naming the mechanism: 'Longer library hours would raise graduation rates.'
cards.a: Model: 'Students who work after school or lack internet at home could use the library's computers in the evening to finish assignments they now leave undone, and fewer missing assignments mean fewer failed courses and fewer seniors short of credits in June.' It links cause to effect through a mechanism: access, then completed work, then passed courses.
cards.h: → cause → mechanism → effect, in one sentence
cards.n: 'Longer hours would help students graduate' repeats the claim; the mechanism, how hours lead to graduation, is what makes it cause-effect.

cards.q: Decide which sentence better develops the claim that the new bus schedule caused the rise in tardies, and explain why. (A) 'Tardies rose from 40 to 95 a week after the schedule changed in January.' (B) 'The January schedule moved the Route 9 bus to a 7:52 arrival for an 8:00 bell, and 41 of the 55 added weekly tardies are Route 9 riders.' (invented figures)
cards.a: (B). It shows the mechanism (a bus arriving eight minutes before the bell) and ties the added tardies to the riders it affects (41 of 55), so the cause explains the effect. (A) shows only that tardies rose after the change, a sequence that could have other causes.
cards.h: → letter + which shows mechanism, not just timing
cards.n: Choosing (A) for its bigger numbers is the trap; a rise after a change shows timing, not cause.

cards.q: Explain why a writer using cause-effect must name the mechanism linking the cause to the effect.
cards.a: Without a mechanism, a cause-effect claim rests on sequence or correlation, which a skeptical reader can explain another way. Naming how the cause produces the effect (the bus arrives eight minutes before the bell) makes the link checkable and rules out rival explanations.
cards.h: → no mechanism = mere sequence → rival explanations stay open → the mechanism makes the link credible
cards.n: 'Because the effect came after the cause' is the trap: timing alone is the flaw REO-1.F warns can make an argument specious.
o: The mechanism is where commentary does its work: it explains how the evidence proves the causal claim.
A named mechanism also tells readers what would have to change to stop the effect, which supports a proposed remedy.

w.a: If two things happen together, one must cause the other.
w.why: correlation is not causation

w.a: The mechanism is obvious, so writers do not need to state it.
w.why: what is obvious to the writer is a missing step to a skeptic

cards.q: Explain why arguing that several causes produced one effect can be more persuasive than blaming a single cause.
cards.a: Most real effects have more than one cause, so a single-cause claim invites the easy rebuttal 'what about X?' Presenting a series of causes answers that in advance, shows the writer has weighed the evidence, and lets the argument target the cause most within the audience's power to change.
cards.h: → real effects have many causes → one cause invites rebuttal → several causes show fairness and pick the fixable one
cards.n: 'More causes means more evidence' misses the reasoning; the gain is accuracy and credibility, not volume.
o: A multi-cause account qualifies the claim, which guards against the oversimplification CLE-1.V warns about.
Naming several causes lets the writer rank them, giving the argument a line of reasoning from minor to decisive.

w.a: Listing many causes makes the argument look more researched.
w.why: appearance is not the reason; accuracy and credibility are

w.a: A single cause is always wrong because readers prefer complexity.
w.why: a single cause can be right; the point is answering rival explanations

cards.q: Explain the method of development called comparison-contrast and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Comparison-contrast develops an idea by presenting a category of comparison and examining the similarities and/or differences between the objects compared (two plans compared on cost, reach, and speed). A writer chooses it to evaluate alternatives or to clarify something unfamiliar by setting it beside something known. Like categories must be used on both sides.
cards.h: → category + similarities/differences + when to choose it
cards.n: Comparing unlike categories (one plan's cost with the other's popularity) is the trap the CED names: such a comparison proves nothing.

cards.q: Contrast point-by-point and block organization for a comparison-contrast essay.
cards.a: Point-by-point alternates between the two subjects category by category (cost for both, then speed for both); block covers all of one subject, then all of the other. Point-by-point keeps like categories side by side; block reads smoothly but can leave two separate summaries the reader must compare alone.
cards.h: → two arrangements + what each does to the categories
cards.n: A block essay whose second half skips a category covered in the first breaks the like-categories rule; check that each category appears on both sides.

cards.q: Identify the objects compared and the categories of comparison in this passage, and explain what the comparison argues: 'A new turf field would cost the district 1.2 million dollars and last about ten years. The same 1.2 million would pay two reading specialists for the same ten years. One serves the 60 students on the varsity roster; the other would reach every one of the 900 students reading below grade level.' (an invented school board comment; figures invented)
cards.a: The objects are a turf field and two reading specialists; the categories are like on both sides: cost (1.2 million each), time (ten years each), and reach (60 students versus 900). Holding cost and time equal lets the difference in reach carry the argument: the same money serves fifteen times as many students through the specialists.
cards.h: → objects + like categories + what the difference shows
cards.n: 'It compares sports and reading' names subjects, not categories; the argument lives in the shared categories of cost, time, and reach.

cards.q: Identify the flaw in this comparison and explain why it weakens the argument: 'The bus plan would cost 3 million dollars a year, while the light-rail plan is supported by 70 percent of residents, so light rail is the better choice.' (an invented council debate)
cards.a: The categories are unlike: the bus plan is measured by cost and the light-rail plan by popularity, so the two are never actually compared. REO-1.K requires like categories; to argue that light rail is better, the writer must compare both plans on cost, both on public support, or both on another shared measure.
cards.h: → the mismatched categories + the repair
cards.n: Arguing that 70 percent is impressive misses the flaw; a strong number in one category cannot be weighed against a number in another.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence comparison that uses like categories to argue that the town should repair its public pool rather than build a splash pad. Use these invented facts: pool, 180,000 dollars to repair, open to all ages, can host swim lessons; splash pad, 90,000 dollars to build, suited to children under 10, no lessons.
cards.a: Model: 'The splash pad costs half as much as repairing the pool, 90,000 dollars against 180,000, but it serves only children under 10, while the pool serves every age. And only the pool can teach a child to swim, so the cheaper choice buys less of what a town pool is for.' Each sentence measures both options on the same category: cost, who is served, lessons.
cards.h: → both options on each category, then the verdict
cards.n: Describing each option in its own sentence ('The pool is... The splash pad is...') leaves the comparing to the reader; set them side by side.

cards.q: Decide which sentence makes a valid comparison, and explain why the other fails. (A) 'Our school spends 900 dollars per student on technology, while Westfield's students score higher on state tests.' (B) 'Our school spends 900 dollars per student on technology and Westfield spends 400, yet Westfield's scores are higher, which suggests spending alone is not the answer.' (invented figures)
cards.a: (B). It measures both schools in the same two categories (spending and scores), so the contrast supports a conclusion. (A) gives spending for one school and scores for the other, unlike categories, so nothing is actually compared.
cards.h: → letter + the categories each sentence uses
cards.n: Choosing (A) because it sounds pointed is the trap; with unlike categories it only hints at a comparison it never makes.

cards.q: Explain why a comparison-contrast argument must use like categories on both sides.
cards.a: A comparison persuades only if both objects are measured the same way: cost against cost, reach against reach. When the categories differ, nothing is actually weighed, so the reader cannot tell which option is better and the conclusion does not follow from the evidence.
cards.h: → like categories = a real measurement → unlike ones weigh nothing → the conclusion doesn't follow
cards.n: 'So the comparison is fair' is too vague; say what unlike categories do to the reasoning: they leave nothing compared.
o: Unlike categories let a writer hide a weakness, showing one option's strength beside the other's flaw, which careful readers see as specious.
Matching the categories makes the differences stand out, because everything else is held equal.

w.a: Writers use like categories so the essay looks balanced.
w.why: the reason is valid reasoning, not appearance

w.a: Any two facts about two things count as a comparison.
w.why: REO-1.K requires like categories of comparison

cards.q: Explain why a writer might compare an unfamiliar proposal with something the audience already knows.
cards.a: A known object gives the audience a reference point: set beside the familiar thing on shared categories, the unfamiliar proposal's features become measurable. The comparison lets readers trace the reasoning through what they already understand, which lowers resistance to something new.
cards.h: → unfamiliar = hard to judge → familiar object on like categories → the proposal becomes measurable
cards.n: Borrows RHS-1.K. A comparison the audience does not share or understand fails, however apt it seems to the writer.
o: If the familiar thing is already trusted, the comparison can transfer that trust to the proposal.
Similarities reassure readers that the proposal is less risky than it looks, while differences show what it adds.

w.a: Comparisons mainly make writing more colorful.
w.why: decoration is not the reasoning a comparison carries

w.a: Readers always prefer familiar things, so comparisons trick them.
w.why: a valid comparison clarifies; it need not trick

cards.q: Explain the method of development called description and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Description develops an idea by relating the characteristics, features, or sensory details of an object or scene, so the audience can judge it as if present. A writer chooses it to make a condition vivid and concrete (a classroom's broken heat, a creek's color), letting the selected details carry an argument without stating it outright.
cards.h: → what it relates + when to choose it
cards.n: Details with no evident point are the trap: description argues only through what it selects, so the details must point toward the claim.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called definition and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Definition develops an idea by relating the characteristics or features of a term, often with examples or illustrations, and by marking what it excludes. A writer chooses it when the argument turns on a contested term such as 'fair' or 'public'; whoever sets the definition shapes what counts as evidence.
cards.h: → what it relates + when to choose it
cards.n: Quoting a dictionary is the trap: an argument's definition must be argued for, since the dispute is over which meaning should govern.

cards.q: Define the spatial organizational pattern and name a typical use.
cards.a: Spatial order arranges material by physical position or location (left to right, entrance to back, street to river). Typical use: descriptions of places, scenes, and physical conditions, where the path the reader's eye takes can build toward the detail that matters most.
cards.h: → pattern + use case
cards.n: Treating spatial order as neutral is the trap: where a description starts and ends decides what the reader sees last.

cards.q: Identify how this passage develops its definition and what the definition lets the writer argue: 'A public space is not simply a place the government owns. A public space is one where you can stay without buying anything, where no one asks why you are there, and where the rules are the same for everyone. By that measure, the new downtown plaza, with its café-only seating and guards who move people along, is not public at all.' (an invented op-ed)
cards.a: It defines by features (you can stay without buying, no one questions your presence, the rules apply equally) and by exclusion (not simply government ownership). Setting out the features first lets the writer use them as a test: café-only seating and guards who move people along fail two of the three, so the plaza is 'not public at all.' The definition supplies the standard the conclusion depends on.
cards.h: → features + exclusion + how the definition becomes a test
cards.n: 'It defines public space' names the method without its work; show how the defined features judge the plaza.

cards.q: Identify the sensory details in this description and explain how they serve the writer's argument that the district must replace Room 114's heating: 'In January the radiator in Room 114 clanks twice an hour and gives no heat. Students write in gloves; the windows fog on the inside; a thermometer taped to the whiteboard read 54 degrees at 9 a.m. last Tuesday.' (an invented letter from a teacher)
cards.a: Sound (the radiator clanks), touch (students writing in gloves), sight (windows fogged on the inside), and a measured detail (54 degrees on a taped thermometer). Together they let readers experience the room as the students do, and the measured reading turns impression into evidence, so the need for new heating seems self-evident without the writer asserting it.
cards.h: → details by sense + what they lead the reader to conclude
cards.n: Listing the details without the claim they serve is the trap; description is evidence only when its details point to the argument.

cards.q: Write a sentence that develops a definition of 'a good neighbor' by stating one characteristic and illustrating it with an example, for an essay arguing that neighborhoods should organize snow-shoveling help for elderly residents.
cards.a: Model: 'A good neighbor notices what you cannot do before you have to ask: the teenager who clears the steps next door on a snowy morning, before the woman who lives there has to phone anyone, has done more for her independence than any city program.' It names a characteristic (noticing unasked needs) and illustrates it with an example that leads toward the claim.
cards.h: → characteristic + an example that serves the claim
cards.n: A definition by synonym ('a good neighbor is a nice person') gives no feature to argue from; name a characteristic and show it.

cards.q: Explain why defining a contested term early can decide an argument before the evidence arrives.
cards.a: The definition sets the criteria the evidence will be judged by. If 'affordable' means rent a teacher can pay on one salary, most new units fail the test before any data appear, while a looser definition would pass them. Whoever defines the term chooses which evidence counts, so the definition itself argues.
cards.h: → definition sets the criteria → criteria decide which evidence counts → the defining writer frames the verdict
cards.n: 'Definitions help the reader understand' is too weak; the point is that the definition sets the test the conclusion depends on.
o: A definition stated early can be applied as a standard in each later paragraph, which gives the argument a line of reasoning.
An opponent who accepts the definition has already conceded the criteria, so the dispute narrows to the facts.

w.a: Defining terms is only for clarity, not for argument.
w.why: a contested definition carries the argument's criteria

w.a: Writers should use the dictionary definition so no one can argue.
w.why: a dictionary cannot settle a contested meaning

cards.q: Explain why a writer might let descriptive details argue without stating the claim outright.
cards.a: Details a reader can picture (gloves worn indoors, 54 degrees at 9 a.m.) lead readers to the conclusion themselves, and a conclusion readers reach on their own meets less resistance than one announced. Stating the claim can seem to overreach, while well-chosen detail makes the verdict feel self-evident.
cards.h: → reader pictures the details → reaches the verdict alone → less resistance than a stated claim
cards.n: 'Description is more interesting' misses the reasoning; the details work as evidence the reader weighs alone.
o: Selection is the argument: which details appear decides what the reader sees, so description can persuade while seeming neutral.
Readers who distrust the writer may still trust what they can picture for themselves.

w.a: Writers leave the claim unstated because they are unsure of it.
w.why: the choice can be strategic, letting details persuade

w.a: Description cannot be argument because it only shows things.
w.why: selected details are evidence that points to a claim

cards.q: Explain the function of a topic sentence.
cards.a: A topic sentence states the paragraph's claim and links it to the thesis, telling the reader what this paragraph will prove and why it comes here. It should assert something arguable, not announce a topic or summarize a source.
cards.h: → two jobs: state the claim + link to the thesis
cards.n: 'In Source B, the author discusses cost' announces a topic; a topic sentence must make a claim the paragraph's evidence can support.

cards.q: Explain the standard structure of an argumentative body paragraph.
cards.a: A claim (the topic sentence); specific evidence introduced with context; commentary explaining how the evidence supports the claim; and a closing link explaining how the paragraph contributes to the argument's reasoning. REO-1.M names the core: claims, evidence, and commentary.
cards.h: → claim + evidence + commentary + link
cards.n: Treating the parts as a fill-in template is the trap: commentary should run through the paragraph, not sit in one sentence after the quotation.

cards.q: Decide when to start a new paragraph.
cards.a: Start a new paragraph when the claim changes, when a new piece of evidence needs its own commentary, when moving from your case to a counterargument, or when a paragraph has grown so long the reader loses its claim. Each paragraph should do one job in the line of reasoning.
cards.h: → the triggers + the one-job principle
cards.n: Breaking at a fixed length ('every five sentences') is the trap; the break follows the claim, not the line count.

cards.q: Contrast a subclaim and a topic sentence.
cards.a: A subclaim is the idea a paragraph exists to prove, an arguable point that supports the thesis; the topic sentence is the actual sentence that states it. A paragraph can have a clear subclaim and a weak topic sentence that hides it.
cards.h: → the idea vs the sentence that states it
cards.n: A topic sentence that names only the subject ('Now for the economy') leaves the subclaim unstated; the sentence must carry the claim.

cards.q: Identify the problem: a body paragraph presents two unrelated pieces of evidence for two different subclaims without transitioning between them.
cards.a: The paragraph lacks unity: a body paragraph should develop one claim, and here two subclaims share a paragraph with nothing connecting them. Split it into two paragraphs, each with its own claim and commentary, or state the claim that joins them and explain how each piece supports it.
cards.h: → named flaw + two possible repairs
cards.n: Adding a transition word alone ('Also,') is the trap; a connective cannot create a relationship the commentary never explains.

cards.q: Explain the concession-turn-refutation pattern for handling a counterargument in one sentence.
cards.a: State the opposing point fairly, mark the pivot with a word such as 'however' or 'yet,' then explain why your position still holds: 'Although the program is costly, the cost of letting the bridge fail would be far higher.' Inside a body paragraph, the move answers the objection while keeping the paragraph's own claim in control.
cards.h: → concede → turn → refute, with an example
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.AA to AC. Conceding without the turn ('The program is costly. Critics are right.') leaves the objection as your last word.

cards.q: Contrast dismissing a counterargument and substantively refuting one.
cards.a: Dismissing rejects a counterargument without engaging its reasoning or evidence ('That argument is ridiculous'); substantively refuting engages the opposing reasoning and shows where it fails or what it overlooks. Refutation is claim, evidence, and commentary aimed at the objection; dismissal is only an assertion.
cards.h: → rejecting vs engaging
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.AC. Calling the other side 'misinformed' without showing how is dismissal, and it costs credibility with fair-minded readers.

cards.q:
Identify the claim, the evidence, and the commentary in this body paragraph, and explain how the paragraph contributes to the thesis that the city should plant more street trees:
'(1) Street trees pay for themselves in cooler summers. (2) In the city's 2023 heat survey, blocks with full tree cover measured up to 9 degrees cooler at street level than treeless blocks nearby. (3) Nine degrees is the difference between a walk to the bus and a health risk for an elderly resident, and cooler blocks draw less on the power grid. (4) If trees cut both danger and demand, the planting budget is not a cost but a savings the city is failing to collect.' (invented)
cards.a: Claim: sentence 1 (trees pay for themselves in cooler summers). Evidence: sentence 2 (up to 9 degrees cooler). Commentary: sentences 3 and 4. Sentence 3 explains what the difference means (health, power demand); sentence 4 explains how the paragraph contributes to the thesis: trees are a savings, so the city should plant more.
cards.h: → claim, evidence, commentary by sentence + its job
cards.n: Dismissing sentence 4 as a restatement misses its job: it explains how this paragraph advances the thesis, which REO-1.M asks commentary to do.

cards.q: Explain the scoring consequence of citing fewer than three sources on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: It caps Row B at 1 of its 4 points. In the College Board's synthesis rubric, the 2-, 3-, and 4-point levels each require evidence from at least three of the provided sources, so an essay that references two can earn only the 1, and one that references fewer than two earns 0, however strong its commentary.
cards.h: → the cap + the rubric levels behind it
cards.n: Rubric recalled from the published 2019-onward guidelines (Exam Craft). Citing six earns nothing extra: past three, Row B scores the commentary.

cards.q: Explain the risk of a body paragraph that opens with evidence instead of a topic sentence.
cards.a: With no claim first, readers must infer the paragraph's point from the evidence, and evidence can support more than one point, so they may infer the wrong one. The commentary then explains a connection to a claim the reader never saw, and the paragraph's contribution to the argument blurs.
cards.h: → no claim first → reader guesses the point → evidence read the wrong way → commentary explains an unseen link
cards.n: 'It confuses the reader' is the vague version; say why: evidence alone does not reveal which claim it supports.
o: A paragraph that states its claim first tells the reader what to look for in the evidence, so the commentary confirms rather than surprises.
Opening with evidence can work in narration, but in an argument's body paragraph it delays the claim the evidence exists to support.

w.a: Opening with evidence is always wrong because the rules say topic sentences go first.
w.why: a formula, not the reason; the risk is misread evidence

w.a: Starting with a quotation is the best hook for a body paragraph.
w.why: hooking the reader is not a body paragraph's job

cards.q: Explain the risk of devoting too much space to a counterargument in a body paragraph.
cards.a: If the objection gets more detail and more vivid evidence than the reply, the paragraph ends up making the other side's case better than the writer's. Readers remember the fuller argument, so the counterargument should be stated fairly and briefly, then answered at greater length.
cards.h: → objection outweighs the reply → the opposing case is the stronger one on the page → the reader leaves unconvinced
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.AA to AC. 'Counterarguments should be short' is a rule without a reason; the risk is that the objection outweighs the answer.
o: A paragraph's weight signals its claim, so a paragraph mostly about the objection seems to argue for it.
Fairness means stating the objection accurately, not developing it fully; the full development belongs to the reply.

w.a: A long counterargument shows the writer is fair, so it always helps.
w.why: fairness does not require making the other side's case stronger

w.a: Writers should leave out counterarguments because they help the other side.
w.why: answering objections builds credibility (CLE-1.AA)

cards.q: Explain how engaging a strong counterargument, rather than a weak one, can earn the Row C sophistication point.
cards.a: Row C rewards a nuanced argument that explores complexities or tensions, and the opposition's strongest point is where the real tension lies. Answering it fully shows the claim has been tested against real resistance; refuting a weak or straw version shows nothing the reader did not already accept.
cards.h: → Row C rewards exploring tensions → the strongest objection is the real tension → answering it shows tested reasoning
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.AA and the Row C rubric. Mentioning a strong objection once and moving on is the trap: the complexity must be sustained.
o: Engaging the best opposing case also marks the argument's limits, and articulating limitations is another route the rubric names.
A reader who holds the strong objection will not be moved by a reply to a weaker one.

w.a: Any counterargument earns the sophistication point.
w.why: Row C needs complexity explored consistently, not a mention

w.a: Refuting an easy objection is safer because the writer can win it.
w.why: a straw objection shows no tested reasoning

cards.q: Define coherence in writing.
cards.a: Coherence is the logical linking of ideas that lets readers follow the movement of thought. REO-1.N places it at three levels: in a sentence, the idea in one clause links to the next; in a paragraph, one sentence's idea links to the next; in a text, one paragraph's ideas link to the next. Transitions, repeated terms, pronoun reference, and consistent order help create it.
cards.h: → definition + the three levels
cards.n: Equating coherence with 'flow' or smooth-sounding prose is the trap; it is about logical links between ideas, testable at each level.

cards.q: Define unity in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence in a paragraph supports the single claim its topic sentence states; nothing wanders into a different claim. Unity concerns what belongs in the paragraph; coherence concerns how its sentences link.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + how it differs from coherence
cards.n: Keeping a strong sentence that proves a different point is the usual cause of lost unity; if it argues another claim, it belongs elsewhere.

cards.q: Contrast unity and coherence in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence supports the one claim in the topic sentence, with nothing off-topic; coherence means each sentence's idea links logically to the next, so the claim's development can be followed. A paragraph can be unified yet incoherent (all on topic, but jumping without links) or coherent yet disunified (smoothly linked, but drifting to a new claim).
cards.h: → belongs vs connects + one can exist without the other
cards.n: Treating them as synonyms is the trap: unity asks whether a sentence belongs; coherence asks whether it links to its neighbor.

cards.q: Contrast cohesion and coherence in writing.
cards.a: Cohesion is the local stitching between sentences (pronouns, repeated terms, transitions); coherence is the logical linking of ideas that makes the whole piece make sense and move toward its purpose. The CED speaks of coherence; cohesion is a common teaching term for the surface devices that support it.
cards.h: → surface devices vs logical links
cards.n: Cohesive devices can be present while the ideas still fail to link: 'however' and 'this' cannot create a coherence the ideas lack.

cards.q: Contrast global coherence and local coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Global coherence is whether the paragraphs link so the whole essay builds toward its thesis (REO-1.N's text level); local coherence is whether clauses and sentences within a paragraph link to one another (its sentence and paragraph levels). An essay can read smoothly sentence to sentence and still fail globally.
cards.h: → text level vs sentence and paragraph levels
cards.n: Fixing only sentence-level transitions is the trap when the paragraphs themselves do not build; global problems need reordering, not connectives.

cards.q:
Identify the level (sentence, paragraph, or text) at which coherence breaks in each case, and name the missing link (all invented):
1. 'The bridge passed its inspection, so the county has closed it for repairs.'
2. A paragraph arguing that bike lanes cut accidents ends: 'Bike lanes are also popular in Europe.'
3. An essay's second paragraph argues that the park is underused; its third, with no bridge, argues that the town's water rates are too high.
4. 'Enrollment in the night program doubled. As a result, the college cut the program's budget.'
5. 'The pantry serves 300 families a week. Its lease ends in March. Volunteers have kept it open for eleven years.'
cards.a:
1 → sentence: 'so' makes the closing a result of passing inspection, which contradicts it; 'but' or 'although' links the clauses
2 → paragraph: the last sentence shifts from safety to popularity, so it does not link to the sentences before it
3 → text: nothing links the two paragraphs' claims; a bridge must show how both serve the thesis, or one does not belong
4 → paragraph: 'As a result' claims the doubling caused the cut, a link the ideas do not support
5 → paragraph: each sentence is a fact, but none links to the next; the paragraph needs the claim that joins them (a pantry this relied on is about to lose its home)
cards.h: → level + the missing link, one per line
cards.n: Item 4 has a transition and still breaks coherence: a connective that asserts a false relationship is worse than none.

cards.q: Write the opening sentence of paragraph 3 so that it links logically to paragraph 2 in an invented essay arguing that the town should keep its east-side library branch open. Paragraph 2 argues that the branch is the only free internet access for many east-side families. Paragraph 3 argues that the branch's after-school program keeps children safe while their parents work.
cards.a: Model: 'Internet access is not the only thing east-side families would lose; for parents who work until six, the branch is also where their children spend the hours between the last bell and the ride home.' It carries paragraph 2's idea forward (what families would lose) and turns to paragraph 3's claim, so the two paragraphs read as steps in one argument.
cards.h: → one sentence: carry the last idea + state the new claim
cards.n: 'Another reason is the after-school program' adds a paragraph without linking ideas; say how the new claim relates to the last one.

cards.q: Explain why an essay can be coherent within every paragraph and still incoherent as a whole.
cards.a: REO-1.N places coherence at three levels. Sentences can link neatly inside each paragraph while the paragraphs' ideas do not link to one another, so each part reads smoothly but the text never builds a line of reasoning, and readers finish unsure how the parts add up.
cards.h: → coherence has three levels → local links don't guarantee paragraph-to-paragraph links → the whole fails to build
cards.n: Adding 'furthermore' between paragraphs is the trap: a connective cannot supply the missing relationship between two paragraphs' ideas.
o: Coherence between paragraphs depends on how their claims relate, and if those claims do not relate, no internal polish links them.
Readers judge an argument by how its main claims connect, which is coherence at the level of the whole text.

w.a: If every paragraph is well written, the essay is coherent.
w.why: coherence at the text level is separate from paragraph polish

w.a: Coherence only matters inside sentences.
w.why: REO-1.N names three levels, including the whole text

cards.q: Explain why reordering sentences can repair a paragraph's coherence without adding any new words.
cards.a: Coherence depends on each idea linking logically to the next. When a claim sits between its pieces of evidence, or an effect comes before its cause, the links exist but are out of sequence; putting sentences in the order the reasoning runs lets each follow from the one before, so the links show without new connectives.
cards.h: → coherence = each idea links to the next → wrong order hides the links → the right order reveals them
cards.n: Adding transitions to a scrambled paragraph is the trap; the words then signal links the sequence does not show.
o: Order is itself a signal: readers assume a sentence relates to the one before it, so the sequence tells them what relates to what.
Reordering often shows that a sentence belongs in a different paragraph, which repairs unity as well.

w.a: Only transition words can make a paragraph coherent.
w.why: order and repeated terms also create links

w.a: The order of sentences does not matter if each sentence is clear.
w.why: clear sentences in the wrong order still fail to link

cards.q: Define pronoun reference as a coherence device and its main risk.
cards.a: Pronoun reference uses words such as it, this, they, and these to point back to an idea already named, linking sentences without repeating the noun and showing that the new sentence develops the same idea. Its main risk is an unclear antecedent, which leaves readers guessing what the pronoun refers to.
cards.h: → how it links + its main risk
cards.n: A 'this' with no noun after it is the riskiest case; adding one word ('this delay') repairs most vague references.

cards.q: Define key-term repetition as a coherence device.
cards.a: Key-term repetition deliberately repeats the thesis's central word or phrase across topic sentences and transitions, so readers track one idea as it develops. It indicates the relationship among paragraphs: each is another step in arguing about the same term.
cards.h: → definition + the relationship it shows
cards.n: Swapping in a new synonym each time 'for variety' is the trap when the term is the argument's focus; readers may think a new idea has started.

cards.q: Define a transitional echo as a coherence device.
cards.a: A transitional echo repeats a key word or idea from the end of one paragraph at the start of the next ('...a cost the town cannot afford. That cost is not only financial.'), so the link between them is explicit. It is repetition working at the text level of coherence.
cards.h: → definition + where it works
cards.n: An echo that repeats the word but not the idea ('Cost is also important') links by sound only; carry the idea forward too.

cards.q: Identify the coherence problem: an essay uses 'this' five times in one paragraph, each time pointing to a different idea from the sentence before.
cards.a: Vague pronoun reference: each 'this' could point to several ideas, so readers must guess and the links between sentences fail. Add a noun after each ('this shortage,' 'this vote') or repeat the key term, so each reference names the idea it develops.
cards.h: → named problem + the repair
cards.n: Replacing 'this' with 'it' does not help; the repair is naming the referent, which turns the pronoun back into a clear link.

cards.q: Identify the repetition, synonym, pronoun reference, and parallel structure in this passage, and explain what relationship each builds: 'The library lends books. It also lends laptops, hotspots, and hours of quiet. For the student with no desk at home, the library is a study hall; for the job seeker with no printer, it is an office; for the retiree with no one to talk to, it is a front porch. Close this refuge, and the town loses more than a building.' (an invented letter)
cards.a: Repetition: 'lends' and 'library' recur, stacking the library's uses on one subject. Synonym: 'refuge' renames the library and adds the idea of shelter. Pronoun reference: 'It' and 'it' point back to the library, keeping each sentence on one subject. Parallel structure: the three 'for the X with no Y, it is a Z' clauses present the uses as equal and cumulative, building toward 'more than a building.'
cards.h: → each device + the relationship it builds
cards.n: Naming the devices without the relationship each builds earns nothing; REO-1.O is about how they link ideas, not the labels.

cards.q: Write a revision of these three sentences that uses pronoun reference and a synonym to link them without repeating 'the stadium proposal' each time: 'The stadium proposal would cost 90 million dollars. The stadium proposal would displace forty businesses. The stadium proposal has not been studied by any independent economist.' (invented)
cards.a: Model: 'The stadium proposal would cost 90 million dollars. It would also displace forty businesses, yet this 90-million-dollar gamble has not been studied by a single independent economist.' 'It' points back to the proposal, and 'gamble' renames it with the writer's judgment, so the sentences read as one developing argument rather than three separate facts.
cards.h: → revised sentences with a pronoun + a renaming
cards.n: Replacing every repetition with 'it' is the trap; three 'it's in a row blur the referent, so mix a pronoun with a renaming synonym.

cards.q: Decide which topic sentence better develops the relationship between paragraphs in an essay whose thesis is that 'food access,' not food supply, is the county's problem, and explain why. The previous paragraph ended: '...the county grows more vegetables than it eats.' (A) 'The real problem, then, is access: the vegetables are here, but the people who need them cannot reach them.' (B) 'Another issue is that some people have trouble with groceries.' (invented)
cards.a: (A). It repeats the thesis's key term, 'access,' and echoes the previous paragraph ('the vegetables are here'), so readers see the new paragraph developing the same argument. (B) drifts into vague wording ('another issue,' 'trouble with groceries') that neither repeats the key term nor links to the last paragraph.
cards.h: → letter + which devices link it
cards.n: Picking (B) as more varied misses the point: at a paragraph's opening, repeating the key term is what shows the relationship.

cards.q: Explain how parallel sentence structure across paragraphs can build coherence in an essay.
cards.a: Repeating a grammatical pattern at each paragraph's opening ('The plan fails the students... The plan fails the teachers... The plan fails the town...') tells readers the paragraphs do comparable work, so the relationship among parts is visible, and a break in the pattern signals a turn in the reasoning.
cards.h: → repeated pattern → paragraphs read as parallel steps → relationship visible; a break in pattern signals a turn
cards.n: Parallelism across unequal ideas is the trap: the pattern claims the paragraphs are equal, so it misleads if one is really a concession.
o: Parallel openings let readers predict the structure, so their attention goes to the evidence instead of the organization.
The repeated frame works like a repeated key term, reminding readers of the thesis each paragraph serves.

w.a: Parallel structure is mainly for making writing sound nice.
w.why: it signals a relationship among parts, not only rhythm

w.a: Every paragraph in every essay should open with the same pattern.
w.why: it misleads when the paragraphs do unequal work

cards.q: Explain why a writer might deliberately repeat a key term instead of varying it with synonyms.
cards.a: In an argument, a new word can suggest a new idea. Repeating the key term (access, access, access) tells readers each sentence develops the same concept, while a synonym may blur whether the writer means the same thing, especially when the term's meaning is itself in dispute.
cards.h: → a new word may signal a new idea → repetition holds the concept steady → the relationship stays clear
cards.n: 'Repetition is bad style' is the trap; in argument, deliberate repetition is a coherence device REO-1.O names.
o: When the writer has defined a term, a synonym can slip in a looser meaning, so repetition keeps the definition in force.
Repetition at paragraph openings shows readers that each paragraph advances the same thesis.

w.a: Writers repeat words because they do not know enough synonyms.
w.why: the repetition is a deliberate link

w.a: Using synonyms is always better because it avoids boring the reader.
w.why: a synonym can suggest a different idea

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal contrast and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Contrast: however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand, conversely. They tell the reader that what follows opposes or turns against what came before, so the reasoning is changing direction.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: 'However' between two sentences that agree is the classic misuse; check that the ideas actually oppose before using it.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal causation and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Causation: therefore, consequently, thus, as a result, because. They tell the reader that what follows is the cause or the result of what came before, a logical relationship rather than mere sequence.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: 'Therefore' after a claim the paragraph has not supported asserts a conclusion the reasoning never earned; the word cannot supply the proof.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal concession and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Concession: admittedly, granted, of course, to be sure, while it is true that. They tell the reader that what follows grants a point to the other side, which sets up a turn back to the writer's claim.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: A concession with no turn after it ('Admittedly, the plan is costly.' and nothing more) reads as agreement; the reader waits for the 'but.'

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal sequence and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Sequence: first, next, subsequently, meanwhile, finally. They tell the reader that what follows comes next in an order of steps, stages, or time.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: 'First, second, third' shows order without showing connection; sequence words can hide the absence of a line of reasoning.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal conclusion and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Conclusion: in short, ultimately, on the whole, in sum, therefore. They tell the reader that what follows draws the argument together or states what it adds up to.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: 'In conclusion' announces an ending without doing anything; the transition should introduce what the reasoning has earned.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal condition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Condition: if, unless, provided that, as long as, in the event that. They tell the reader that what follows holds only under a stated circumstance, narrowing the claim to where it can be defended.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: Reading a conditional as a weak hedge is the trap: 'if' limits a claim's scope on purpose, which can make it stronger, not weaker.

cards.q: Explain the most common misuse of transitions.
cards.a: Using a transition whose relationship the ideas do not have: 'however' between agreeing sentences, 'therefore' where no cause was shown, 'for example' before something that is not an instance. The word promises a logical link the paragraph never delivers, which breaks coherence more than no transition would.
cards.h: → the misuse + why it breaks coherence
cards.n: Scattering transitions to 'improve flow' is the trap; writing questions reward the connective that matches the actual relationship.

cards.q: Explain the difference between macro transitions and micro transitions.
cards.a: Macro transitions link paragraphs or sections, often through a whole sentence or clause that shows how one paragraph's claim relates to the last; micro transitions link sentences within a paragraph, often through a word or phrase. REO-1.P covers both: transitional elements can be words, phrases, clauses, sentences, or whole paragraphs.
cards.h: → two levels + what each links
cards.n: Opening a paragraph with a lone 'However,' is the common macro failure: it never says what the new claim contrasts with.

cards.q: Contrast a coordinating conjunction and a conjunctive adverb as transitional tools.
cards.a: A coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses with a comma before it; a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover) cannot join them with a comma alone: it needs a semicolon before it, usually with a comma after, or it begins a new sentence. Both show relationships; they are punctuated differently.
cards.h: → two tools + how each joins clauses
cards.n: Borrows STL-1.N. 'The plan is costly, however it works' is a comma splice; writing questions test exactly this.

cards.q: Identify the turn word doing the work in: 'Critics are right that the program is costly. Yet the cost of inaction is far higher.'
cards.a: 'Yet.' It marks the pivot from conceding the critics' point (the program is costly) to answering it (inaction costs more), signaling that the second sentence reframes the first rather than denying it.
cards.h: → the word + the turn it marks
cards.n: Answering 'are right' misses the turn: that phrase grants the point, and 'Yet' is what turns the passage back to the writer's claim.

cards.q: Identify the transitional element in this passage that is a whole sentence, and explain the relationship it shows: '...Fares have risen three times in four years, and ridership has fallen each time. So far, the case against the fare increase has been about riders. But the drivers have a stake too. Since 2022 the transit agency has cut 40 driver positions, and those who remain work longer routes.' (an invented op-ed)
cards.a: 'So far, the case against the fare increase has been about riders.' It sums up the preceding section and, with the next sentence ('But the drivers have a stake too'), turns the argument to a new group, showing that what follows adds a second line of evidence for the same claim. Transitional elements can be whole sentences, not only single words.
cards.h: → the sentence + the relationship it shows
cards.n: Pointing only to 'But' misses the task: REO-1.P says phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs can be transitional elements.

cards.q: Explain why the choice of transition changes the argument a reader perceives, not just its flow.
cards.a: A transition states a logical relationship: 'therefore' makes the next idea a consequence, 'however' an opposition, 'for example' an instance. Swapping one for another changes what the writer claims about how the ideas relate, so the choice is part of the reasoning, not decoration.
cards.h: → each transition asserts a relationship → a different word asserts a different logic → the reasoning changes
cards.n: Calling transitions 'words that help the essay flow' is the trap; each one makes a claim about how two ideas relate.
o: Readers interpret a sentence through the transition before it, so the word decides how the evidence is read.
Writing questions ask for the transition that fits the relationship because the wrong one misstates the argument.

w.a: Any transition works as long as the sentences sound smooth.
w.why: each transition asserts a specific relationship

w.a: Transitions are optional because readers can work out the logic.
w.why: the transition tells readers which logic the writer intends

cards.q: Explain why a whole transitional paragraph can be worth its space in a long argument.
cards.a: At a major turn (from problem to solution, or from the writer's case to the objections), a single word cannot show how the sections relate. A short transitional paragraph can sum up what has been established and preview what comes next, keeping readers oriented across sections.
cards.h: → a major turn between sections → a word is too small → a brief paragraph sums up + previews → readers stay oriented
cards.n: A transitional paragraph that only repeats the introduction is the trap; it must say how the section just ended relates to the next.
o: REO-1.P names paragraphs among transitional elements, recognizing that coherence between sections can need more than a word.
Summing up before a turn reminds readers what has been proved, so the next section builds on it.

w.a: Transitional paragraphs just pad the essay.
w.why: they show the relationship between major sections

w.a: Every paragraph should simply begin with a transition word instead.
w.why: a word cannot sum up a section's reasoning

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal addition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Addition: furthermore, moreover, in addition, also. They tell the reader that what follows adds another piece of evidence or another reason of the same kind, supporting the same claim.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: Stacking 'furthermore' and 'moreover' makes a list look like reasoning; addition shows more evidence, not how the evidence builds.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal exemplification and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Exemplification: for example, for instance, specifically, to illustrate, namely. They introduce evidence, telling the reader that what follows is a specific instance of the general claim just made.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: 'For example' before something that is not an instance of the claim is worse than no transition: it promises a fit the evidence lacks.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal emphasis and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Emphasis: indeed, above all, in fact, most important. They tell the reader that what follows is the weightiest point or evidence so far, ranking it against what came before.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: These make a claim about rank, so using one on every point flattens the very hierarchy they exist to create.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal comparison and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Comparison: similarly, likewise, in the same way, by the same token. They tell the reader that the evidence that follows is alike in kind to evidence already given, so the two support the claim together.
cards.h: → sample words + relationship
cards.n: Confusing comparison with addition is the trap: 'likewise' asserts that two things are alike; 'also' only adds another item.

cards.q: Define an attributive tag (signal phrase) and give two examples.
cards.a: An attributive tag (signal phrase) introduces borrowed material and names its source, so readers know where the evidence comes from and how to weigh it: 'As economist Dana Ruiz notes,' or 'Source B counters that.' Its verb also indicates the evidence's relationship to other ideas: 'concedes,' 'claims,' and 'demonstrates' position a source differently.
cards.h: → definition + two examples + what the verb does
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.E. Using 'says' for every source is the trap: the tag's verb can show agreement, doubt, or concession, and a flat verb wastes it.

cards.q: Explain how to cite sources in-text on the synthesis essay.
cards.a: Name each source in a signal phrase or in parentheses, by its letter or by the description the packet gives: 'Chen argues that...' or '(Source C).' The CED allows either the letter or the description in parentheses, and a works cited list is not required. The citation is part of introducing the evidence: it tells readers whose voice they are hearing.
cards.h: → the two accepted forms + what citation does
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.N. Uncited source material leaves readers unable to tell your reasoning from the source's, which weakens the essay's evidence.

cards.q: Define a parenthetical citation used for a source identified only by letter in the AP Lang synthesis source set.
cards.a: A parenthetical such as (Source C) that identifies synthesis evidence by the letter the exam assigns (the six sources run A through F). The CED allows the letter or the source's description in parentheses, so it is the exam's shorthand for showing whose evidence you are introducing.
cards.h: → form + where the letter comes from
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.N. The letter alone is allowed but thin: a tag naming the source's type or author also tells readers how to weigh it.

cards.q: Explain how to cite a graph or chart source with no named author in an AP Lang synthesis essay.
cards.a: By its source label, (Source D), or by the description the packet gives, such as (county ridership chart), ideally introduced with a signal phrase that says what the graph shows: 'A county chart of ridership (Source D) shows...'
cards.h: → label or description + a signal phrase
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.N. Inventing an author or leaving the graph uncited are both traps; use the label or description the packet supplies.

cards.q: Explain how many sources the AP Lang synthesis essay requires and how to use them.
cards.a: At least three of the six sources, used as evidence for your own position: introduce each with a signal phrase or citation, quote, paraphrase, or summarize only what the claim needs, and use transitions and commentary to show how each relates to your reasoning and to the other sources. One source may appear in more than one paragraph.
cards.h: → the number + how to bring each in
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.P. Citing more than three earns nothing by itself; thin commentary on six sources scores below strong commentary on three.

cards.q: Explain how to integrate a quotation grammatically into your own sentence.
cards.a: Make the quotation part of your own sentence: introduce it with a signal phrase and a comma (As Ruiz writes, '...'), blend it in with 'that' and no comma (Ruiz argues that '...'), or weave short phrases into your own clause. The finished sentence must read grammatically with the quotation marks removed.
cards.h: → three ways to introduce a quotation
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.E. A quotation dropped in as its own sentence, with no introducing words, is the trap: nothing tells readers how it relates to the claim.

cards.q: Explain how to put two sources in conversation rather than listing them.
cards.a: Build the paragraph around your claim, then use transitional elements to show how the sources relate: one extends, complicates, or answers the other ('While Source A treats cost as decisive, Source D shows the cost falls unevenly'). Then explain what that relationship proves. The paragraph is organized by idea, not by source.
cards.h: → claim first + a transition naming the relationship
cards.n: Two back-to-back summaries joined by 'Also,' is the trap; the transition must name the relationship between the sources.

cards.q: Explain how to put a statistic from a graph source into conversation with a claim from a prose source in the same paragraph.
cards.a: State the prose source's claim, then introduce the graph's figure with a transition that names the relationship ('The county's own data confirm this:' or 'Yet the chart complicates that claim:'), and explain what the pairing shows. The two sources then visibly respond to each other within one line of reasoning.
cards.h: → claim + relational transition + the figure + commentary
cards.n: Putting the chart and the prose source in separate paragraphs is the trap; the relationship shows only when a transition joins them.

cards.q: Explain when and how to use an ellipsis in a quotation.
cards.a: Use an ellipsis (three spaced periods) to cut words from the middle of a quotation so only the words your claim needs remain, and only when the cut does not change the source's meaning. A short phrase woven into your own sentence usually needs none at its start or end. Trimming this way lets the evidence arrive inside your sentence, ready for commentary.
cards.h: → what it marks + the one rule + why trim
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.E. Cutting a qualifier ('may,' 'in some districts') with an ellipsis changes the claim and misrepresents the evidence.

cards.q: Explain when to use square brackets inside a quotation.
cards.a: Use square brackets to insert or change words so a quotation fits your sentence or makes sense out of context: naming a pronoun's referent ('it [the tariff] failed'), adjusting a verb's tense, or changing a letter's capitalization. The brackets tell readers those words are yours, so the evidence reads smoothly without misquoting the source.
cards.h: → purpose + three typical changes
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.E. Brackets may change the fit of a quotation, never its meaning; a bracketed word that alters the source's claim misquotes it.

cards.q: Explain why citing a source by letter alone, with no attributive tag, is weaker than naming what the source is.
cards.a: '(Source B)' identifies the evidence but says nothing about its kind or credibility; a tag such as 'a 2021 county health report (Source B) found' introduces the evidence and signals how much weight it deserves, so readers can judge it as they read.
cards.h: → a letter only identifies → a tag adds type and credibility → the reader weighs the evidence while reading
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.Q. The letter alone is acceptable citation; the trap is thinking citing a source and introducing it are the same job.
o: A tag lets the writer set sources against each other ('an industry group... a university study...'), which shows relationships among evidence.
Naming the source's type prepares commentary about its reliability, which the CED ties to strong arguments (CLE-1.S).

w.a: Citing by letter alone is wrong and loses points.
w.why: the CED allows citation by letter; it is weaker, not wrong

w.a: Naming the source only matters when the author is famous.
w.why: type and credibility matter whatever the fame

cards.q: Explain why a transition that introduces evidence should signal the evidence's relationship to the claim, not just its arrival.
cards.a: 'Another quote is' tells readers only that evidence is coming. 'The clearest proof comes from the county's own audit' or 'Even the plan's supporters concede' tells them what the evidence will do: confirm, rank, or complicate. Readers then weigh it as the writer intends before the commentary begins.
cards.h: → bare arrival tells nothing → a relational lead-in says confirm, rank, or complicate → evidence read as intended
cards.n: 'Here is a quote that shows this' announces evidence without relating it; REO-1.Q asks the transition to indicate the relationship.
o: A lead-in that names the relationship starts the commentary early, so the evidence arrives already connected to the claim.
When sources disagree, a lead-in such as 'Source C disputes this' shows readers the conversation the paragraph is building.

w.a: Any lead-in is fine as long as the quotation is cited.
w.why: citation identifies the source; it does not relate the evidence

w.a: Transitions before evidence are unnecessary if the commentary is good.
w.why: the lead-in frames how the evidence is read

cards.q: Explain why a chart, photograph, or cartoon in a synthesis source set counts as a citable source.
cards.a: Every lettered source is evidence the essay may use, whatever its form, and a visual makes its case through data or images instead of sentences. CLE-1.N extends acknowledgment to images, so a visual used as evidence must be introduced and cited like prose, and it counts toward the three-source minimum.
cards.h: → each lettered source is evidence → a visual argues through data or image → introduce and cite it → it counts
cards.n: Borrows CLE-1.N. Using a chart's figure with no '(Source D)' leaves the evidence unattributed, and it adds nothing toward the three sources.
o: The exam builds two visual sources into every set, so the task assumes they may be used and cited like the rest.
A chart's numbers and a photograph's framing are someone else's work and choices, so citing them credits the source and tells readers how to weigh it.

w.a: Only the prose sources count, because a chart has no argument to cite.
w.why: a visual presents evidence and often a stance

w.a: A cartoon can be mentioned but not cited, since it has no author or page number.
w.why: the exam allows citing by letter or by description

cards.q: Define denotation.
cards.a: Denotation is a word's literal, dictionary meaning, apart from the feelings or associations it carries. The CED's point is that every word has both a denotative and a connotative meaning: 'house' and 'home' share a denotation (a dwelling) but differ in what they suggest.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + a shared-denotation pair
cards.n: Calling denotation 'the neutral word a writer should use' misses the point: analysis lives in connotation; denotation matters when a writer insists on a literal sense.

cards.q: Contrast denotation and connotation.
cards.a: Denotation is what a word literally means; connotation is what it suggests, the positive, negative, or other associations it carries.
