cards.a: Antimetabole: the same words ('company,' 'workers,' 'choose') return in reversed order (ABBA) across two balanced clauses. The reversal carries the point, flipping who holds the power, and the mirrored shape makes the line memorable.
cards.h: → device + the reversed words + effect
cards.n: Antimetabole is a kind of chiasmus, so 'chiasmus' is not wrong, only less precise. Neither name is a CED term; the reversal's effect earns credit.

cards.q: Identify the device in Kennedy's inaugural: 'Ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: Antimetabole: the same words return in reversed order ('your country... you,' then 'you... your country'), a chiasmus that also works as antithesis between receiving and giving. The mirrored halves make the reversal of duty feel inevitable, and highly quotable.
cards.h: → device + the reversal + what it asks of the audience
cards.n: Naming antimetabole rather than the broader chiasmus shows you see the exact structure, but the credit comes from what the reversal asks of the audience.

cards.q: Contrast the two devices at work in Kennedy's line 'ask not what your country can do for you - ask what you can do for your country.'
cards.a: Antithesis sets two opposed ideas side by side (what the country gives versus what the citizen gives); chiasmus, here antimetabole, reverses the order of the same words ('country... you,' 'you... country'). The antithesis supplies the contrast in meaning; the reversal supplies the mirrored shape that makes the contrast memorable.
cards.h: → what each device contributes to the line
cards.n: A single line can carry two devices at once: the contrast lies in the ideas and the reversal in the word order, so say what each contributes.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might present two competing goals in a compound sentence joined by 'and' rather than subordinating one of them.
cards.a: Coordination puts both goals in independent clauses of equal rank, illustrating balance: neither goal outweighs the other. Subordinating one ('Although safety matters, cost...') would rank it as background, taking a side the writer may want readers to see as a genuine tradeoff.
cards.h: → coordination = equal rank → both goals weigh the same → the tradeoff stays open; subordination would rank them
cards.n: 'To make the sentence flow' earns nothing; tie coordination to the equality between ideas the writer intends.
o: Keeping both goals equal can hold an audience split between the two values, since neither group sees its concern demoted.

w.a: The writer uses 'and' because it is the simplest conjunction.
w.why: simplicity is not the reason; equality is

w.a: Coordination shows the writer thinks the two goals are the same thing.
w.why: equal weight is not identity

cards.q: Explain why parallel structure in a series makes a writer's items seem equally important.
cards.a: When each item takes the same grammatical form, readers process the items as members of one class, and none is marked as primary or secondary. The matching form becomes a signal of matching weight, so the structure itself argues that the items deserve equal attention.
cards.h: → same form for each item → read as one class → none ranked above the rest → equal importance
cards.n: 'Parallelism makes writing sound good' names a side effect; the credited point is what the matched form tells readers about the ideas.
o: A break in parallelism draws the eye to the odd item, which is why writers who want balance keep every item in the same form.

w.a: Parallel structure means the items are listed in order of importance.
w.why: order can rank; matched form signals equality

w.a: Writers use parallelism to make their sentences longer.
w.why: length is not the effect

cards.q: Define subordination and give an example.
cards.a: Subordination places one idea in a dependent clause so that it supports, rather than competes with, the idea in the main clause. Example: 'Because the data were incomplete, the panel withheld judgment.' Writers frequently use it to illustrate an imbalance or inequality between ideas: the main clause is the point, the dependent clause its condition.
cards.h: → definition + example + the imbalance it creates
cards.n: Subordinated does not mean unimportant; it means ranked as background (cause, condition, concession) to the claim in the main clause.

cards.q: Apply subordination to this pair to emphasize the job loss: 'The town lost its factory. Three hundred jobs disappeared overnight.'
cards.a: 'When the town lost its factory, three hundred jobs disappeared overnight.' The closing moves into a dependent clause as background, and the job loss takes the independent clause, where the sentence's main assertion and emphasis fall.
cards.h: → one combined sentence + where the emphasis falls
cards.n: Subordinating the wrong idea ('When three hundred jobs disappeared, the town lost its factory') reverses the emphasis and garbles the sequence.

cards.q: Identify which idea the writer treats as more important in this sentence from an invented mayor's statement, and explain how the grammar shows it: 'While some residents have raised concerns about noise, the new rail line will cut commute times in half.'
cards.a: The commute savings. 'While' places the residents' noise concerns in a dependent clause, acknowledging them as background, and the independent clause carries the benefit as the main assertion, so the grammar ranks the benefit above the complaint.
cards.h: → the main idea + the subordinator + the ranking
cards.n: 'The mayor addresses both sides' misses the imbalance: the concession is real but grammatically demoted.

cards.q: Decide which version better serves a writer who wants to stress the danger of a road rather than the cost of fixing it, and explain why. (A) 'Although repaving Route 9 will cost two million dollars, the road has had eleven serious crashes this year.' (B) 'Although Route 9 has had eleven serious crashes this year, repaving it will cost two million dollars.'
cards.a: (A). The cost sits in the 'although' clause as a conceded detail, and the crash count takes the independent clause, where the emphasis falls. (B) subordinates the crashes and makes the price the main assertion, which would suit a writer arguing that the repair costs too much.
cards.h: → choice + where each idea sits
cards.n: Both versions hold the same facts; only the grammar ranks them. Choosing by content rather than by which idea is subordinated misses the point.

cards.q: Write a sentence for an invented op-ed that concedes the opposing view in a subordinate clause and places the writer's claim in the main clause, using these ideas: 'The new phone policy is unpopular with students.' 'Focus in class has improved.'
cards.a: Model: 'Although the new phone policy is unpopular with students, focus in class has clearly improved.' The concession, the policy's unpopularity, is acknowledged in the 'although' clause but ranked beneath the writer's claim, which takes the independent clause and the sentence's emphasis.
cards.h: → one sentence + which clause holds which idea
cards.n: Reversing the clauses ('Although focus has improved, students dislike the policy') hands the emphasis to the opposing view.

cards.q: Identify the problem with the emphasis in this sentence from an invented news brief, and write a revision that fixes it: 'The mayor was finishing her speech when the stage collapsed.'
cards.a: The main event, the stage's collapse, is buried in the dependent 'when' clause, while the routine detail (finishing the speech) holds the independent clause, so the grammar ranks the minor above the major. Revision: 'As the mayor was finishing her speech, the stage collapsed,' which gives the collapse the main assertion.
cards.h: → what is subordinated wrongly + a revision
cards.n: In a story the trailing 'when' clause can be a deliberate surprise; in a news brief it buries the event readers most need.

cards.q: Explain why a writer often subordinates the less important of two ideas rather than presenting them as separate sentences.
cards.a: Subordinating the lesser idea tells readers which point is secondary, so the sentence argues for a hierarchy of importance instead of listing facts as equals. Two separate simple sentences give each idea the same weight and leave readers to guess what matters.
cards.h: → lesser idea in a dependent clause → it becomes background → the main clause holds the point → hierarchy is clear
cards.n: A string of equal simple sentences can be flawless and still unpersuasive, because it never tells readers what matters most.
o: Subordination also names the relationship ('because,' 'although'), which separate sentences leave for readers to infer.

w.a: Subordinating ideas makes the writing sound more sophisticated.
w.why: about sound, not the relationship between ideas

w.a: Separate sentences are always clearer, so subordination is only a style preference.
w.why: ignores the ranking subordination supplies

cards.q: Explain why a writer conceding a point often places the concession in an 'although' clause.
cards.a: The 'although' clause acknowledges the opposing point, which shows fairness, while subordinating it: the concession becomes background and the writer's claim takes the independent clause. The imbalance lets the writer grant the point without granting it equal weight.
cards.h: → 'although' clause grants the point → it is subordinated → claim holds the main clause → imbalance favors the writer
cards.n: Borrows concession from Claims and Evidence. 'Although shows contrast' is too thin; name the ranking: conceded idea subordinate, claim dominant.
o: Readers who hold the opposing view hear it acknowledged first, so they are likelier to keep reading into the writer's claim.

w.a: The writer puts the concession in an 'although' clause to show both sides are equally valid.
w.why: subordination ranks them unequally

w.a: 'Although' is used because it is a transition word that starts sentences.
w.why: a label, not the effect

cards.q: Define anaphora and give an example.
cards.a: Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences. Example: 'Every child deserves a safe school. Every child deserves a full meal. Every child deserves a teacher who knows her name.' Placing the repeated words first makes them the frame for each clause, building rhythm and momentum around the idea they carry.
cards.h: → definition + example + what the position does
cards.n: Naming anaphora earns nothing by itself; say what the repeated opening builds toward and why that emphasis serves the purpose.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We will rebuild after the flood. We will rebuild after the fire. We will rebuild after every disaster.'
cards.a: Anaphora: 'We will rebuild' begins each sentence. Because the repeated phrase holds the opening position while the disaster changes, the arrangement emphasizes the constant, the resolve to rebuild, and builds toward the widest case, 'every disaster.'
cards.h: → device + what stays fixed + what it builds to
cards.n: Anaphora is easy to spot and easy to under-analyze; commentary must name what stays fixed, what changes, and what the sequence builds to.

cards.q: Contrast anaphora and epistrophe by where the repeated words fall.
cards.a: Anaphora repeats words at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences; epistrophe repeats them at the end. Position sets the emphasis: anaphora puts the repeated idea up front as a frame that drives each clause forward, while epistrophe lands every clause on the same words, so the audience leaves holding them.
cards.h: → where each repeats + the emphasis each creates
cards.n: Some passages use both at once; trace where the repeated words physically fall before naming the device.
x: repetition at the start vs. the end

cards.q: Define periodic sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A periodic sentence withholds its main clause until the end, after introductory phrases or clauses. Example: 'Despite the rain, the delays, and the cold that cut through every coat, we marched.' The arrangement creates suspense and lands the main idea with force in the final position.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect of the delay
cards.n: 'Periodic' has nothing to do with periods or time; it names the delayed main clause. Say what the delay makes the reader wait for.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'After the vote failed, after the funding dried up, after the last volunteer quit, the clinic finally closed.'
cards.a: A periodic sentence: the main clause, 'the clinic finally closed,' is withheld until the end, after three parallel 'after' clauses. The delay piles up the losses so that the closing lands as their inevitable result, emphasizing the finality of 'finally closed.'
cards.h: → sentence type + the withheld clause + its effect
cards.n: Periodic sentences are less common, so finding one usually signals that the withheld clause carries the weight; say what the delay builds.

cards.q: Define loose (cumulative) sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A loose (cumulative) sentence states its main clause first and then adds modifying phrases. Example: 'We marched, soaked to the skin, exhausted, still singing.' The arrangement gives immediate clarity, then enriches the idea detail by detail, often ending on the most telling one.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect
cards.n: Loose is not a criticism; the cumulative sentence is the English default, and its effect comes from what the added details build to.

cards.q: Identify the sentence type: 'The clinic closed, its doors locked, its equipment sold, its patients scattered to clinics an hour away.'
cards.a: A loose (cumulative) sentence: the main clause, 'The clinic closed,' comes first, and three modifying phrases pile up after it. The arrangement states the fact plainly, then lets the consequences accumulate, ending on the human cost, patients scattered an hour away.
cards.h: → sentence type + the order + its effect
cards.n: Identifying the type earns nothing without the effect; here the order moves from the event to its widening consequences.

cards.q: Define passive voice and give an example.
cards.a: In the passive voice the grammatical subject receives the action, and the actor appears in a 'by' phrase or disappears. Example: 'The proposal was rejected (by the board).' The arrangement puts the thing acted upon first, emphasizing it, and can erase the actor altogether.
cards.h: → definition + example + what the arrangement does
cards.n: Passive is not past tense and not 'weak writing' by definition; the test is whether the subject performs or receives the action.

cards.q: Identify the voice and its likely rhetorical purpose: 'Mistakes were made in the handling of the funds.'
cards.a: Passive voice. The sentence names the mistakes but not who made them, so it admits a problem while avoiding blame for any specific actor, a common evasive use of the passive. The active version, 'The treasurer mishandled the funds,' would put the responsible person first.
cards.h: → voice + who disappears + the purpose
cards.n: 'Passive voice is bad writing' earns nothing; ask who disappears from the sentence and who benefits from the disappearance.

cards.q: Write a periodic version of this loose sentence from an invented speech so that the main clause lands last, and explain what the new arrangement emphasizes: 'The levee held, despite three days of rain, a river two feet above flood stage, and a crew of only eleven volunteers.'
cards.a: Periodic version: 'Despite three days of rain, a river two feet above flood stage, and a crew of only eleven volunteers, the levee held.' Now the obstacles build suspense and the main clause arrives last, emphasizing the levee's survival as a triumph; the loose original states the outcome first and lets the obstacles trail after it.
cards.h: → the rearranged sentence + what the final position stresses
cards.n: Changing the words instead of their order misses the task; the same clauses, rearranged, are what shift the emphasis.

cards.q: Define repetition as a rhetorical strategy and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition is the deliberate reuse of a word, phrase, or structure for emphasis. Example: 'Free at last, free at last, thank God Almighty, we are free at last' (King, 1963). Where the repeated words sit (at the opening, at the close, or back to back) determines what the repetition emphasizes.
cards.h: → definition + example + why position matters
cards.n: 'The writer repeats words for emphasis' restates the definition; say what idea the repetition fixes in the audience's mind and why that serves the purpose.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'This is a plan built by workers, tested by workers, and paid for by workers.'
cards.a: Epistrophe: 'by workers' repeats at the end of each successive phrase. Placing the repeated words last means every phrase lands on 'workers,' so the audience leaves holding the idea that the plan belongs to them.
cards.h: → device + where the repetition falls + effect
cards.n: Epistrophe stresses what the phrases share (here, workers); anaphora stresses what changes after the repeated opening.

cards.q: Identify the scheme in Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: 'we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate, we can not hallow this ground.'
cards.a: Anaphora: 'we can not' opens each of three parallel clauses, rising from 'dedicate' to 'consecrate' to 'hallow.' The repeated denial builds toward Lincoln's point that the soldiers have already consecrated the ground beyond anything the living can add.
cards.h: → device + what the repetition builds toward
cards.n: Lincoln uses the repetition to deflate the ceremony before turning to the unfinished work of the living; name that turn, not just the device.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.'
cards.a: Anaphora: 'we shall fight' opens each clause (Churchill, 1940). The repeated phrase holds still while the place changes, so the arrangement emphasizes a resolve that will not shift however the ground does.
cards.h: → device + what stays fixed + what changes
cards.n: Anaphora is easy to name; the credit comes from what stays fixed (the resolve) and what changes (the battleground).

cards.q: Contrast periodic and loose sentences by effect.
cards.a: A periodic sentence withholds its main clause until the end, building suspense and landing the main idea with force; a loose (cumulative) sentence gives the main clause first and adds detail after, sounding immediate and natural. The choice decides where the emphasis falls: on the delayed payoff or on the opening statement enriched by what follows.
cards.h: → each sentence type + where its emphasis falls
cards.n: Naming which one a writer chose, and what the delay or the immediacy does to the reader, is textbook Row B commentary.

cards.q: Define active voice and give an example.
cards.a: In the active voice the grammatical subject performs the action. Example: 'The board rejected the proposal.' Putting the actor first names who is responsible and keeps prose direct; the passive 'The proposal was rejected' moves the actor to a 'by' phrase or drops it.
cards.h: → definition + example + contrast with passive
cards.n: Active is not 'better' by rule; the question is whom the writer wants in the subject position and whether the actor should be seen.

cards.q: Explain when passive voice is a deliberate rhetorical choice rather than a flaw.
cards.a: Passive voice is deliberate when the actor is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant; when the receiver of the action deserves the emphasis ('The patient was stabilized'); when a neutral, institutional tone is wanted; or when the writer means to obscure responsibility ('mistakes were made').
cards.h: → passive puts the receiver first → shifts emphasis or hides the actor → chosen when that serves the purpose
cards.n: Do not call passive voice weak writing on the exam; ask who disappears from the sentence and who benefits.
o: A lab report says 'the samples were heated' because the procedure, not the person, is what readers need in order to repeat it.

w.a: Passive voice is always a mistake that makes writing wordy.
w.why: ignores cases where emphasis on the receiver is the point

w.a: Writers use passive voice because it sounds more formal and intelligent.
w.why: about sound, not emphasis or responsibility

cards.q: Explain why placing a key word at the end of a sentence can emphasize it.
cards.a: The end of a sentence is where the idea completes and the reader pauses, so attention peaks there. Arranging the sentence so the key word arrives last ('What the town lost was its trust') gives that word the final stress and makes it the idea that lingers.
cards.h: → the sentence builds toward its end → attention peaks at the close → the final word lingers → emphasis
cards.n: 'It is the last word, so readers remember it' is close but thin; explain that the arrangement builds toward the final position.
o: Speakers naturally stress the end of a sentence, so a written sentence that ends on the key word reads with the stress already in place.

w.a: Words at the end are emphasized because they come right before the period.
w.why: punctuation is not the cause; position after the build is

w.a: The first word of a sentence is always the most important, so ending on a key word hides it.
w.why: reverses how end position works

cards.q: Explain how the repeated opening in anaphora emphasizes an idea differently from stating the idea once.
cards.a: Stated once, an idea passes; repeated at the start of each clause, it becomes the frame through which every new detail is read, so readers meet it again as the details change. The cumulative rhythm turns a claim into a refrain the audience carries away.
cards.h: → same opening each clause → the idea frames every new detail → repetition builds rhythm → the idea becomes a refrain
cards.n: 'Repetition makes the point stronger' is too vague; say that the opening position makes the repeated idea frame each changing detail.
o: The changing ends of the clauses show the idea applying case after case, which argues its reach without stating it.

w.a: Anaphora is used so that readers will not forget what the writer said.
w.why: memory is part of it, but the framing emphasis is missing

w.a: The writer repeats the phrase because the writer had nothing new to say.
w.why: treats a deliberate scheme as padding

cards.q: State what grammar and mechanics that follow established conventions enable, according to the CED, and explain why that matters to an argument.
cards.a: They enable clear communication. Conventional grammar and mechanics let readers parse each sentence the way the writer intends, so their attention stays on the argument rather than on decoding it; errors that change meaning or force rereading cost clarity and, often, the writer's credibility.
cards.h: → the CED's claim + why it matters to readers
cards.n: 'Grammar makes writing correct' misses the CED's reason: conventions serve clear communication, and that is the standard exam items apply.

cards.q: Define a comma splice and give an example.
cards.a: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Example: 'The evidence was strong, the jury still hesitated.' Conventional fixes are a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction ('The evidence was strong, but the jury still hesitated'), and the conjunction also states the relationship.
cards.h: → definition + example + the conventional fixes
cards.n: In writing-set items the best fix usually expresses the relationship too; 'but' beats a bare period when the two ideas contrast.
x: two sentences joined by only a comma

cards.q: Contrast 'who' and 'whom' in formal usage.
cards.a: 'Who' is a subject pronoun, used when the pronoun performs the action ('the senator who wrote the letter'); 'whom' is an object pronoun, used when it receives the action or follows a preposition ('the voters whom she thanked,' 'to whom it may concern').
cards.h: → the role of each + an example of each
cards.n: Test it: if 'he' fits, use 'who'; if 'him' fits, use 'whom.' Rewording to avoid the choice is also acceptable.

cards.q: Explain the parallel structure error in 'The policy will reduce costs, improving morale, and it protects jobs.'
cards.a: The three items in the series should share one grammatical form, but the sentence mixes a verb ('reduce costs'), a participle ('improving morale'), and a full clause ('it protects jobs'). Corrected: 'The policy will reduce costs, improve morale, and protect jobs,' which lets the three benefits read as equals.
cards.h: → the mismatched forms + a corrected version
cards.n: Broken parallelism is easy to miss because each piece sounds fine alone; test each item after the shared words ('The policy will...').

cards.q: Identify the error in each sentence from an invented student letter to the school board, and explain how it obscures meaning: (1) 'Each of the new buses have broken heaters.' (2) 'When the board met with the teachers, they agreed to delay the vote.'
cards.a: (1) Subject-verb agreement: the subject 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has'; the plural 'have' follows the nearby noun 'buses.' (2) Unclear pronoun reference: 'they' could mean the board or the teachers, so readers cannot tell who agreed; revise to 'the board agreed' or 'the teachers agreed.'
cards.h: → the error + how it blurs meaning, per sentence
cards.n: Saying sentence 2 'sounds awkward' earns nothing; name the ambiguous pronoun and the two readings it allows.

cards.q:
Write a corrected version of each sentence, following established conventions. All sentences are invented:
1. The council approved the budget, the mayor vetoed it.
2. Neither the mayor nor the council members was present.
3. Its the district's responsibility to fix the roof.
4. The report, which was released Tuesday, show a rise in absences.
5. Between you and I, the plan is flawed.
6. The members of the committee disagrees about the proposal.
7. The board has three goals: raising scores, to hire teachers, and repairs to the gym.
8. The team lost it's final game.
9. Less students enrolled this year.
10. The principal, along with two teachers, are attending.
cards.a:
1 → 'The council approved the budget, but the mayor vetoed it.' (comma splice)
2 → '...nor the council members were present.' (after 'neither...nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject)
3 → 'It's the district's responsibility...' (it's = it is)
4 → '...released Tuesday, shows a rise...' (subject 'report')
5 → 'Between you and me...' (object of a preposition)
6 → '...the committee disagree about...' (subject 'members')
7 → '...raising scores, hiring teachers, and repairing the gym.' (parallelism)
8 → '...lost its final game.' (possessive 'its' has no apostrophe)
9 → 'Fewer students enrolled...' ('fewer' for things counted)
10 → '...along with two teachers, is attending.' (the 'along with' phrase does not change the subject)
cards.h: → one corrected sentence + the convention, per line
cards.n: Items 2 and 10 are the traps: after 'neither...nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, but an 'along with' phrase never changes the subject.

cards.q: Explain why subject-verb agreement errors increase when a long prepositional phrase sits between the subject and the verb.
cards.a: A writer's ear tends to match the verb to the noun nearest it rather than to the true subject, so in 'The list of items are long' the plural 'items' pulls the verb to 'are,' though the subject, 'list,' is singular and needs 'is.' The longer the phrase, the farther away the true subject sits.
cards.h: → a phrase separates subject and verb → the nearest noun pulls the verb → the true subject is lost → agreement error
cards.n: Cross out the prepositional phrase and reread; the sentence usually corrects itself once the intervening noun is gone.
o: The noun inside the phrase is the object of a preposition, so it can never be the subject, yet it sits exactly where the ear expects one.

w.a: Agreement errors happen because long sentences are harder to punctuate.
w.why: punctuation is not the cause

w.a: The verb should agree with whichever noun is closest to it.
w.why: states the error as if it were the rule

cards.q: Explain why an unclear pronoun reference can damage an argument more than a minor spelling error does.
cards.a: A spelling slip rarely changes what a sentence says, but an unclear pronoun can: in 'The board blamed the teachers because they ignored the budget,' readers cannot tell who ignored it, so the claim itself blurs. Conventions matter most where breaking them blocks clear communication.
cards.h: → a spelling slip keeps the meaning → an unclear pronoun splits it → the claim blurs → communication fails
cards.n: 'Both are just grammar mistakes' misses the CED's standard: conventions matter because they enable clear communication, and meaning-changing errors fail it.
o: Readers forced to reread a sentence to work out who did what lose track of the line of reasoning around it.

w.a: All grammar errors are equally bad, since every error breaks a rule.
w.why: treats all conventions alike; the CED ties them to clear communication

w.a: Spelling errors are worse because readers notice them more easily.
w.why: noticeability is not lost meaning

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the semicolon and give an example.
cards.a: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, or separates list items that already contain commas. Example: 'The vote failed; the coalition held anyway.' It demonstrates that the clauses are linked and roughly equal, leaving readers to infer the exact relationship (here, contrast).
cards.h: → two uses + example + the relationship it shows
cards.n: Outside lists, a semicolon needs an independent clause on each side; putting one before a fragment is the most common semicolon error.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The vote was close; the consequences were not.'
cards.a: The semicolon binds two short independent clauses into one unit, demonstrating that they belong together and should be weighed against each other: the narrow margin set against the lopsided consequences. The balanced halves sharpen the irony without subordinating either one.
cards.h: → what the semicolon joins + the relationship it shows
cards.n: The compression is the point: a period would let the first clause settle before the second overturns it.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a semicolon, a colon, and a dash used at the same junction in a sentence.
cards.a: A semicolon presents the two parts as balanced, closely related equals; a colon announces that what follows explains, specifies, or delivers on what came before; a dash breaks in abruptly, giving what follows emphasis or the feel of an aside. The same two ideas take on a different relationship with each mark.
cards.h: → the relationship each mark shows
cards.n: The three marks can often join the same clauses, so the question is never which is correct but which relationship the writer means to show.

cards.q: Identify the relationship between ideas that the colon demonstrates in this sentence from an invented op-ed, and explain its effect: 'The study found one reliable predictor of whether students finished the program: a single adult at school who knew their name.'
cards.a: The colon demonstrates specification: the clause before it promises 'one reliable predictor,' and what follows names it. Delaying the answer to the end and setting it off gives the simple, human finding, an adult who knew their name, the weight of a revelation.
cards.h: → the relationship + what the colon sets up and delivers
cards.n: 'The colon introduces a list' is wrong here: a colon can introduce a single item, and the credited point is the promise-then-delivery relationship.

cards.q: Decide which punctuation best demonstrates the intended relationship, and explain why: a writer wants the second clause to explain the first in 'The school board had one choice left ___ it had to close the pool.' (A) a comma (B) a semicolon (C) a colon (D) no punctuation
cards.a: (C) a colon. The second clause explains and specifies the 'one choice' the first announces, the relationship a colon signals. A semicolon (B) would present the clauses as parallel equals rather than as statement and explanation; a comma (A) makes a comma splice; no punctuation (D) makes a run-on.
cards.h: → choice + why each other option fails
cards.n: Choosing the semicolon because both clauses are independent is the trap: it is grammatical but shows balance, not explanation.

cards.q: Write one sentence joining these two invented ideas with punctuation that shows they contrast as equals, and one that shows the second as an abrupt, emphatic addition: 'The bridge cost forty million dollars.' 'It has never carried a train.'
cards.a: Equals in contrast: 'The bridge cost forty million dollars; it has never carried a train.' Abrupt emphasis: 'The bridge cost forty million dollars — and it has never carried a train.' The semicolon balances the price against the result for readers to weigh; the dash breaks in, isolating the failure as a pointed afterthought.
cards.h: → two sentences + the relationship each mark shows
cards.n: A comma alone in either version makes a comma splice; the mark must be one that can join two independent clauses.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might join two independent clauses with a semicolon rather than separating them with a period.
cards.a: A period separates the clauses into two complete thoughts; a semicolon keeps them in one sentence, demonstrating that they are closely related and should be read together, often as a balance or contrast. Readers take the second clause as completing the first rather than starting a new point.
cards.h: → a period separates → a semicolon joins → the clauses read as one related unit → balance or contrast shown
cards.n: 'A semicolon makes the sentence longer' earns nothing; name the relationship between the ideas that the mark demonstrates.
o: Because the semicolon names no relationship, readers must infer it, which can make a contrast feel sharper than 'but' would.

w.a: Semicolons are used to make writing look more advanced.
w.why: about appearance, not relationship

w.a: A semicolon shows that the second clause is less important than the first.
w.why: a semicolon joins equals; it does not subordinate

cards.q: Explain why a writer who ends a sentence with 'and no one noticed' might set that phrase off with a dash rather than a comma.
cards.a: A comma would fold the phrase smoothly into the sentence as one more detail; the dash creates a break that isolates it, so 'and no one noticed' lands as a pointed, separate revelation. The punctuation shows that the final idea stands apart from, and comments on, everything before it.
cards.h: → a comma blends the phrase in → a dash breaks the flow → the phrase is isolated → it lands as a pointed comment
cards.n: 'The dash adds drama' is only a start; name what the break does to the relationship between the final phrase and the rest.
o: The pause the dash forces mimics a speaker's timing before a punch line, which gives the ending an ironic edge.

w.a: A dash and a comma mean the same thing, so the choice does not matter.
w.why: ignores the different relationships they show

w.a: The writer used a dash because the sentence already had too many commas.
w.why: a mechanical reason, not the effect

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the colon and give an example.
cards.a: A colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces what explains, specifies, or lists it: an explanation, a list, an appositive, or a quotation. Example: 'The problem was simple: nobody had read the bill.' It organizes and emphasizes, promising something and then delivering it in the spotlight position.
cards.h: → what precedes and follows + example + its purposes
cards.n: A colon after an incomplete clause ('The goals are: speed and cost') is an error; what precedes the colon must be able to stand alone.

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The board had one option left: resign.'
cards.a: The colon sets up the single word 'resign' as a blunt, delayed payoff: the clause announces 'one option,' and the colon makes readers wait an instant for it. Isolated at the end, the word lands with more force than 'The board's one option was to resign.'
cards.h: → what the colon sets up + the effect of the payoff
cards.n: A colon promises that what follows delivers on what came before; here the delivery is one word, which is why it hits so hard.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the dash and give an example.
cards.a: A dash sets off an interruption, an appositive, or an emphatic addition, singly at the end of a sentence or in pairs mid-sentence. Example: 'The new policy — announced without warning on a Friday — took effect Monday.' It emphasizes the set-off material or gives it the feel of speech breaking in.
cards.h: → uses + example + effect
cards.n: Dashes are louder than commas or parentheses; say why this material deserves the extra attention, not just that the dash 'adds emphasis.'

cards.q: Identify the punctuation choice's effect: 'The plan was approved - barely - after three hours of debate.'
cards.a: The paired dashes interrupt the sentence to insert 'barely' as a pointed aside, forcing readers to notice how narrow the approval was. The interruption undercuts the official-sounding 'was approved' and adds a skeptical, wry tone.
cards.h: → what the dashes insert + the effect on meaning and tone
cards.n: Dashes read as more abrupt than parentheses, which would cushion the aside and make 'barely' sound like a quiet footnote.

cards.q: Define rhetorical question and give an example.
cards.a: A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer, because the answer is implied. Example: 'Are we to stand by and do nothing?' Its end mark signals a question while its content makes a claim, so readers supply the answer themselves and feel the conclusion is their own.
cards.h: → definition + example + how the end mark works
cards.n: 'It makes the reader think' earns little; say what answer it implies and why having readers supply it serves the purpose.

cards.q:
Identify the purpose each punctuation choice primarily serves: clarifying, organizing, emphasizing, indicating purpose, supplementing information, or contributing to tone. All sentences are invented:
1. The mayor's 'transparency' has so far produced two press releases.
2. We need three things: funding, staff, and time.
3. The vote passed (by a single ballot) on Tuesday.
4. The plan helps small-business owners.
5. The inspector found one problem — the roof.
6. The fire drill lasted an hour!
7. The members, who had waited all night, left angry; the reporters, who had not, stayed.
8. Is this the best a city of 90,000 can do?
9. Before eating, the volunteers washed their hands.
10. The report — all 400 pages of it — arrived Friday.
cards.a:
1 → contributing to tone: the scare quotes signal skepticism about the mayor's word
2 → organizing: the colon introduces and frames the list
3 → supplementing information: the parentheses add a detail as an aside
4 → clarifying: the hyphen shows 'small' describes the businesses, not the owners
5 → emphasizing: the dash isolates 'the roof' as the payoff
6 → contributing to tone: the exclamation point conveys exasperation
7 → organizing: the semicolon separates halves that already contain commas
8 → indicating purpose: the question mark marks a question, here a rhetorical challenge
9 → clarifying: the comma prevents the misreading 'eating the volunteers'
10 → supplementing information, with emphasis: the dashes set off a pointed aside
cards.h: → one purpose + how the mark serves it, per line
cards.n: Some marks serve two purposes (item 10 supplements and emphasizes); name the primary one and how the mark achieves it, as MC items require.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'How much longer can this city pretend the water is safe to drink?'
cards.a: A rhetorical question: it is asked not to get an answer but to imply one (the city cannot keep pretending). The question mark turns an accusation into a challenge, so readers supply the charge themselves.
cards.h: → device + the implied answer + effect
cards.n: A rhetorical question is answered by silence, while hypophora answers itself aloud; that difference is what MC items test.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might put a word in quotation marks when it is not a quotation, as in the city's 'improvements' to the park.
cards.a: The quotation marks (scare quotes) distance the writer from the word, signaling that it is someone else's term and that the writer doubts it. Readers hear 'improvements' ironically, so the punctuation contributes a skeptical tone without the writer having to argue that the changes made the park worse.
cards.h: → quotation marks on a non-quotation → the word becomes someone else's → the writer doubts it → skeptical tone
cards.n: 'The quotation marks emphasize the word' misreads them; scare quotes question a word rather than stress it.
o: Scare quotes let the writer turn the other side's own label against it, which can feel sharper than an open accusation.

w.a: The writer is quoting the city's report, so the quotation marks are required.
w.why: the question says it is not a quotation

w.a: The quotation marks show that 'improvements' is an important word.
w.why: confuses scare quotes with emphasis

cards.q: Explain why a writer might close a paragraph with a rhetorical question rather than a direct statement of the same idea.
cards.a: A statement asserts the conclusion; a rhetorical question makes readers supply it, so the conclusion feels like their own and is harder to resist. The question mark also shifts the tone toward challenge, pressing the audience to respond rather than simply nod along.
cards.h: → question mark invites an answer → readers supply the conclusion → it feels like their own → harder to resist
cards.n: 'To make the reader think' is too vague; say what answer the question implies and why supplying it persuades.
o: A question can voice indignation a statement cannot, since it implies the answer is too obvious to need saying.

w.a: The writer asks a question because the writer does not know the answer.
w.why: misreads a rhetorical question as a real one

w.a: Questions are more interesting than statements, so they keep readers engaged.
w.why: generic; no implied answer and no purpose

cards.q: State what design features such as italics or boldface do in a text, according to the CED.
cards.a: They create emphasis. Setting a word or phrase in italics or boldface marks it as more important than the words around it, directing the reader's attention to it or signaling the stress a speaker would give it aloud.
cards.h: → the CED's claim + how the emphasis works
cards.n: 'Italics are for titles' is one convention only; the CED's point is the rhetorical one, that design features create emphasis.

cards.q: Identify what the italics emphasize in this sentence from an invented principal's letter, where the word 'every' is printed in italics, and explain the effect: 'The new policy applies to every student, including the seniors.'
cards.a: The italics stress 'every,' emphasizing that the policy has no exceptions. The emphasis anticipates the objection some families would raise, that seniors are exempt, and answers it before it is voiced, which 'including the seniors' then confirms.
cards.h: → the stressed word + the objection it heads off
cards.n: 'The italics make the word stand out' repeats the question; say why this word needs stress for this audience.

cards.q:
Identify how the meaning of this invented sentence changes as the italicized word moves: 'I did not say she took the money.'
1. 'I' in italics
2. 'say' in italics
3. 'she' in italics
4. 'money' in italics
cards.a:
1 → someone else said it, not I
2 → I may have implied it, but I never said it
3 → I said someone took it, but not her
4 → she may have taken something, but not the money
cards.h: → one meaning per placement
cards.n: The words never change; only the emphasis does. The trap is treating design features as decoration rather than as part of the meaning.

cards.q: Identify the design feature and its effect in this invented email from a coach to players: 'Practice is CANCELED today because of the lightning warning.'
cards.a: Capital letters on 'CANCELED' work like boldface: they create emphasis, so players who skim the email catch the one fact that changes their plans. In informal messages all capitals can read as shouting, but a single capitalized word is a clear, sparing signal.
cards.h: → the feature + what it emphasizes + its risk
cards.n: The CED statement says 'such as' italics or boldface; treat capitals as another design feature that creates emphasis, not as a spelling error.

cards.q: Decide which use of boldface better serves an invented school safety notice, and explain why. (A) boldface on the single instruction 'Do not use the east stairwell' (B) boldface on every sentence of the notice
cards.a: (A). Emphasis works by contrast: boldface on the one instruction readers must not miss makes it stand out from everything else. Boldfacing every sentence (B) emphasizes nothing, since when all the text is bold no part of it stands out, and the key instruction is lost.
cards.h: → choice + the contrast principle
cards.n: Choosing (B) because 'safety is important' confuses importance with emphasis; emphasis needs plain text around it.

cards.q: Write a sentence for an invented flyer reminding students of the deadline to register for a student council election, and state which one word you would set in boldface and why.
cards.a: Model: 'Registration closes Friday at 3:00, and late forms will not be accepted.' Set 'not' in boldface: students tend to assume a deadline will bend, so emphasizing the refusal is what makes them act by Friday.
cards.h: → one sentence + the word to emphasize + the reason
cards.n: Emphasizing the date alone repeats what readers expect; stress the word that corrects the likeliest misunderstanding.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might italicize the word a speaker would stress aloud.
cards.a: Print loses the stress a voice supplies, so a sentence can be misread; italics restore it, telling readers which word carries the meaning ('I said the report was late, not wrong,' with 'late' italicized). The design feature creates the emphasis the voice would have given.
cards.h: → print loses vocal stress → misreading possible → italics restore the stress → the intended meaning is emphasized
cards.n: 'Italics make the word look important' is thin; say what misreading the emphasis prevents or what contrast it creates.
o: Italics can also mimic a speaker's disbelief or indignation, contributing to tone as well as emphasis.

w.a: Italics are used for words from other languages, so the writer must be using a foreign word.
w.why: one convention, not the emphasis asked about

w.a: The writer italicizes the word to decorate a confusing sentence.
w.why: decoration is not emphasis; name the stressed meaning

cards.q: Explain why emphasis from boldface or italics works only when most of the surrounding text is left plain.
cards.a: Emphasis is a contrast: a word stands out only against words that do not. Used sparingly, each design feature signals importance; used everywhere, the contrast disappears and readers can no longer tell which idea the writer most wants them to notice.
cards.h: → emphasis = contrast with plain text → sparing use keeps the signal → overuse erases the contrast → nothing stands out
cards.n: 'Too much bold is annoying' is a reaction, not a reason; the credited point is that emphasis depends on contrast.
o: Heavy formatting can make a writer seem to be shouting, which undercuts the calm authority an argument needs.

w.a: Boldface should only be used in titles and headings.
w.why: a rule, not the reason emphasis depends on contrast

w.a: Using boldface everywhere makes the whole text more important.
w.why: without contrast, nothing is emphasized

cards.q: Define style in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: Style is the mix of word choice, syntax, and conventions a writer employs (the CED's definition): the characteristic way a writer uses language, from diction and sentence structure to figurative language and punctuation, that distinguishes one writer's prose from another's and shapes how an audience receives the argument.
cards.h: → CED definition + what it includes + why it matters
cards.n: Style is never neutral decoration; describe the specific mix and connect it to purpose, or the observation earns nothing.
x: the mix of word choice, syntax, and conventions

cards.q: Define syntax.
cards.a: Syntax is the arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses in sentences: sentence length, type, and the order of elements. With word choice and conventions, it is one of the three ingredients of style the CED names.
cards.h: → one-sentence definition + its place in style
cards.n: Syntax commentary is the fastest way out of a diction-only essay; describe the pattern (a periodic sentence, a run of fragments), then its effect.

cards.q: Define voice in writing.
cards.a: Voice is the distinctive personality a reader hears in a writer's prose, produced by the writer's habitual mix of word choice, syntax, rhythm, and stance. Tone can shift from passage to passage; voice is the consistent style behind the shifts.
cards.h: → definition + how it differs from tone
cards.n: 'Voice' is not a CED term; on the exam, describe the style that creates it (word choice, syntax, conventions) rather than just asserting a voice.

cards.q: Define extended metaphor and give an example.
cards.a: An extended metaphor sustains a single comparison across several sentences or a whole passage, developing its details. Example: describing a campaign as a voyage, then continuing with charts, storms, mutiny, and landfall. It becomes part of the writer's style, a controlling frame through which readers interpret the argument.
cards.h: → definition + example + its effect on reading
cards.n: Quoting one line of an extended metaphor misses its force; trace how the comparison develops and what it leads readers to assume by the end.

cards.q: Identify the device: 'Every reform since has been measured against that summer, the district's own Waterloo.'
cards.a: Allusion: a brief, unexplained reference to Waterloo, Napoleon's final defeat in 1815. It borrows that shared meaning, a decisive, crushing loss, to cast the summer's failure as the end of an era, without the writer spelling it out.
cards.h: → device + the reference + the meaning it borrows
cards.n: An allusion is a bet on shared knowledge, so it also reveals what the writer assumes the audience knows; explain the borrowed meaning, not just the reference.

cards.q: Define colloquialism and give an example.
cards.a: A colloquialism is an informal word or expression from everyday speech used in writing. Example: 'gonna,' 'no big deal,' 'y'all.' As a style choice it shortens the distance between writer and audience and can signal candor or membership in a shared community, though it can cost authority in a formal setting.
cards.h: → definition + examples + effect and risk
cards.n: Colloquial language is not an error in itself; judge it by audience and occasion, and say what closeness or candor it buys.

cards.q: Describe the style of this excerpt from an invented commencement speech by a retired firefighter, naming its word choice, syntax, and conventions: 'You will be told to be bold. Fine. Be bold. But bold is cheap. Bold is a word on a poster. What costs something is showing up: at 3 a.m., in the rain, for people who will never learn your name.'
cards.a: The style is plain, blunt, and emphatic. Word choice is short and concrete ('cheap,' 'poster,' '3 a.m.,' 'rain'); syntax relies on short sentences, a fragment ('Fine.'), repetition of 'bold,' and a colon that delivers the definition of courage; conventions are informal (direct 'you,' a sentence opening with 'But'). The mix sounds like hard-won experience, not ceremony.
cards.h: → overall style + word choice, syntax, conventions + effect
cards.n: Listing devices without naming the overall style they make up misses the statement: style is the mix, so describe the mix and its effect.

cards.q: Write a version of this formal sentence from an invented city notice in a plain, conversational style for a flyer to residents, changing word choice, syntax, and conventions: 'Residents are hereby notified that, owing to scheduled infrastructure maintenance, potable water service will be temporarily suspended between the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. on Tuesday.'
cards.a: Model: 'Heads up: your tap water will be off Tuesday from 9 to 3 while crews fix the pipes.' Word choice moves from Latinate terms ('potable,' 'suspended,' 'infrastructure') to plain ones ('tap water,' 'off,' 'pipes'); syntax moves from a long passive construction to a short active one; conventions loosen with a colloquial opener and a colon.
cards.h: → the rewritten sentence + the change in each element
cards.n: Shortening the sentence without changing its diction and structure only trims it; the style changes when all three elements change.

cards.q: Define analogy and give an example.
cards.a: An analogy is an extended comparison that maps the relationships in a familiar case onto an unfamiliar one in order to explain or argue. Example: 'A city that skips pipe repairs to save money is like a driver who skips oil changes: the savings last until the engine seizes.' It makes reasoning concrete, but it persuades only as far as the mapping holds.
cards.h: → definition + example + its limit
cards.n: An analogy that breaks at a key point can be rebutted there; test whether the relationships, not just the surfaces, match. Analogy is a comparison (skill 7.A).

cards.q: Define personification and give an example.
cards.a: Personification gives human qualities or actions to an object, animal, or abstraction. Example: 'The old mill watched the town shrink around it.' It makes an object or idea feel like an agent with feelings, so readers respond to it as they would to a person.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect
cards.n: 'It makes the writing come alive' earns nothing; say what attitude the human trait assigns to the subject (here, a silent, grieving witness).

cards.q: Define vernacular.
cards.a: Vernacular is the everyday language of a particular region, group, or class, including its own grammar and idiom, as opposed to standardized or literary language. As a style choice, writing in the vernacular claims that a community's own speech belongs on the page and brings readers close to its speakers.
cards.h: → definition + what choosing it claims
cards.n: Vernacular is not an error to be corrected; analyze what writing in it claims about whose voice counts.

cards.q: Define pedantic diction.
cards.a: Pedantic diction is ostentatiously scholarly or overly precise word choice that calls attention to the speaker's learning. It can build authority with an academic audience or, when a writer mocks a persona, expose the speaker as pompous and out of touch.
cards.h: → definition + its two possible effects
cards.n: 'Pedantic' is a criticism, not a synonym for 'academic'; use it when learning is displayed for its own sake.

cards.q: Define monosyllabic diction and give an example.
cards.a: Monosyllabic diction relies mostly on one-syllable words, which read as plain, blunt, and direct. Example: 'We must act now, or we lose all we have built.' As part of a writer's style, it strips away ornament so the claim lands with the force of plain speech.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect
cards.n: Counting syllables is only the evidence; the analysis is the effect (plainness, urgency, sincerity) at that moment.

cards.q: Define polysyllabic diction and give an example.
cards.a: Polysyllabic diction relies on long, many-syllabled words, which read as elevated, formal, or technical. Example: 'the unprecedented deterioration of institutional accountability.' It can signal expertise and gravity, but it can also sound evasive or distant to a general audience.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect and risk
cards.n: A switch between polysyllabic and monosyllabic words is often the most analyzable moment; notice the shift, not just the level.

cards.q: Explain why a writer might choose a plain style of short sentences and common words for an argument aimed at a general audience.
cards.a: A general audience varies in background, so plain words and short sentences reduce confusion and let every reader follow the reasoning. The style also signals candor: a writer who avoids jargon seems to have nothing to hide, which builds trust with readers wary of experts.
cards.h: → mixed audience → plain words, short sentences → everyone follows + the writer seems candid → argument trusted
cards.n: Borrows audience from Rhetorical Situation. 'Plain style is easier to read' is half the answer; add what the style signals about the writer.
o: Plain style keeps attention on the claim itself, so the argument seems to stand on its merits rather than on the writer's eloquence.

w.a: Writers use a plain style because they cannot write in an elevated one.
w.why: treats a choice as a limitation

w.a: A plain style is always the best style for any argument.
w.why: ignores audience and occasion

cards.q: Explain why a writer might build an entire essay around one extended metaphor rather than several unrelated comparisons.
cards.a: A sustained metaphor gives readers one controlling frame, so each new detail extends the comparison and the reader's assumptions accumulate in a single direction. Several unrelated comparisons pull in different directions and dilute the attitude the writer wants readers to adopt.
cards.h: → one sustained comparison → a single frame → details build in one direction → readers adopt the writer's view
cards.n: 'It makes the essay more creative' earns nothing; explain how a sustained frame shapes the reader's interpretation.
o: Returning to the same metaphor also unifies the essay's style, so the comparison doubles as a thread of coherence.

w.a: An extended metaphor is used because the writer only thought of one comparison.
w.why: treats a design choice as a lack of ideas

w.a: Several comparisons would be better, because variety is always more interesting.
w.why: ignores the cumulative force of one frame

cards.q: Explain why an allusion can persuade an audience that shares the reference but fall flat with one that does not.
cards.a: An allusion borrows meaning the audience already holds: readers who know the reference supply its emotions and associations instantly and feel included. Readers who do not know it get no borrowed meaning and may feel excluded, so the same choice builds or breaks the writer's connection.
cards.h: → allusion borrows shared meaning → insiders supply it and feel included → outsiders get nothing and feel shut out
cards.n: Borrows audience from Rhetorical Situation. 'The allusion shows the writer is well read' is about the writer, not the audience's response.
o: An allusion also defines the audience as people who share a culture, which can flatter insiders or alienate everyone else.

w.a: Allusions always strengthen an argument because they add evidence from history.
w.why: ignores whether the audience knows the reference

w.a: The writer uses an allusion to show off a knowledge of history.
w.why: about the writer's image, not the audience's response

cards.q: Define verbal irony and give an example.
cards.a: Verbal irony says the opposite of, or something different from, what is meant, with the gap available to the audience. Example: remarking 'What lovely weather' during a downpour. In argument it signals a complex or ironic perspective: readers who catch the gap share the writer's judgment of the target.
cards.h: → definition + example + what it signals
cards.n: Irony is not just 'something unexpected'; verbal irony needs a gap between what is said and what is meant, and the analysis names both.

cards.q: Define situational irony and give an example.
cards.a: Situational irony is a gap between what is expected to happen and what actually happens. Example: a fire station burning down, or a safety campaign whose billboards block drivers' view of a crosswalk. Writers point to it to expose the distance between plans and outcomes, often to criticize overconfident institutions.
cards.h: → definition + examples + its use in argument
cards.n: Coincidence is not irony; the outcome must contradict a reasonable expectation in a way that means something.

cards.q: Define satire and give an example.
cards.a: Satire uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose vice, folly, or abuse and imply that reform is needed. Example: Jonathan Swift's 'A Modest Proposal' (1729), which 'recommends' selling poor children as food to attack English policy toward Ireland. Its irony emerges from the gap between the argument and readers' values.
cards.h: → definition + example + where the irony comes from
cards.n: Satire is not mere mockery; it has a corrective target. If you cannot name what the writer wants changed, you have not found the satire.

cards.q: Contrast Horatian and Juvenalian satire.
cards.a: Horatian satire is light, witty, and tolerant, treating folly as laughably human; Juvenalian satire is harsh, bitter, and moralizing, treating vice as intolerable. The difference lies in tone and in the severity of the implied indictment.
cards.h: → the tone of each + what separates them
cards.n: Naming the kind of satire earns little alone; say why the writer needed that severity for that target and audience. Neither term is in the CED.

cards.q: Define paradox and give an example.
cards.a: A paradox is a statement that seems self-contradictory but reveals a truth on reflection. Example: 'The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know.' It signals a complex perspective: the writer refuses a simple view and makes readers work out how both halves can be true.
cards.h: → definition + example + the perspective it signals
cards.n: A paradox is not a logical error; the analysis must explain the truth that resolves the apparent contradiction.

cards.q: Contrast paradox and oxymoron.
cards.a: An oxymoron is a compressed contradiction within a phrase ('deafening silence,' 'cruel kindness'); a paradox is a whole statement or situation that seems contradictory but proves meaningful. The difference is scale, phrase versus proposition, though both signal a subject that resists a simple label.
cards.h: → each defined + the difference in scale
cards.n: Students label every paradox an oxymoron; if it is a whole idea rather than a two-word pair, call it a paradox.

cards.q: Define apophasis and give an example.
cards.a: Apophasis raises a subject by claiming to pass over it, so the audience registers the point while the speaker denies making it. Example: 'I won't mention his three arrests, since they have nothing to do with tonight's vote.' It is an ironic move: what is said contradicts the stated intention.
cards.h: → definition + example + why it is ironic
cards.n: Not a CED term. The credited observation is the gap between 'I won't mention' and the mention, and the deniability it buys.

cards.q: Identify the technique Swift leans on in A Modest Proposal by having an economist calmly recommend eating Irish infants.
cards.a: A sustained ironic persona: the calm, reasonable projector presents a monstrous plan in the language of economics, and the gap between his tone and his proposal exposes the real cruelty of policies that already treated the Irish poor as commodities, a critique Swift never states directly.
cards.h: → the technique + how the gap exposes the target
cards.n: The persona is the device, so quoting the narrator's cold arithmetic proves the irony better than quoting the shocking proposal itself.

cards.q: Identify the satire type in A Modest Proposal.
cards.a: Juvenalian satire: the proposal is bitter and biting, using shocking irony to condemn real suffering rather than to amuse. Its target, policy that left the Irish poor starving, calls for indignation, not light teasing.
cards.h: → satire type + the evidence of its severity
cards.n: Because the target is real, ongoing suffering rather than a harmless habit, calling this Horatian would badly undersell the essay's anger.

cards.q: Identify the irony in this excerpt from an invented op-ed, and explain how it emerges from the difference between the argument and readers' expectations or values: 'Our district has found a bold way to raise test scores: stop testing the students who struggle. Last spring, 140 of them were quietly placed in a program exempt from the state exam, and our average rose four points. Congratulations are in order.'
cards.a: The irony is verbal: 'bold' and 'Congratulations are in order' praise what the writer condemns. It emerges because readers expect raising scores to mean helping students learn, and they value honesty about students who struggle; the plan games the average by hiding those students, so the praise exposes the district's priorities.
cards.h: → the ironic words + the expectation or value they violate
cards.n: Reading the praise as sincere is the trap; the gap between 'bold' and what the plan actually does is the evidence for irony.

cards.q: Define sarcasm and give an example.
cards.a: Sarcasm is sharp, mocking verbal irony aimed at a target. Example: saying 'Nice work' after a coworker drops a tray of dishes. Unlike gentler irony it is meant to wound, so it can alienate readers who sympathize with the target.
cards.h: → definition + example + how it differs from gentler irony
cards.n: Sarcasm is a kind of verbal irony, not a synonym for it: all sarcasm is ironic, but irony need not mock anyone.

cards.q: Define Horatian satire and give an example.
cards.a: Horatian satire is gentle, amused satire that laughs at human folly rather than condemning it. Example: a light send-up of parents who treat a third-grade soccer league like the World Cup. Its tolerant tone keeps readers comfortable enough to recognize themselves in the target instead of getting defensive.
cards.h: → definition + example + why the mildness works
cards.n: Not a CED term. The credited point is the tone and why the writer chose mildness for this audience, not the label.

cards.q: Define oxymoron and give an example.
cards.a: An oxymoron places two contradictory terms side by side in a single phrase. Example: 'an open secret,' 'a working vacation.' It compresses a complex perspective into two words, signaling that the subject resists a simple label.
cards.h: → definition + examples + what it signals
cards.n: A whole contradictory statement is a paradox, not an oxymoron; an oxymoron is a collision inside one phrase.

cards.q: Explain why A Modest Proposal's title is itself ironic.
cards.a: Calling a proposal to eat infants 'modest' opens a gap between the word and the plan, since nothing could be less modest. The adjective signals from the first word that the speaker's calm reasonableness cannot be trusted, priming readers to look past the surface argument.
cards.h: → 'modest' clashes with a monstrous plan → the speaker can't be trusted → readers look for the real target
cards.n: The irony works at the level of one adjective, which makes the title the cheapest quotable evidence in the whole essay.
o: 'Modest' also mimics the humble pose of the reform pamphlets of Swift's day, mocking a genre that made such schemes sound respectable.

w.a: The title is ironic because the proposal is actually long, not short.
w.why: confuses 'modest' with length

w.a: The title is ironic because Swift really wanted people to eat children.
w.why: misreads the satire as sincere

cards.q: Explain why a writer might use irony rather than direct criticism to challenge readers' values.
cards.a: Direct criticism invites readers to defend their values; irony lets them discover the problem themselves as they notice the gap between the argument and what they believe. The recognition feels like their own insight, so it is harder to reject, and the writer seems clever rather than preachy.
cards.h: → direct attack → readers defend; irony → readers find the gap → the insight feels their own → harder to reject
cards.n: 'Irony makes the essay funny' misses the purpose; explain how the gap between argument and values moves readers.
o: Irony builds an in-group of readers who catch it, and the wish to belong to it pulls readers toward the writer's judgment.

w.a: Writers use irony when they are afraid to say what they mean.
w.why: treats a strategy as timidity

w.a: Irony is used to confuse readers so that they keep reading.
w.why: irony depends on readers catching the gap, not on confusion

cards.q: Explain why ironic praise, such as calling a failed project 'a triumph of planning,' signals a complex perspective rather than simple disapproval.
cards.a: Ironic praise holds two views at once: the official claim ('a triumph') and the writer's judgment of the failure. Readers must register both to get the point, so the phrase conveys more than disapproval: it mocks the gap between the planners' confidence and the result.
cards.h: → praise word + failed result → two views held at once → readers see the gap → mockery of the planners' confidence
cards.n: 'The writer is being sarcastic' names a tone without the gap; a complex perspective means explaining the two views the irony holds together.
o: The praise borrows the planners' own language, so the irony turns their words against them.

w.a: The writer genuinely thinks the project was a success.
w.why: misreads the irony as sincere

w.a: The writer is simply saying the project was bad in a funny way.
w.why: reduces the double view to plain disapproval

cards.q: Define a dangling modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A dangling modifier has no word in the sentence that it can logically modify, so it attaches to the wrong one. Example: 'Having finished the report, the printer jammed,' which says the printer finished the report. Fix it by naming the doer right after the modifier: 'Having finished the report, Ana watched the printer jam.'
cards.h: → definition + example + the fix
cards.n: An opening phrase modifies the subject that follows it; if that subject cannot perform the action, the modifier dangles, however clear the intent seems.

cards.q: Define a misplaced modifier and give an example.
cards.a: A misplaced modifier sits too far from the word it modifies, so it seems to modify another. Example: 'She almost drove her kids to school every day' suggests she nearly drove but never did; 'She drove her kids to school almost every day' says what is meant. The CED's rule: place modifiers closest to what they modify to reduce ambiguity.
cards.h: → definition + example + the CED's placement rule
cards.n: Limiting words (only, almost, just, nearly) are the usual culprits; each placement of 'only' in a sentence can produce a different meaning.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The crowd fell silent, its collective breath held, as the verdict was read.'
cards.a: An absolute phrase: 'its collective breath held' (a noun plus a participle) modifies the whole main clause rather than a single word, adding a vivid, simultaneous detail that specifies how the crowd fell silent.
cards.h: → structure + what it modifies + its effect
cards.n: Absolute phrases modify the whole clause, not one noun, so they cannot dangle; that is how to tell them from participial phrases.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'Determined to finish before dark, the crew worked through the storm.'
cards.a: A participial phrase: 'Determined to finish before dark' modifies 'the crew,' the subject placed directly after it. Opening the sentence with it front-loads the crew's motive before their action, qualifying the action as a choice rather than a necessity.
cards.h: → structure + what it modifies + its effect
cards.n: A participial phrase modifies the noun beside it, so it must sit next to the subject it describes; an absolute phrase has its own noun and modifies the whole clause.

cards.q: Contrast the rhetorical effect of a single absolute phrase versus a full subordinate clause conveying the same idea.
cards.a: An absolute phrase ('her voice shaking') is compressed and image-like, placing a detail beside the action without stating how they relate; a subordinate clause ('because her voice was shaking') names the relationship, whether cause, time, or condition, and so reads as more logically explicit and argumentative.
cards.h: → effect of each + what the clause adds
cards.n: Both can convey simultaneity or cause; choose the absolute for the image and the clause when the reader must see the logical link.

cards.q:
Write a revision of each sentence that places the modifier closest to what it modifies, removing the ambiguity. All sentences are invented:
1. Walking into the gym, the new scoreboard caught everyone's eye.
2. The council only approved two of the five proposals.
3. The mayor announced a plan to fix the potholes at Tuesday's meeting.
4. Covered in graffiti, the students repainted the underpass.
5. We saw a deer driving to school.
6. The coach told the players on Friday they would travel.
7. Burned beyond repair, the fire chief inspected the house.
cards.a:
1 → 'Walking into the gym, everyone noticed the new scoreboard.'
2 → 'The council approved only two of the five proposals.'
3 → 'At Tuesday's meeting, the mayor announced a plan to fix the potholes.'
4 → 'The students repainted the underpass, which was covered in graffiti.'
5 → 'Driving to school, we saw a deer.'
6 → 'On Friday, the coach told the players they would travel,' or 'The coach told the players they would travel on Friday' (the two mean different things)
7 → 'The fire chief inspected the house, which was burned beyond repair.'
cards.h: → one revised sentence per line
cards.n: Item 6 has two correct answers because the original is ambiguous; say which meaning you chose. Moving a modifier can change meaning, not just clarity.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of stacking two absolute phrases in one sentence.
cards.a: Stacked absolute phrases layer several simultaneous details onto one main action without subordinating any of them, so readers see the moment from several angles at once, a slow-motion, cinematic effect. Each phrase specifies the scene further while the main clause holds still.
cards.h: → two absolute phrases → details layered on one action → none subordinated → a slow-motion, cinematic moment
cards.n: Overused across many sentences, the move feels overwritten; its force comes from saving it for the one moment the writer wants readers to linger on.
o: Because absolute phrases name no causal link, stacking them lets images accumulate and leaves readers to feel the connection.

w.a: Stacking absolute phrases makes the sentence longer, so it seems more descriptive.
w.why: length is not the effect

w.a: Two absolute phrases show that the writer knows advanced grammar.
w.why: about the writer, not the reader's experience

cards.q: Explain the effect of opening a sentence with a participial phrase rather than the subject.
cards.a: It delays the subject and verb, so readers hold a condition or motive in mind before learning who acted, which can build suspense or foreground cause. Because the phrase modifies the subject that follows, that subject must come right after it, or the modifier dangles.
cards.h: → phrase first → subject and verb delayed → reader holds the motive or condition → suspense or foregrounded cause
cards.n: The risk is a dangling modifier: the opening phrase attaches to whatever subject follows, so name the right subject immediately.
o: Opening with the phrase also varies how sentences begin, giving a paragraph of subject-first sentences a change of rhythm at a chosen moment.

w.a: Opening with a participial phrase is an error, because sentences should start with the subject.
w.why: it is conventional when the right subject follows

w.a: The writer opens with the phrase to make the sentence sound more formal.
w.why: names a register, not the effect on emphasis

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of parentheses and give an example.
cards.a: Parentheses enclose supplementary material that interrupts the main sentence. Example: 'The measure passed (barely) on the third vote.' They lower the volume, marking the material as an aside, a qualification, or a wry comment the writer chooses not to elevate, while still supplying what some readers need.
cards.h: → definition + example + effect
cards.n: Parentheses can hold information a reader needs (a definition, a date); calling everything in them 'unimportant' misreads their purpose.

cards.q: Identify the structure: 'The senator, a decorated veteran, refused to discuss the vote.'
cards.a: An appositive: 'a decorated veteran' renames 'The senator.' Set off by commas as a parenthetical element, it is not needed to identify her but supplies a credential that shapes how readers judge her refusal, adding weight without a new clause.
cards.h: → structure + what it renames + its effect
cards.n: An appositive can slip characterization into a sentence; ask why the writer chose this detail about the senator at this moment.

cards.q: Apply an appositive to add a credential to this sentence: 'The engineer warned that the bridge was unsafe.'
cards.a: 'The engineer, a thirty-year veteran of municipal bridge inspections, warned that the bridge was unsafe.' The appositive interrupts to supply the credential readers need to trust the warning, advancing the writer's purpose without a separate sentence.
cards.h: → revised sentence + what the appositive supplies
cards.n: An appositive is a noun phrase set off by commas; 'The engineer, who has worked for thirty years,' is a clause, not an appositive.

cards.q: Contrast 'which' and 'that' in formal written English.
cards.a: 'That' introduces a restrictive clause, essential to identifying the noun, with no commas ('the bridge that failed inspection'); 'which' introduces a nonrestrictive clause, a parenthetical addition set off by commas ('the Elm Street bridge, which opened in 1962,'). The comma-bound 'which' clause can be removed without changing which thing is meant.
cards.h: → restrictive vs nonrestrictive + the comma signal
cards.n: The comma is the signal readers use; a 'which' clause without commas blurs whether the information is essential. American style guides enforce this more than British usage.

cards.q: Contrast a restrictive and a nonrestrictive clause.
cards.a: A restrictive clause narrows down which thing is meant and cannot be removed without changing the meaning ('Students who missed the test must retake it'). A nonrestrictive clause is a parenthetical element: it adds information about something already identified and is set off by commas ('Ms. Ruiz, who wrote the test, will proctor').
cards.h: → each defined + an example of each
cards.n: Adding commas changes the meaning: 'The students, who missed the test, must retake it' now says that all the students missed it.
