cards.q: Identify the parenthetical element in this sentence from an invented hospital newsletter for patients' families, and explain what audience need it addresses: 'Your relative may be moved to the step-down unit (a floor for patients who no longer need intensive care but still need close monitoring) within a day or two.'
cards.a: The parenthetical is the definition in parentheses. Families may not know hospital jargon, so it defines 'step-down unit' without interrupting readers who already know it, and its reassuring wording ('no longer need intensive care') presents the move as progress rather than a cause for alarm.
cards.h: → the element + the audience need + its effect on purpose
cards.n: 'The parentheses add extra information' repeats the definition; the credited answer says whose need the information meets and how.

cards.q: Explain why a writer would set an appositive off with dashes instead of commas.
cards.a: Dashes make the appositive an emphatic interruption that draws the reader's eye, while commas fold it in quietly as background. The grammar is the same; the dashes tell readers that this added information matters to the writer's purpose.
cards.h: → same appositive → commas blend it in; dashes break in → the reader's attention lands on it → emphasis
cards.n: The grammar is identical either way; the punctuation choice is entirely about how much attention the parenthetical element should get.
o: Dashes can also give the aside a tone of surprise or indignation that commas cannot carry.

w.a: Dashes are used when the appositive is too long for commas.
w.why: length is not the reason

w.a: Commas and dashes are interchangeable here, so it is just a preference.
w.why: ignores the difference in emphasis

cards.q: Explain why a writer addressing both experts and newcomers might define a term in a parenthetical element rather than in a separate sentence.
cards.a: The parenthetical supplies the definition newcomers need while marking it as supplementary, so experts can skip it without losing the thread. A separate sentence would halt the argument for everyone and could seem condescending to the experts.
cards.h: → newcomers need the term → parenthetical supplies it → marked as optional → experts read on → both served
cards.n: 'To give more information' misses the audience point: the parenthetical meets one group's need without slowing the other.
o: Keeping the definition inside the sentence keeps the term and its meaning together, so newcomers never hold an unknown word in mind.

w.a: The writer uses parentheses because the definition is not important.
w.why: the definition matters to part of the audience

w.a: A separate sentence is better, because definitions should always stand alone.
w.why: a rule that ignores the mixed audience

cards.q: Explain how an invented student's proposal for a later school start should change its evidence, organization, and language when its audience changes from the school board to the parents of ninth graders.
cards.a: The claim stays; the choices around it change. For the board, lead with costs and logistics (bus tiers, the district's attendance data) in its technical terms. For parents, lead with what they value and fear, their children's sleep and the dark 6:40 a.m. bus stop, answer the worry about after-school jobs early, and write in plain, concrete words. Evidence, order, and language are all chosen for the audience's needs.
cards.h: → what stays + evidence, order, language for each
cards.n: Changing only the vocabulary is the trap: the audience also decides which evidence leads and what order the reasons take.

cards.q: Decide which piece of evidence should lead an invented proposal to a town finance committee for a crossing guard at one intersection, and explain why: (A) a parent's story of a near miss last October; (B) a morning count of 212 children crossing there, against a cost of about $9,000 a year; (C) a national safety group's statement that every child deserves a safe route to school.
cards.a: (B). A finance committee weighs cost against benefit, so the count and the price answer its question directly: $9,000 protects 212 children, about $42 a child a year. (A) can follow as the case that makes the number real, and (C) states a value the committee already accepts, so it adds nothing the committee needs. Strategically selected evidence relates to this audience's values.
cards.h: → letter + what this audience weighs
cards.n: Picking the most moving evidence (A) is the trap; the right lead is the evidence that answers the question this audience is asking.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented line of commentary from a rhetorical analysis and correct it: 'The writer uses statistics because statistics are the strongest kind of evidence.'
cards.a: Error: it ranks evidence in the abstract instead of explaining why this evidence suits this claim and audience. Corrected: 'The writer cites the 38 percent drop in late buses because her audience, a budget committee, trusts figures it can check, so the number meets the committee on its own terms.' Evidence is strong only relative to the claim it supports and the audience it must persuade.
cards.h: → the error in a clause + corrected commentary
cards.n: Tempting because statistics often do persuade; the credited move says whom they persuade and why they fit here.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence from a rhetorical analysis and correct it: 'Because the audience is teenagers, the writer uses simple words so they can understand.'
cards.a: Error: it treats the audience as a stereotype (teenagers need simple words) instead of naming the belief, value, or need the choice answers, and 'simple words' names no effect. Corrected: 'Because her readers are students who expect a lecture about phones, the principal writes short, plain sentences and admits she checks her own phone too often, so the letter reads as a conversation rather than a rule.'
cards.h: → the error in a clause + corrected sentence
cards.n: Tempting because it does name the audience; but an age group is not a belief or a need, and the analysis must say what the choice does.

cards.q: Contrast sufficient evidence (Claims and Evidence) and evidence that meets an audience's needs (Rhetorical Situation), and explain how the two interact.
cards.a: Sufficiency concerns the claim: evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality give apt support for what is asserted. Audience needs concern the reader: what this audience must see before it will accept the claim. They interact because a skeptical or expert audience raises the bar: two anecdotes may satisfy supporters but not a board that expects data, so the audience helps decide what counts as apt support.
cards.h: → each definition + how the audience moves the bar
cards.n: Treating sufficiency as a fixed number of examples is the trap; 'apt support' depends on the claim and on who must be convinced.

cards.q: Decide what an invented writer arguing that 'the city should turn the Dunmore Street parking lot into a pocket park' should lead with for each audience, and why: 1. downtown shop owners 2. parents at the nearby elementary school 3. the city council's budget committee 4. members of the senior center across the street 5. readers of a regional architecture magazine 6. commuters who park in the lot now
cards.a:
1 → customers: foot traffic and where shoppers will park instead (their need is sales)
2 → a safe place for children to play near school (their value is safety)
3 → cost, upkeep, and what the lot earns now (their duty is the budget)
4 → benches, shade, and a short walk (their need is access)
5 → the design and how it fits the street (their interest is form)
6 → where they will park instead, conceded first (their loss must be answered before anything else is heard)
cards.h: → one lead + the need it answers, per line
cards.n: The claim never changes across the six; the trap is thinking a new audience needs a new position rather than new evidence and a new order.

cards.q: Write a revision of the invented claim 'Kids need recess' for school board members whose main worry is test scores, keeping the writer's position.
cards.a: Model: 'Restoring a twenty-minute afternoon recess is likely to protect, not cost, the instructional time the board values, because students return from a break better able to focus.' It keeps the position, turns an obvious claim into one that requires a defense, and frames the benefit in the board's own terms, so the evidence that follows answers the board's worry.
cards.h: → one sentence in the board's terms + why it works
cards.n: Adding the words 'test scores' without a reason is the trap; the claim must show how recess serves what the board already values.

cards.q: Decide whether an invented writer should define the term 'induced demand' in a letter to a neighborhood association or in a letter to a state transportation board, and explain the choice.
cards.a: Define it for the neighborhood association, not the board. Residents may not know the term, so a short definition by description (new lanes draw new drivers until traffic returns) lets them trace the reasoning. Transportation officials already share the term, and defining it for them would suggest the writer misjudges their expertise. How precise and how explained a word must be depends on what the audience already knows.
cards.h: → which audience + what defining does for each
cards.n: 'Always define technical terms' is the trap; for experts, a definition can cost credibility by talking down to them.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented plan for an argument to a skeptical audience and correct it: 'I will open with my strongest claim and call the other side uninformed, so readers know I am confident.'
cards.a: Error: calling opponents 'uninformed' insults the readers who share their view, the very audience the writer must move, and the loaded word signals bias. Corrected plan: open with a value both sides share (safe streets), concede what the other side gets right, then rebut with evidence. Writers enhance their credibility when they concede and rebut rather than dismiss.
cards.h: → the error in a clause + a revised opening plan
cards.n: Tempting because confidence feels persuasive; a skeptical audience hears 'uninformed' as a verdict on itself, not as confidence.

cards.q: Explain how an invented writer's decision to open a letter to a skeptical city council with the council's own 2023 traffic study shapes both the audience's trust and the argument's line of reasoning.
cards.a: Opening with the council's own study makes the first evidence something the audience already accepts, so it trusts the writer before reaching the disputed claim. It also sets the line of reasoning: each later paragraph can build from a shared fact toward the conclusion the council resists. The same study placed last would read as a rebuttal rather than a foundation.
cards.h: → effect on trust + effect on the order of reasons
cards.n: Saying only 'it builds ethos' misses the structural half: the shared starting point makes every later step easier to accept.

cards.q: Identify which component of the rhetorical situation differs between these two invented versions of a letter to a town council, and explain what the difference changes in the claim, the evidence, and the tone: Version 1, written in March, asks the council to hire a lifeguard for Miller Pond 'before swimming season.' Version 2, written in July, the day after a child was pulled from the pond, asks for the same lifeguard 'this week.'
cards.a: The exigence and the context differ: a routine planning request in March, a near-drowning in July; writer, audience, and purpose stay the same. The new exigence changes the claim's urgency ('this week'), makes the rescue the lead evidence where the March letter could offer only risk, and shifts the tone from measured planning to urgency. One component moves, and choices across several Big Ideas move with it.
cards.h: → the component that changed + three effects
cards.n: Answering 'the audience changed' is the trap: the council is the same; what changed is the event prompting the letter and its moment.

cards.q: Explain why the same statistic can strengthen an argument for one audience and weaken it for another.
cards.a: Evidence works through the audience's values: a figure showing a school closure saves $2 million persuades a budget committee that values cost, but parents who value their children's school may hear it as proof the writer counts money over children, so it costs credibility with them.
cards.h: → evidence meets values → same number, different values → trust from one audience, suspicion from another
cards.n: 'Statistics are always strong' is the one-unit answer; the credited point is that evidence's force depends on who reads it.
o: Strategically selected evidence relates to an audience's emotions and values, so the fit to the audience, not the number itself, decides its effect.
An audience that distrusts the source of a figure discounts it, so the same statistic can read as proof to one group and as spin to another.

w.a: Statistics are the strongest evidence, so they strengthen an argument for any audience.
w.why: ignores that evidence works through the audience's values

w.a: Some audiences are not smart enough to understand statistics.
w.why: blames the audience instead of naming the values the evidence touches

w.a: A statistic weakens an argument only if it is inaccurate.
w.why: an accurate figure can still cost trust with an audience that values something else

cards.q: Explain why a writer facing a hostile audience may lead readers through a line of reasoning before stating the thesis.
cards.a: A hostile audience stops listening once it hears the claim it rejects, so the writer first builds agreement step by step, shared facts and then reasons, and arrives at the thesis after readers have accepted most of its support; the delayed thesis follows from reading the audience.
cards.h: → hostile readers reject the claim on sight → build agreement first → thesis arrives as a conclusion they half accept
cards.n: 'To build suspense' is the trap: the delay is a choice about this audience, not a device for drama.
o: Stating the thesis last lets it read as the reader's own conclusion rather than the writer's demand.
Early agreement on shared values makes the later disagreement smaller, so the claim meets less resistance when it appears.

w.a: The writer delays the thesis to create suspense and keep readers interested.
w.why: names no link to the audience's hostility

w.a: A thesis should always come in the first paragraph, so delaying it is a mistake.
w.why: a one-unit rule that ignores the rhetorical situation

w.a: The writer is not sure of the claim yet, so it comes at the end.
w.why: confuses a strategic delay with uncertainty

cards.q: Explain why the sufficiency of evidence depends on the audience, not only on the claim.
cards.a: Evidence is sufficient when its quantity and quality give apt support, and what is apt depends on who must be convinced: supporters may accept one vivid case, while a skeptical or expert audience needs more, and more rigorous, support before the same claim is defended.
cards.h: → sufficient = apt support → apt for whom? → skeptics and experts raise the bar → same claim, more evidence
cards.n: 'More evidence is always better' misses it: support this audience does not need can bury the reasoning it does need.
o: The CED says writers consider an audience's needs when choosing evidence, so sufficiency is judged against the readers' doubts, not an abstract standard.
An argument that satisfies its supporters but not the undecided has not yet met the audience it needs, because the undecided bring doubts the supporters never raised.

w.a: Evidence is sufficient when there are at least three examples.
w.why: a fixed count ignores quality and audience

w.a: If the claim is true, any amount of evidence is sufficient.
w.why: truth does not make support apt for a doubtful reader

w.a: The audience does not matter because evidence is objective.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses whom the evidence must convince

cards.q: Explain why defining a technical term helps an argument with a general audience but can cost credibility with experts.
cards.a: A definition lets a general audience trace reasoning that depends on the term, so it meets their need; experts already share the term, so defining it signals that the writer has misjudged them, and a writer who seems to misjudge the audience is trusted less.
cards.h: → definition serves readers who lack the term → experts already have it → defining reads as talking down → trust drops
cards.n: 'Definitions always clarify' is the one-unit answer; clarity for one audience can read as condescension to another.
o: Precise, undefined technical language signals membership in the experts' community, which experts reward with trust, while a general audience needs the definition to follow the reasoning.

A writer facing a mixed audience can use a brief appositive definition that informs the newcomer without lecturing the expert, which shows both effects at work: one reader needs the term, the other resents the lesson.

w.a: Defining terms always makes an argument clearer, so it can never hurt.
w.why: ignores how experts perceive the writer

w.a: Experts do not read arguments carefully, so definitions are wasted on them.
w.why: an unsupported claim about experts, not an effect on credibility

w.a: Technical terms should be avoided entirely in arguments.
w.why: a rule that ignores what the expert audience expects

cards.q: Explain why the order of paragraphs in an argument reveals what the writer assumes about the audience.
cards.a: Writers put first what the audience must accept before anything else will work, often a shared value or its biggest objection; since the sequence of paragraphs reveals the line of reasoning, it also shows what the writer thinks readers believe and doubt.
cards.h: → order = line of reasoning → lead with what readers must grant or most doubt → order reveals the assumed audience
cards.n: 'The writer saves the best point for last' is a one-unit habit; the order answers what this audience needs first.
o: An argument that opens by answering an objection assumes a skeptical audience; one that opens with a call to action assumes readers already agree.
Reordering the same paragraphs for a new audience changes the argument's effect without changing a single claim, so the order a writer chose shows which audience it was built for.

w.a: The order of paragraphs just follows the order in which the writer thought of the ideas.
w.why: treats a strategic choice as an accident

w.a: Paragraphs go from strongest to weakest so the argument starts strong.
w.why: a fixed formula that ignores the audience

w.a: Order shows the writer's organization skills, not anything about the audience.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the link to audience

cards.q: Contrast pathos (Rhetorical Situation) and tone (Style), using this invented line from a firefighter's statement at a budget hearing: 'Last winter we reached the Ortiz house four minutes late. I carried their daughter out myself.'
cards.a: Pathos is the appeal to the audience's emotions: the late arrival and the rescued child make council members feel fear and responsibility. Tone is the speaker's attitude, here restrained and grave, conveyed by two short, plain sentences with no adjectives. The two work together, since the restraint keeps the appeal from sounding manipulative, but pathos concerns the audience's feeling and tone the writer's attitude.
cards.h: → each term applied to the line + how they work together
cards.n: Calling the tone 'pathos' is the trap: tone belongs to the writer, pathos to what the audience is moved to feel.

cards.q: Contrast an emotional appeal that supports a claim and one that replaces evidence, using these invented sentences about a proposed reservoir: (A) 'The valley holds 140 family farms; the reservoir would drown 38 of them, including the Hale farm, worked by five generations.' (B) 'Only a heartless person could support drowning this beautiful valley.'
cards.a: (A) supports the claim: its emotional pull (five generations of one family) rests on evidence, a count showing that more than a quarter of the valley's farms would be lost, so readers feel what the facts justify. (B) replaces evidence: it offers no fact about the reservoir and tries to make disagreement feel shameful, which also insults undecided readers. An appeal to emotion persuades best when it grows out of evidence and reasoning.
cards.h: → which supports, which replaces, and the test
cards.n: Tempting to call both 'pathos' and stop; the credited contrast is whether the feeling rests on evidence.

cards.q: Explain how the anecdote in this invented testimony works at once as evidence, as a method of development, and as an emotional appeal: a nurse urging state legislators to limit patient loads describes a night she cared for nine patients and noticed one man's rising fever two hours late.
cards.a: As evidence it is an anecdote, a concrete case supporting the claim that heavy loads endanger patients. As development it is narration: real experience whose significance she draws out (the delay came from the load, not carelessness). As an appeal it makes legislators imagine the patient, and her firsthand account builds her credibility. One choice serves claim, reasoning, and audience at once.
cards.h: → three roles, one sentence each + the link
cards.n: Naming only 'pathos' is the trap: the story also carries the claim and organizes the reasoning, which is what makes it persuasive.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented line of commentary and correct it: 'The writer's tone is pathos because the passage is very emotional.'
cards.a: Error: it confuses tone, the writer's attitude, with pathos, an appeal to the audience's emotions. Corrected: 'The writer's tone is grieving but controlled; that restraint lets the details of the flooded classroom carry the pathos, so readers feel the loss without feeling pushed.' Name the attitude, then explain how it shapes the audience's response.
cards.h: → the confusion named + corrected commentary
cards.n: Tempting because both involve feeling; tone describes the writer's attitude, pathos the emotions the writer aims to stir in readers.

cards.q: Identify whether the emotional effect of each invented sentence comes mainly from its evidence, its word choice, or its sentence structure: 1. 'Forty-one children in this district slept in cars last year.' 2. 'The shelter is a warehouse for the forgotten.' 3. 'They waited. They waited through the fall, through the first snow, through the holidays.' 4. 'The Moreno twins did their homework by the dome light of a Buick.' 5. 'We have, in our generosity, given them a parking lot.' 6. 'No bed. No desk. No door that locks.' 7. 'The county spends more on the courthouse fountain than on shelter beds.'
cards.a:
1 → evidence: a plain statistic whose scale carries the feeling
2 → word choice: 'warehouse' and 'forgotten' make people into stored goods
3 → structure: repetition and a lengthening series stretch the wait
4 → evidence: an anecdote whose concrete detail makes one family visible
5 → word choice: 'generosity' is ironic, so the praise condemns
6 → structure: parallel fragments strip the scene to what is missing
7 → evidence: a comparison of two facts that exposes priorities
cards.h: → evidence, word choice, or structure per line + the tell
cards.n: Most lines use more than one; name the source doing the most work, since commentary must point at a specific choice, not at 'emotion'.

cards.q: Explain how subordination helps this invented speaker establish credibility without shifting attention to herself: 'Although I have taught chemistry here for nineteen years, tonight's question is not about me but about the lab's broken ventilation.'
cards.a: Placing her nineteen years in the dependent 'although' clause gives the audience her credentials but marks them as secondary; the independent clause carries the point, the ventilation. Because subordination shows an imbalance between ideas, her authority supports the claim instead of competing with it, and the modesty itself adds to her credibility.
cards.h: → what each clause holds + the effect on credibility
cards.n: 'She builds ethos by mentioning experience' misses how: the credit lies in the subordination, which keeps the claim in front.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented student claim and correct it: 'Because the writer uses statistics, the passage appeals only to logos and has no emotional appeal.'
cards.a: Error: it sorts appeals by type of evidence, when one piece of evidence can build several. Corrected: 'The statistic that one in five children in the county goes to bed hungry appeals to logic through its scale and to emotion through what it asks readers to imagine.' Strategically selected evidence strengthens reasoning, relates to the audience's emotions and values, and adds credibility at once.
cards.h: → the false sorting named + corrected claim
cards.n: Tempting because classroom charts pair statistics with logos; numbers about people routinely carry emotional weight.

cards.q: Write one sentence of commentary explaining how the word 'abandoned' in this invented sentence builds an emotional appeal: 'The county has abandoned the Route 9 bridge.'
cards.a: Model: 'By calling the county's inaction abandonment, the writer casts the county as a caretaker who walked away from the people who depend on it, so readers feel the bridge's neglect as a betrayal rather than a scheduling delay, which makes the repair feel owed.' The sentence names the connotation, the feeling it produces, and what that feeling does for the argument.
cards.h: → one sentence: connotation + feeling + purpose
cards.n: 'Abandoned is a strong word' names nothing; the credited sentence says what the word suggests and what the suggestion does.

cards.q: Decide which invented closing sentence better serves a speech urging a city council to fund a teen center, and explain: (A) 'If you vote no tonight, whatever happens to these kids is on your hands.' (B) 'Vote yes, and the next time a fifteen-year-old has nowhere to go at 9 p.m., she will have somewhere.'
cards.a: (B). It calls the audience to act and leaves a compelling image, two of a conclusion's jobs, and its emotional pull rests on a concrete case the council can picture. (A) threatens the people whose votes the speaker needs; its accusatory tone makes the council defensive, so the emotional appeal costs the speaker credibility.
cards.h: → letter + the conclusion's job + tone's effect
cards.n: (A) is tempting because it is forceful; blaming the decision-makers turns an emotional appeal into an attack on the audience.

cards.q: Explain how the concrete details in this invented description appeal to emotion without naming any emotion: 'The gym roof leaks over the free-throw line. Buckets sit on the bleachers. The scoreboard clock stopped in 1998.'
cards.a: Description relates sensory details (a leak, buckets, a dead clock), and readers supply the feeling themselves: neglect, embarrassment, years of waiting. Because the writer never says 'sad' or 'shameful,' the audience experiences the emotion as its own conclusion from evidence, which is harder to dismiss than an announced feeling.
cards.h: → what the details are + how readers supply the feeling
cards.n: 'The details create imagery' stops at the device; the credited point is that readers infer the emotion, so it feels earned.

cards.q: Explain why a restrained tone often makes an emotional anecdote more persuasive than an openly outraged one.
cards.a: When the tone is calm, the facts of the anecdote carry the emotion and readers feel it as their own response; outrage tells them what to feel, which invites resistance and makes the writer seem less credible, so the same story moves the audience less.
cards.h: → calm tone → facts carry the feeling → readers own the emotion → writer stays credible → the appeal lands
cards.n: 'Outrage is unprofessional' is a rule, not a reason; the point is who supplies the emotion, the writer or the reader.
o: An understated account signals that the writer is not exaggerating, which makes the events themselves seem more serious.
Readers who feel pushed tend to push back; restraint lowers that resistance while keeping the emotional content.

w.a: A calm tone is better because emotions have no place in arguments.
w.why: misreads the case: the emotion still works, through the facts

w.a: Outrage is more persuasive because it shows the writer really cares.
w.why: ignores how audiences resist being told what to feel

w.a: Tone and anecdotes are separate choices, so one cannot affect the other.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses how style shapes the appeal

cards.q: Explain why tone and pathos are different even when a sad tone helps an emotional appeal.
cards.a: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject, conveyed through word choice and style; pathos is an appeal to the audience's emotions. A sad tone can support pathos, but a writer can also stir anger or hope in a calm tone, so naming the tone does not explain what the audience is meant to feel or why.
cards.h: → tone = writer's attitude → pathos = audience's emotion aimed at → they can differ → analyze both
cards.n: Using the two terms interchangeably earns nothing; an analysis must say whose feeling it means.
o: A satirist can write in an amused tone while stirring the audience's outrage, so the two can point in different directions.
Tone is inferred from the writer's words; pathos is judged by the response the writer seeks from a particular audience.

w.a: Tone and pathos are the same thing because both are about emotions.
w.why: erases the writer-versus-audience distinction

w.a: Pathos is only for sad writing, so a sad tone always means pathos.
w.why: emotional appeals include anger, fear, hope, and pride

w.a: Tone is a style term, so it has nothing to do with persuasion.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses how tone shapes the appeal

cards.q: Explain why a single piece of evidence can build logos, pathos, and ethos at once.
cards.a: Strategically selected evidence does several jobs: a specific, sourced figure about local children strengthens the reasoning, makes readers feel the scale of the problem, and shows that the writer did the research, so one choice serves claim, audience, and credibility together.
cards.h: → evidence supports reasoning → it touches values → its care shows research → three appeals from one choice
cards.n: Sorting each piece of evidence into one appeal is the trap; the CED lists all three effects for well-chosen evidence.
o: Appeals are effects on an audience, not labels on sentences, so one sentence can produce several effects.
A firsthand account supports a claim, shows the writer's standing to make it, and, through its human detail, moves readers, all at once.

w.a: Each piece of evidence can only be ethos, pathos, or logos, never more than one.
w.why: treats appeals as exclusive categories

w.a: Statistics are logos and stories are pathos.
w.why: sorts by evidence type instead of by effect

w.a: Evidence proves the claim, and appeals are something separate the writer adds.
w.why: the one-unit answer that splits evidence from audience

cards.q: Explain why an emotional appeal in a conclusion works best when the body has already supplied the evidence behind it.
cards.a: A conclusion can engage readers with a compelling image or a call to act, but they accept the feeling only if the argument has earned it; after the evidence, the image reads as the claim made vivid, whereas without it the same image reads as manipulation.
cards.h: → body supplies evidence → the closing image recalls it → the feeling seems earned → readers act rather than resist
cards.n: 'End with emotion to leave an impression' is a formula; placement after evidence is what makes the emotion credible.
o: The line of reasoning leads readers to the conclusion, so an emotional close confirms what they already accept instead of asking them to feel first.
An emotional appeal with no evidence behind it can be dismissed as a trick, which damages the writer's credibility.

w.a: Emotional appeals belong in the introduction to hook readers.
w.why: ignores why placement after the evidence matters

w.a: Conclusions should only summarize, so emotion does not belong there.
w.why: the CED lists images and calls to action among a conclusion's moves

w.a: The emotion works anywhere as long as the story is sad enough.
w.why: ignores the evidence needed to earn the feeling

cards.q: Explain why short, fragmentary sentences can intensify an emotional appeal in an argument.
cards.a: Short fragments slow the reader and isolate each detail, so every item lands with its own weight; the arrangement emphasizes the losses, and the audience dwells on them long enough to feel them, which one long list would hurry past.
cards.h: → fragments isolate details → each gets its own weight → readers linger → the feeling builds
cards.n: 'Fragments are grammatically wrong' is the one-unit reflex; used deliberately, they are an arrangement choice that serves the appeal.
o: Breaking a series into fragments turns a list into a sequence of pauses, which mimics how a person absorbs bad news.
The stripped syntax also sets a tone of restraint, which keeps the appeal from sounding overwrought.

w.a: Short sentences are easier to read, so they are always more emotional.
w.why: ease of reading is not the mechanism

w.a: Fragments are errors and weaken any argument.
w.why: ignores deliberate arrangement for emphasis

w.a: The emotion comes from the words, not from sentence length.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses how syntax shapes the appeal

cards.q: Contrast a text's purpose (Rhetorical Situation) and its thesis (Claims and Evidence), using an invented op-ed that argues a proposed warehouse's truck traffic will clog Route 4 and urges readers to attend Tuesday's zoning hearing.
cards.a: The purpose is what the writer hopes to accomplish: to get readers to the hearing to oppose the permit. The thesis is the main claim the writer defends: that the warehouse's truck traffic will clog Route 4. The thesis serves the purpose, since readers must accept the claim before they will act, but the two differ: a writer may have several purposes and still one overarching claim.
cards.h: → purpose (what it aims to do) vs thesis (what it claims)
cards.n: Giving the thesis when asked for the purpose is the trap; a purpose is an action on the audience, a thesis a claim to defend.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented thesis and the body plan that follows it, then correct both: 'In this essay I will discuss the pros and cons of year-round school.' Paragraph 1: benefits. Paragraph 2: drawbacks. Paragraph 3: conclusion.
cards.a: Error: the thesis announces a topic but takes no position, so the body has no line of reasoning, only a sorted list. Corrected: 'Year-round school is worth adopting, because shorter breaks reduce the learning students lose over a long summer, and families' objections about vacations can be met with a longer spring break.' Paragraph 1 shows the loss, paragraph 2 the benefit of shorter breaks, paragraph 3 answers the vacation objection, each step building toward the claim.
cards.h: → the error in a clause + a revised thesis and plan
cards.n: Tempting because it looks balanced; a plan that only sorts pros and cons cannot reveal a line of reasoning, since nothing is argued.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented student's revision and correct it: after finding a source showing that the district's electric buses saved far less on fuel than predicted, the student kept the thesis 'Electric buses will save the district a fortune on fuel' and placed the new source in the last paragraph.
cards.a: Error: evidence that contradicts the thesis should lead to revising the thesis or the line of reasoning, not to burying it at the end. Corrected thesis: 'Electric buses are worth their cost less for fuel savings, which proved small, than for cleaner air at the stops where students wait.' The order changes too: the fuel evidence becomes an early concession, and the air-quality evidence carries the argument.
cards.h: → the error + revised thesis + what moves
cards.n: Tempting because the thesis 'still has evidence'; contradicting evidence tucked at the end tells readers the writer will not follow the evidence.

cards.q: Decide which invented topic sentence better advances this thesis, and explain: 'Our school should grade homework for completion only, because grading practice punishes the mistakes practice exists to produce.' (A) 'Many students have homework in several classes each night.' (B) 'A student who gets a problem wrong on Tuesday's homework and right on Friday's test has learned exactly what practice is for.'
cards.a: (B). A body paragraph makes a claim that advances the line of reasoning; (B) claims that early mistakes are part of learning, the thesis's own reason, and invites evidence. (A) is an obvious fact that requires no defense and connects to nothing in the thesis.
cards.h: → letter + what a topic sentence must do
cards.n: (A) is tempting because it sounds like a safe opening; an obvious fact advances no step in the line of reasoning.

cards.q: Identify where the thesis appears in this invented passage and what its placement does: '(1) In 2019 the town planted forty maples on Grant Street. (2) By 2024, shop owners there reported that customers lingered longer in summer. (3) On a July afternoon, Grant Street's pavement measured nine degrees cooler than bare Pine Street's. (4) Shade, it turns out, is not decoration; it is infrastructure, and the town should budget for it like roads.'
cards.a: The thesis is sentence 4, at the end. The passage leads readers through evidence (the plantings, the lingering customers, the cooler pavement) and then arrives at the claim, so the claim reads as the conclusion the evidence has already made likely. The metaphor 'infrastructure' reframes trees as a budget item just when readers are ready to accept it.
cards.h: → sentence number + the reasoning before it + effect
cards.n: Picking sentence 1 because theses 'come first' is the trap; here the first sentence is evidence and the claim arrives last.

cards.q: Write a thesis statement for this invented column, which never states one: the columnist describes her town's pool closing for lack of lifeguards, notes that the county pays lifeguards less than the drive-through across the street pays cashiers, and ends by listing the three summers the pool has now been closed.
cards.a: Model: 'The town's pool will stay closed until the county pays lifeguards at least what the jobs across the street pay, because the shortage is a wage problem, not a lack of willing teenagers.' The column's sequence (the closing, the pay gap, the lost summers) reveals a cause-then-consequence line of reasoning, so the thesis names the cause and the remedy the evidence points to.
cards.h: → one defensible sentence + how the order revealed it
cards.n: Writing 'the pool is closed' restates the topic; an implied thesis is the claim the evidence is arranged to prove.

cards.q: Contrast how the arrangement of sentences within a paragraph (Style) and the sequence of paragraphs in a text (Reasoning and Organization) each shape what readers take from an argument.
cards.a: Within a paragraph, arrangement emphasizes by position: the sentence placed last, or set apart, gets the reader's attention, as when a short final sentence lands a point. Across a text, sequence reveals the line of reasoning: which reason comes first, which builds on which, and which the argument ends on. The first shapes what readers notice in the moment; the second shapes what they conclude overall.
cards.h: → sentence-level emphasis vs text-level reasoning
cards.n: Treating both as 'organization' is the trap; one is emphasis within a unit, the other the logic of the whole.

cards.q: Write a thesis for a rhetorical analysis of this invented situation: a volunteer fire chief writes to residents asking them to approve a $24 yearly fee; she opens with the department's 11-minute average response time and closes by naming the three volunteers who retired this year.
cards.a: Model: 'To win a fee from residents who doubt they need it, the chief opens with the eleven-minute response time to make the danger measurable and closes with the names of the retired volunteers to make the shortage personal, so that paying $24 a year reads as protecting neighbors rather than funding a department.' It names the purpose, the audience's doubt, two choices in order, and what each does.
cards.h: → purpose + audience + choices in order + effect
cards.n: Listing 'statistics and names' without the purpose they serve restates the passage; the thesis must say what the choices accomplish.

cards.q: Decide whether this invented speaker states her claim first and then justifies it or leads through reasoning to arrive at it, and explain what the choice suggests about her audience: 'The library should open on Sundays. Sunday is the only day many shift workers are free. It is the day students cram for Monday tests. And the building, already heated, sits empty.'
cards.a: She states the claim first and then justifies it with three reasons. The choice suggests she expects a receptive or at least open audience: naming the claim at once risks little resistance, and the reasons read as support for a proposal already on the table rather than as steps toward a surprise.
cards.h: → which structure + what it assumes about readers
cards.n: Answering only 'claim first' earns half; the credited answer ties the structure to what the writer assumes about the audience.

cards.q: Explain how the conclusion of this invented essay connects to its introduction and what the connection does for the thesis: the essay opens with a grandmother's 1962 photograph of the town square full of market stalls, and closes by asking readers to picture the same square, now a parking lot, filled with stalls again next spring.
cards.a: The conclusion returns to the introduction's image and transforms it: a scene from the past becomes a future readers can help create. The frame unifies the argument and turns the thesis (the town should license a weekly market in the square) from a claim about what was lost into a call to action, one of the jobs the CED gives a conclusion.
cards.h: → the frame + what changes + what it does for the thesis
cards.n: 'The conclusion restates the introduction' is the trap; the credited answer says what changes between the two images and why.

cards.q: Identify the exigence of this invented letter and explain how it shapes both the introduction and the thesis: a week after a van carrying a youth soccer team slid off an unguarded curve on County Road 9, a retired highway engineer writes to the county newspaper, opens with the date of the crash, and argues that the county should install guardrails on its four sharpest curves before winter.
cards.a: The exigence is the crash, the event that prompted the letter. It shapes the introduction, which opens with the date so readers begin from an event they already know and fear, and it shapes the thesis, a narrow, urgent policy claim (four curves, before winter) rather than a general complaint about road safety, because the crash makes a specific, timely remedy easy to defend.
cards.h: → the exigence + its effect on the intro + on the thesis
cards.n: Naming 'road safety' as the exigence is the trap: the exigence is the specific event that prompted this text, not its general topic.

cards.q: Explain why a thesis that is an obvious fact leaves an essay without a line of reasoning.
cards.a: An obvious fact requires no defense, so the body paragraphs have nothing to prove; they can only add more facts, and without a claim to advance, their order reveals no reasoning, so the essay reads as a list.
cards.h: → obvious fact needs no defense → nothing to prove → paragraphs just accumulate → no sequence, no reasoning
cards.n: 'The thesis is too simple' misses the mechanism: a claim that needs no defense gives the body no job.
o: The line of reasoning is the path from evidence to claim, and a fact everyone accepts has no path because readers are already there.
Body paragraphs make claims that advance the thesis, and a factual thesis gives them nothing to advance.

w.a: The thesis is fine as long as the body has a lot of evidence.
w.why: evidence with no claim to support is not an argument

w.a: An obvious fact makes a strong thesis because nobody can disagree with it.
w.why: the CED says an effective claim requires a defense

w.a: The only problem is that the essay will be boring.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the missing line of reasoning

cards.q: Explain why new evidence that contradicts a thesis can change the order of an essay's paragraphs, not only the thesis sentence.
cards.a: The sequence of paragraphs reveals the line of reasoning, so when new evidence forces a revised thesis, the steps toward it change too: evidence that once led may become an early concession, and a minor reason may now carry the argument.
cards.h: → new evidence → revised thesis → different steps to reach it → paragraphs reorder
cards.n: Editing only the thesis sentence is the trap; a new claim over the old order leaves the body arguing for the thesis you abandoned.
o: A revised thesis with an unrevised body makes the introduction promise one argument and the paragraphs deliver another.
Contradicting evidence often becomes the concession the revised thesis answers, which changes where it belongs.

w.a: Only the thesis sentence needs to change, since the evidence is the same.
w.why: ignores that the sequence carries the reasoning

w.a: Contradicting evidence should be left out so the thesis can stay.
w.why: the CED says new evidence may require revision

w.a: The order of paragraphs never matters as long as each one is good.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the line of reasoning

cards.q: Explain why a rhetorical-analysis claim about a writer's choice needs the writer's purpose to be defensible.
cards.a: A choice has an effect only relative to what the writer wants from an audience; 'she uses statistics' is an observable fact, but 'the statistics make the cost seem small to a budget board' is a claim someone could dispute, and defending it requires the purpose.
cards.h: → choices matter relative to a goal → a device named is a fact → a device tied to purpose is a defensible claim
cards.n: Listing devices is the trap: 'she uses anaphora' is observable, so it needs no defense and makes no claim.
o: Two writers can use the same device for opposite purposes, so the device alone cannot support any claim about the text.
The purpose is what lets commentary explain why a choice works, which is the point of the analysis.

w.a: The thesis should list as many devices as possible to show knowledge.
w.why: a list of devices is not a claim

w.a: The purpose is obvious, so the thesis can skip it.
w.why: without the purpose, no effect can be argued

w.a: The claim only needs to say the writer is persuasive.
w.why: a verdict with no choices or purpose defends nothing

cards.q: Explain why a thesis statement need not list an essay's points, yet the essay still needs a visible line of reasoning.
cards.a: The CED lets a thesis preview the reasoning but does not require a list; the reasoning can become visible instead through the sequence of body paragraphs, each making a claim that advances the thesis, so readers follow the argument without a roadmap sentence.
cards.h: → a preview is optional → the reasoning must still show → body claims in sequence carry it → readers can trace it
cards.n: 'A thesis must have three points' is the trap: the CED says outright that a thesis need not list them.
o: A thesis that lists points can make an essay mechanical; one that states a claim with a reason leaves room for the reasoning to develop, which readers can follow only if each body paragraph visibly advances the claim.
Topic sentences that each advance the thesis do the work a listed preview would do.

w.a: A thesis must always list three points so readers know the structure.
w.why: the CED says a thesis need not list points

w.a: If the thesis does not list points, the essay does not need organization.
w.why: the line of reasoning still has to be traceable

w.a: The line of reasoning just means the thesis.
w.why: confuses the claim with the path that supports it

cards.q: Explain why an introduction's anecdote should point toward the thesis rather than only grab attention.
cards.a: An introduction may engage readers with an anecdote, but it also orients and focuses them; a story that embodies the problem the thesis answers does both at once, while a disconnected one forces readers to switch topics when the claim arrives.
cards.h: → anecdote engages → if it points to the claim, it also orients → readers carry it into the argument
cards.n: 'Hook the reader' is the trap: the CED says an introduction orients and focuses as well as engages.
o: An anecdote the conclusion can return to gives the argument a frame and grounds the thesis in a real case.
A disconnected hook wastes the audience's first attention, the most valuable space in the text.

w.a: Any interesting story works as an introduction because it gets attention.
w.why: attention without orientation delays the argument

w.a: Anecdotes do not belong in arguments, only in narratives.
w.why: the CED lists anecdotes among introduction moves and evidence types

w.a: The anecdote should come after the thesis so readers know what it proves.
w.why: misses the introduction's job of orienting before the claim

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented line of commentary on a speaker who calls the district's roof repair 'a patch on a patch,' and correct it: 'This quote shows that the speaker feels strongly about the issue.'
cards.a: Error: the commentary is generic; it could follow any quotation and says nothing about how this evidence advances the line of reasoning. Corrected: 'By calling the repair "a patch on a patch," the speaker shrinks the district's plan to a temporary fix already tried once, which prepares her claim that only replacing the roof will last.' Commentary names the choice, its connotation, and its role in the argument.
cards.h: → the error in a clause + commentary that names the choice
cards.n: Tempting because it sounds analytical; 'feels strongly' fits every quotation ever written, so it explains nothing about this one.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented body paragraph plan and correct it: topic sentence; a quotation from Source A; a quotation from Source D; a statistic from Source F; next paragraph.
cards.a: Error: the evidence is stacked with no commentary, so nothing explains how the sources support the claim or relate to one another. Corrected: topic sentence (claim); Source A's quotation, then a sentence on how it supports the claim; Source F's statistic, then a sentence on how it extends or limits A (Source D only if it adds a step); a closing sentence tying the paragraph to the thesis. A body paragraph makes a claim, supports it, and explains its contribution.
cards.h: → the missing element + a rebuilt plan
cards.n: Tempting because three sources look thorough; without commentary the reader must guess how each one supports the claim.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented passage from a synthesis essay and correct it: 'Schools should start later. "Teen drivers who slept eight hours had fewer crashes" (Source C).'
cards.a: Error: the quotation is dropped in, neither introduced nor embedded in the writer's sentence, and no commentary connects it to the claim. Corrected: 'Later start times protect students beyond the classroom: Source C, a study of teen drivers, found that those "who slept eight hours had fewer crashes," so an extra hour of sleep is also a safety measure for the morning commute.'
cards.h: → the error + an embedded, explained version
cards.n: Tempting because the citation is correct; a cited quotation does no work until the writer's own sentence says what it shows.

cards.q: Contrast evidence used to illustrate a claim and evidence used to amplify it (Claims and Evidence), and say what the commentary for each must do (Reasoning and Organization).
cards.a: Evidence that illustrates gives a concrete case of the claim, so its commentary must show the case is representative, not a lucky exception. Evidence that amplifies enlarges the claim's stakes or scale, so its commentary must connect the larger stakes back to the specific claim. Either way, commentary explains the evidence's significance and relevance to the line of reasoning.
cards.h: → each purpose + the commentary it needs
cards.n: The CED lists illustrate and amplify without defining them (these are working glosses); the trap is commentary that only repeats the evidence.

cards.q: Write one or two sentences of commentary connecting this invented evidence to the claim. Claim: 'The town should keep the pool open through August.' Evidence: 'Last August the pool logged 1,900 visits, 700 of them by children in the free summer lunch program.'
cards.a: Model: 'More than a third of August's visits came from children in the lunch program, the families least able to pay for another way to spend a hot afternoon. Closing the pool in August would take the town's cheapest summer refuge from exactly the residents who have no substitute.' The commentary interprets the number (who the visitors are) and ties it to why August matters, instead of repeating the figure.
cards.h: → interpret the number + tie it to the claim
cards.n: Restating '700 of 1,900 visits were lunch-program children' is summary; commentary says why that share matters to the claim.

cards.q: Decide which invented line of commentary better explains this evidence, and why. Evidence: two of the three bus routes the city plans to cut serve the county hospital's night shift. (A) 'This statistic is very persuasive and makes a strong point.' (B) 'The council has called the cuts trimming waste; showing that the routes carry hospital workers recasts the waste as service the city cannot spare.'
cards.a: (B). It explains the evidence's significance in relation to the line of reasoning: it answers the council's own framing ('waste') and shows why these riders matter. (A) evaluates the evidence without explaining it; 'persuasive' and 'strong' could describe any fact.
cards.h: → letter + what the better one does
cards.n: (A) is tempting because it praises the evidence; praise is a verdict, and commentary must give the reasons.

cards.q: Identify the job each sentence does in this invented body paragraph (claim, transition into evidence, evidence, or commentary): '(1) Parking meters on Main Street hurt the shops they were meant to help. (2) Consider the city's own survey. (3) After the meters went in, 41 percent of shoppers said they now drive to the mall instead. (4) A meter meant to free up spaces for customers has instead sent customers where parking is free.'
cards.a: (1) claim, the paragraph's topic sentence; (2) transition that introduces the evidence and signals its source; (3) evidence, a statistic from that survey; (4) commentary, which explains that the meters defeat their own purpose and so ties the number to the claim. The pattern is the CED's body paragraph: a claim, evidence, and commentary, linked by transitional elements.
cards.h: → one job per sentence + which one reasons
cards.n: Labeling (2) as evidence is the trap: it points to evidence but supplies none; transitions can introduce evidence as well as link ideas.

cards.q: Write one sentence of commentary for a rhetorical analysis explaining how this invented speaker's phrase serves her purpose with city council members: she calls the vacant lot on Fifth Street 'a tire graveyard.'
cards.a: Model: 'By calling the lot a "tire graveyard," the speaker turns an empty parcel into a place where things are dumped and left to rot, so council members who might see a harmless vacancy see instead a hazard they are responsible for, and her cleanup proposal looks like overdue maintenance.' It names the choice, its connotation, and its effect on this audience's view of the claim.
cards.h: → one sentence: choice + connotation + effect on readers
cards.n: Stopping at 'the metaphor creates an image' is the trap; the point is what the image makes this audience believe.

cards.q: Write one sentence that embeds a paraphrase of this invented source into your own claim and signals how it supports it. Source B, a county health department survey, found that 62 percent of 1,200 households surveyed had no smoke detector with a working battery. Claim: the fire department should run a free detector program.
cards.a: Model: 'A free detector program would reach a danger hiding in plain sight: the county health department found that 744 of the 1,200 households it surveyed, 62 percent, had no working smoke detector (Source B), so the problem is common, not rare.' The paraphrase sits inside the writer's claim, is attributed, and is followed by a clause saying what it shows.
cards.h: → claim + attributed paraphrase + what it shows
cards.n: Opening with 'Source B says' makes the source the subject; the credited sentence keeps the writer's claim in charge and the source in support.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented line of commentary and correct it: 'This survey, in which 58 of 80 Lincoln High students chose a later start, proves that all teenagers want later start times.'
cards.a: Error: the commentary claims more than the evidence can support, leaping from one school's 80 students to all teenagers. Corrected: 'The survey suggests that most Lincoln students who answered, 58 of 80, want a later start, which gives the board local evidence worth testing with a larger sample.' Commentary should state what the evidence shows and no more.
cards.h: → the overreach named + a claim sized to the evidence
cards.n: Tempting because 58 of 80 is a clear majority; a clear majority of one small sample is still one small sample.

cards.q: Explain why strong evidence without commentary rarely advances a line of reasoning.
cards.a: Evidence does not explain itself: commentary establishes the logical relationship between evidence and claim, saying why it matters at this step of the argument. Without it, readers must guess the connection, and readers who connect it differently may even take it as support for the other side.
cards.h: → evidence alone is ambiguous → commentary states the link → without it readers guess → the reasoning stalls
cards.n: 'The evidence speaks for itself' is the trap; the CED puts the reasoning in the commentary, not in the evidence.
o: The same statistic can support opposite claims, so only commentary fixes which claim it supports here.
Commentary explains significance and relevance; a strong fact with no stated relevance is just information.

w.a: Strong evidence speaks for itself, so commentary is only needed for weak evidence.
w.why: evidence never states its own relation to the claim

w.a: Commentary just repeats the evidence in different words.
w.why: confuses commentary with paraphrase

w.a: As long as the evidence is cited correctly, the paragraph is complete.
w.why: the one-unit answer that stops at the source

cards.q: Explain why commentary on a single word's connotation counts as reasoning in a rhetorical analysis, not just description.
cards.a: Naming a connotation describes; explaining what it makes the audience believe, and how that belief serves the writer's purpose, is reasoning, because it links a specific choice to the analysis's claim, which is what commentary must do.
cards.h: → connotation named = description → its effect on the audience + link to purpose = reasoning
cards.n: Stopping at 'the word has a negative connotation' is the trap; description becomes reasoning only when it reaches audience and purpose.
o: A thesis about a writer's strategy is defended by specific choices; one word's connotation is evidence, and its effect is the commentary.
Close attention to one word can trace how that choice serves the writer's purpose with this audience, which is reasoning, while a survey of many devices only names them.

w.a: Talking about one word is too small to count as analysis.
w.why: size is not the test; the link to purpose is

w.a: Identifying the connotation is enough to show analysis.
w.why: naming the connotation without its effect is description

w.a: Word choice belongs to style, so it cannot support a claim about purpose.
w.why: the one-unit answer that separates style from purpose

cards.q: Explain why introducing a quotation with a signal phrase does part of commentary's work.
cards.a: A signal phrase names the source and frames the quotation ('the district's own engineer admits'), so readers know who speaks and how the writer is using the words before they see them; it begins integrating the source into the line of reasoning, which is commentary's job.
cards.h: → signal phrase names source and stance → the quotation arrives framed → integration begins before the quote
cards.n: 'Signal phrases are just for citation' is the trap; a verb like 'admits' already argues something about the evidence.
o: The verb in a signal phrase (claims, admits, warns) tells readers how much weight to give the quotation.
A transition that introduces evidence shows its relationship to the idea before it, which is part of explaining it.

w.a: Signal phrases are only needed to avoid plagiarism.
w.why: misses their role in framing the evidence

w.a: The quotation should come first so readers can judge it without the writer's influence.
w.why: an unframed quotation leaves its role unexplained

w.a: Any signal phrase works, such as 'Source A says.'
w.why: a neutral phrase frames nothing about the evidence's role

cards.q: Explain why the same quotation needs different commentary in two essays with different claims.
cards.a: Commentary explains evidence's significance in relation to a particular line of reasoning, so a quotation that supports one claim is read for one feature and, under another claim, for a different one; the words stay the same, but their relevance does not.
cards.h: → commentary ties evidence to a claim → a different claim asks a different question → same words, new relevance
cards.n: Reusing a canned explanation for a favorite quotation is the trap; commentary is written for the claim, not for the quote.
o: A mayor's line that the budget is 'balanced for now' supports a claim about her caution in one essay and about future deficits in another, so each essay's commentary must explain a different part of it, 'balanced' or 'for now.'
Because evidence can support, complement, or contradict a thesis, its role depends on the thesis it meets.

w.a: A quotation always means the same thing, so the commentary should be the same.
w.why: confuses what a quotation means with what it does in an argument

w.a: Commentary explains the quotation, not the claim.
w.why: the CED ties commentary to the claim and the line of reasoning

w.a: Only the evidence matters; commentary is decoration.
w.why: the reasoning lives in the commentary

cards.q: Explain why commentary should follow each piece of evidence rather than wait until the end of the paragraph.
cards.a: Coherence depends on each sentence linking logically to the next; commentary placed right after a piece of evidence explains it while it is in the reader's mind, whereas commentary saved for the end leaves readers sorting out which explanation fits which evidence.
cards.h: → each sentence should link to the next → commentary beside its evidence keeps the link → delay blurs the match
cards.n: 'One summary sentence at the end covers it' is the trap; stacked evidence reads as a list until the explanation finally arrives.
o: When two sources sit side by side with commentary between them, the commentary can also show how the second extends or limits the first.
A reader who meets unexplained evidence may draw a different conclusion before the writer's explanation arrives.

w.a: It does not matter where the commentary goes as long as it is in the paragraph.
w.why: placement decides whether readers can match explanation to evidence

w.a: Commentary belongs only at the end, to wrap up the paragraph.
w.why: a wrap-up cannot explain each piece of evidence

w.a: More evidence before any commentary makes the paragraph stronger.
w.why: the one-unit answer that treats quantity as reasoning

cards.q: Contrast a modifier that qualifies a claim (Claims and Evidence) and a modifier as a matter of sentence clarity (Style), using this invented sentence: 'Most commuters who drive alone would switch to the bus if it ran every ten minutes.'
cards.a: As qualification, 'most,' 'who drive alone,' and 'if it ran every ten minutes' limit the argument's scope: not all commuters, only solo drivers, only with frequent service, so the claim is easier to defend. As clarity, each modifier must sit next to what it modifies; 'who drive alone' belongs right after 'commuters.' Misplace one and the sentence says something else, so a grammar slip can change the claim's scope.
cards.h: → the scope each modifier limits + the placement rule
cards.n: Treating these as two unrelated topics is the trap: in an argument, where a modifier sits decides what the claim covers.

cards.q: Explain how changing this invented sentence from coordination to subordination changes both the balance of ideas and the force of the claim: (A) 'The plan is expensive, and it will save lives.' (B) 'Although the plan is expensive, it will save lives.'
cards.a: (A) coordinates two independent clauses, presenting cost and lives as equal ideas, so the reader weighs them evenly. (B) puts the cost in a dependent 'although' clause, conceding it while making it secondary, and the independent clause, 'it will save lives,' carries the claim. The syntax performs the concession: the writer grants the objection and still makes the benefit dominant.
cards.h: → balance in A + imbalance in B + what B concedes
cards.n: Calling the versions equivalent is the trap; 'and' or 'although' decides which idea the reader takes as the point.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented thesis and correct it: 'Social media might possibly be somewhat harmful to some teenagers in certain cases.'
cards.a: Error: stacked hedges ('might possibly,' 'somewhat,' 'some,' 'in certain cases') qualify the claim until it takes no clear position and needs no defense. Corrected: 'Social media harms teenagers most when it cuts into sleep, so schools should teach students to protect the hour before bed.' One precise limit ('when it cuts into sleep') sets the scope and leaves a position to defend.
cards.h: → the error + one precise qualifier in its place
cards.n: Tempting because the CED values qualified claims; qualification limits scope precisely, while vague hedges only blur it.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented concession and correct it: 'Some people say the curfew keeps teens safe, but they are just wrong.'
cards.a: Error: it names the opposing view but neither concedes any part of it nor rebuts it with evidence, and 'just wrong' is dismissive diction that costs credibility. Corrected: 'Supporters are right that most late-night incidents involving teens happen after 11 p.m.; but in the year since the curfew began, those incidents have not fallen, so the rule has not delivered the safety it promised.' Concede a portion, then rebut with evidence.
cards.h: → the error + a concede-then-rebut version
cards.n: Tempting because it mentions the other side; naming a view in order to dismiss it is neither a concession nor a rebuttal.

cards.q: Decide whether each invented sentence from an argument for a later school start concedes, rebuts, or qualifies (limits the writer's own claim): 1. 'Critics are right that the new schedule costs more in its first year.' 2. 'But the study they cite measured one school in its first month.' 3. 'The later start helps most students, though not those who work early shifts.' 4. 'Granted, some parents will need new morning childcare.' 5. 'That objection assumes buses cannot be rerouted, and the district's own plan reroutes them.' 6. 'In districts with long bus routes, the benefit is likely smaller.' 7. 'Yes, scores fell that year, but they fell statewide, and by more.'
cards.a:
1 → concedes (grants the critics' point)
2 → rebuts (questions the evidence behind the objection)
3 → qualifies (limits whom the claim covers)
4 → concedes (accepts a cost of the writer's plan)
5 → rebuts (shows the objection's assumption is false)
6 → qualifies (limits where the claim holds)
7 → concedes, then rebuts (grants the drop, then recasts it with wider evidence)
cards.h: → one move per line + the tell
cards.n: Turn words ('granted,' 'but,' 'though') are clues, not proof: line 7 makes two moves, and lines 3 and 6 limit the writer's own claim.

cards.q: Identify the shift in tone in this invented passage and what it suggests about the writer's perspective: 'For years I mocked school gardens as photo opportunities for principals. Then I spent a month at Harlan Valley Middle School, where students grow a third of the cafeteria's lettuce. I still doubt it would work at a school our size, but I no longer laugh.'
cards.a: The tone shifts from mocking ('photo opportunities for principals') to measured respect ('I still doubt... but I no longer laugh'). The shift signals a refined perspective: the writer has reconsidered without converting, qualifying the old dismissal while keeping a reservation. Showing that change of mind makes the writer credible to skeptical readers, who are invited to make the same move.
cards.h: → from what tone to what + what the shift qualifies
cards.n: Calling it 'a change of opinion' overstates it: 'I still doubt' keeps a reservation, which is exactly what makes it a qualification.

cards.q: Identify how the parenthetical element in this invented sentence qualifies the claim and serves the audience, a school board that has seen the data: 'The later start raised attendance at all four high schools (at Lincoln, only slightly), so the board should keep it.'
cards.a: The parenthesis limits the claim honestly: attendance rose everywhere, but not evenly. Set off as nonessential, it supplies information without interrupting the main claim, and it anticipates board members who know Lincoln's numbers, so the writer names the weak case before anyone can use it against her. The qualification protects credibility without changing the position.
cards.h: → what it limits + why it is set off + effect on the board
cards.n: Calling the parenthesis 'extra information' misses its job: it is a qualification placed where it costs the claim least.

cards.q: Write a qualified version of this invented absolute claim, keeping the writer's position and using a modifying phrase or clause: 'Homework is useless.'
cards.a: Model: 'Homework that only repeats what students mastered in class does little for learning, so teachers should assign less of it and more practice on what students have not yet mastered.' The relative clause limits the claim to one kind of homework, so no single counterexample of useful homework refutes it, and the argument against pointless assignments stands.
cards.h: → one sentence with a limiting clause + what it limits
cards.n: Adding 'maybe' or 'some people think' weakens without qualifying; a real qualifier says exactly where the claim holds.

cards.q: Decide which placement of 'only' makes this invented claim say what the writer means, that a bus ban should apply to one street and no other: (A) 'The council should only ban buses on Main Street.' (B) 'The council should ban buses only on Main Street.'
cards.a: (B). 'Only' placed before 'on Main Street' limits the location, which is the writer's qualification. In (A), 'only' sits before the verb, so it can be read as limiting the action (the council should do nothing but ban buses), which leaves the claim's scope ambiguous. Modifiers belong next to what they modify, and in an argument that placement decides what is claimed.
cards.h: → letter + what each placement limits
cards.n: (A) is how people talk, which makes it tempting; in writing, a misplaced 'only' can change the scope a reader holds you to.

cards.q: Explain how opening with a summary of an existing debate, in this invented introduction, both qualifies the writer's claim and does an introduction's job: 'Parents who want phones banned from classrooms and students who want them allowed agree on one thing: attention is the problem. They disagree about who should manage it.'
cards.a: By first stating what both sides already argue, the writer enters an ongoing conversation rather than claiming the subject from scratch, and signals that her claim will answer those positions instead of ignoring them. As an introduction, it orients and focuses the audience: the shared concern (attention) is common ground, and the disagreement (who manages it) is the question her thesis will answer.
cards.h: → what engaging prior positions does + the intro's job
cards.n: Calling the opening 'background' misses that summarizing both sides fairly is itself a credibility move and sets the terms of the claim.

cards.q: Explain why putting a concession in a subordinate clause keeps the writer's claim dominant.
cards.a: Subordination shows an imbalance between ideas: the dependent clause holds the conceded point and the independent clause holds the claim, so readers register the concession but take the main clause as the writer's position; the concession adds fairness without shifting the weight.
cards.h: → dependent clause = secondary idea → concession goes there → claim sits in the main clause → fair, still firm
cards.n: 'Although is a transition word' names the word and misses the grammar that ranks the two ideas.
o: Coordinating the two ideas with 'and' would present the objection as equal to the claim, inviting readers to weigh them evenly.
Placing the claim in the main clause at the end of the sentence also gives it the emphasis of the final position.

w.a: A concession always weakens an argument, so it should be hidden in a subordinate clause.
w.why: misreads subordination as hiding rather than ranking

w.a: Subordinate and independent clauses carry equal weight, so the order does not matter.
w.why: the CED says subordination shows imbalance

w.a: A fair concession deserves its own sentence, so subordinating it is dishonest.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores how syntax ranks ideas

cards.q: Explain why a shift in tone partway through an argument can strengthen the writer's credibility rather than weaken it.
cards.a: A tone shift can signal that the writer has qualified or reconsidered a perspective; readers who watch a writer adjust in response to evidence trust that the final position was earned, so the shift works as an implicit concession rather than as inconsistency.
cards.h: → shift signals refinement → refinement shows responsiveness to evidence → readers trust the final position
cards.n: 'The tone shifts to keep readers interested' is the trap; the CED ties tone shifts to qualification and reconsideration.
o: A writer who moves from mockery to respect models the change of mind the argument asks of skeptical readers.
Avoiding absolute terms in an ongoing debate makes a writer seem fair, and a tone shift can show that fairness in action.

w.a: Changing tone makes the writer seem inconsistent, so it always weakens the argument.
w.why: ignores the CED's link between tone shifts and qualification

w.a: The tone shifts because the writer ran out of things to say.
w.why: treats a choice as an accident

w.a: Tone shifts are only about style, not about the argument.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the link to the claim

cards.q: Explain why a qualified claim can persuade an informed audience more than an absolute one.
cards.a: Informed readers know the exceptions; an absolute claim invites them to refute it with one counterexample, while a claim limited to where the evidence holds is harder to attack and shows the writer grasps the subject's complexity, which earns credibility with exactly those readers.
cards.h: → informed readers know exceptions → absolutes invite counterexamples → limits show knowledge → trust rises
cards.n: 'Qualified claims are more polite' misses the logic: a limited claim is harder to refute and signals command of the subject.
o: An absolute claim oversimplifies, and the CED ties oversimplification to a lack of understanding that informed readers will notice.
A precise limit tells the audience exactly what the writer is defending, so it can be tested and accepted.

w.a: Absolute claims are stronger because they show confidence.
w.why: confidence does not survive a known counterexample

w.a: Qualifying a claim shows the writer is unsure.
w.why: confuses a precise limit with hedging

w.a: The audience's knowledge does not matter if the evidence is good.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores who must be convinced

cards.q: Explain why a misplaced modifier can change an argument's claim, not just its grammar.
cards.a: Modifiers qualify or specify whatever they sit next to; misplace one and it attaches to a different word, so the sentence limits something the writer did not intend, and readers hold the writer to the claim as written, not as meant.
cards.h: → a modifier attaches to its neighbor → misplaced, it limits the wrong thing → the claim's scope changes
cards.n: 'It is just a grammar mistake' is the one-unit answer; in an argument, grammar sets the claim's scope.
o: Qualifying words like 'only' and 'most' are modifiers, so their position decides the scope of the claim.
An ambiguous modifier hands an opponent a reading to attack that the writer never intended.

w.a: Misplaced modifiers only matter on grammar tests, not in arguments.
w.why: ignores how placement sets a claim's scope

w.a: Readers always know what the writer meant, so placement does not matter.
w.why: readers judge the claim as written

w.a: A modifier can go anywhere in the sentence as long as it is included.
w.why: the CED says to place modifiers closest to what they modify

cards.q: Explain why conceding a point to an opponent can make the audience more willing to accept the writer's rebuttal.
cards.a: Conceding shows the writer has weighed the opposing position fairly, which enhances credibility; readers who hold that view feel heard, so they are likelier to follow the rebuttal that comes next than to reject it as partisan.
cards.h: → concession shows fairness → credibility rises → opposed readers feel heard → they follow the rebuttal
cards.n: 'Conceding admits you are wrong' is the trap: a concession grants a portion, and the CED says it enhances credibility.
o: A concession narrows the disagreement to the point the writer can win, so the rebuttal meets less resistance.
Readers are more willing to accept evidence from a writer who has shown she accepts evidence against herself.

w.a: Conceding a point makes the writer look weak, so it should be avoided.
w.why: the CED says concession enhances credibility

w.a: Concessions are only polite and do not affect persuasion.
w.why: misses the effect on the opposed audience
