w.a: The rebuttal works because its evidence is stronger, not because of the concession.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores the audience

cards.q: Contrast 'although' (a subordinating conjunction, Style) and 'however' (a transitional element, Reasoning and Organization) as ways to show contrast, using these invented sentences: (A) 'Although the fee is small, many families cannot pay it.' (B) 'The fee is small. However, many families cannot pay it.'
cards.a: 'Although' makes 'the fee is small' a dependent clause inside one sentence, so the contrast is also a ranking: the smallness is conceded and the families' hardship dominates. 'However' links two independent sentences, keeping both ideas grammatically equal while signaling the contrast. Punctuation follows the grammar: a comma after the 'although' clause, a period or semicolon before 'however.'
cards.h: → what each does to the two ideas + the punctuation
cards.n: Treating the two as interchangeable is the trap; both signal contrast, but only 'although' ranks the ideas.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence from an argument that cutting the late bus hurt tutoring, and correct it: 'The district cut the late bus, and attendance at after-school tutoring fell by half.'
cards.a: Error: coordinating with 'and' presents the two events as equal, separate facts and hides the causal relationship the writer wants to argue. Corrected: 'After the district cut the late bus, attendance at after-school tutoring fell by half, because students without rides could no longer stay.' Subordination and 'because' state the relationship, which also commits the writer to defending that cause with evidence.
cards.h: → the error + a sentence that states the relationship
cards.n: Tempting because 'and' is grammatically correct; the error is rhetorical: the sentence never makes the causal claim the argument needs.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented pair of sentences and correct it: 'Many students work after school until 6 p.m. Furthermore, the library closes at 4 p.m.'
cards.a: Error: 'furthermore' signals addition, but the relationship is conflict: the closing time shuts working students out. Corrected: 'Many students work after school until 6 p.m., yet the library closes at 4 p.m., two hours before most of them are free.' A transitional element must name the actual relationship between ideas, or coherence breaks even though each sentence is true.
cards.h: → the mismatched relationship + a corrected link
cards.n: Tempting because both sentences support the argument; 'furthermore' makes the second sound like a new point, not the problem the first creates.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence and correct it in a way that shows how the two ideas relate: 'The pilot program worked, attendance rose in every grade.'
cards.a: Error: a comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma, so the sentence breaks convention and leaves the relationship unstated. Corrected: 'The pilot program worked: attendance rose in every grade.' The colon signals that the second clause is the evidence for the first, a relationship a period (separation) or a semicolon (two related, equal statements) would not show as clearly.
cards.h: → the error named + a fix that shows the relationship
cards.n: Tempting because the sentence reads smoothly aloud; every fix is correct, but only the colon shows that the second clause proves the first.

cards.q: Decide how to join each invented pair of ideas (coordinate, subordinate, or use a colon), and say why: 1. 'The bike lane is cheap.' / 'It is safe.' (two equal reasons) 2. 'The bridge closed.' / 'Traffic doubled on Elm.' (cause, then effect) 3. 'The council has one choice left.' / 'It must raise the fee.' (the second names the first) 4. 'The fee is unpopular.' / 'It is necessary.' (the claim is the second) 5. 'Some residents object.' / 'Most support it.' (a contrast of groups) 6. 'The study was small.' / 'Its results were striking.' (concede the first)
cards.a:
1 → coordinate: 'The bike lane is cheap, and it is safe' (balance of equal reasons)
2 → subordinate: 'Because the bridge closed, traffic doubled on Elm' (the dependent clause states the cause)
3 → colon: 'The council has one choice left: it must raise the fee' (what follows specifies what came before)
4 → subordinate: 'Although the fee is unpopular, it is necessary' (the claim takes the main clause)
5 → coordinate: 'Some residents object, but most support it' (a balanced contrast; the end position still favors the majority)
6 → subordinate: 'Although the study was small, its results were striking' (concede, then the point)
cards.h: → the join + a model sentence + why, per line
cards.n: Pairs 4 and 6 are the trap: 'and' would make the objection equal to the claim; the conceded idea belongs in the dependent clause.

cards.q: Identify how parallel structure links the paragraphs of this invented speech and what it emphasizes: paragraph 1 opens 'We built the road for the trucks.' Paragraph 2 opens 'We built the school for the children.' Paragraph 3 opens 'Now we must build the bridge for both.'
cards.a: The repeated frame 'We built the ___ for the ___' ties the paragraphs together, creating coherence across the text, and moves the line of reasoning from past to present: two separate goods the town once built, then one project that serves both. The break in the pattern ('Now we must') marks the third paragraph as the claim the first two prepared.
cards.h: → the frame + its movement + what the break stresses
cards.n: Naming 'parallelism' or 'anaphora' earns nothing alone; the credited answer says how the pattern builds toward the third paragraph.

cards.q: Decide which order of these two invented sentences better ends a paragraph arguing that a flood wall is worth its cost, and explain: (A) 'The wall will protect 300 homes. It will cost $4 million.' (B) 'The wall will cost $4 million. It will protect 300 homes.'
cards.a: (B). The end of a sequence is the position of emphasis, so (B) acknowledges the cost first and leaves the reader with the homes protected, the writer's reason. (A) ends on the price, making the cost the last thing the reader weighs, which works against the claim.
cards.h: → letter + the position of emphasis
cards.n: Both orders state the same facts, which makes the choice seem trivial; what a paragraph ends on is what the reader carries forward.

cards.q: Write one sentence that combines these invented ideas so the second is clearly the more important: 'The park is small.' 'It is the only green space within a mile of Garfield Elementary.'
cards.a: Model: 'Although the park is small, it is the only green space within a mile of Garfield Elementary.' Subordinating the size concedes the obvious objection and puts the writer's point, the park's irreplaceability, in the independent clause at the end of the sentence, where it carries both grammatical weight and the emphasis of the final position.
cards.h: → one sentence + why the clause order works
cards.n: 'The park is small, and it is the only green space' makes size and scarcity equal; the reader should finish on scarcity.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence and correct it: 'The council told the parents' group that they had ignored the traffic data.'
cards.a: Error: 'they' could refer to the council or to the parents' group, so the reader cannot tell who ignored the data, and the accusation lands on no one. Corrected, depending on the meaning: 'The council admitted to the parents' group that it had ignored the traffic data' or 'The council told the parents' group that the group had ignored the traffic data.' A pronoun builds coherence only when its antecedent is clear.
cards.h: → the ambiguity named + a revision for each meaning
cards.n: Tempting because the writer knows who 'they' is; the reader does not, and in an argument the ambiguity decides who is blamed.

cards.q: Explain how a one-sentence paragraph such as 'Then the money ran out.' can act both as a transitional element and as emphasis in an invented essay about a town's failed recycling program.
cards.a: As a transition, the paragraph marks the turn in the line of reasoning, from the program's early success to its collapse, linking the sections before and after it. As emphasis, isolating one short sentence in its own paragraph slows the reader and makes the reversal land. The CED counts whole paragraphs among transitional elements, and the arrangement of sentences can emphasize an idea.
cards.h: → its transitional job + its emphatic job
cards.n: Calling it 'a short paragraph for effect' names no effect; say what it turns from and to, and why isolation stresses it.

cards.q: Explain why choosing between coordination and subordination is also a claim about which idea matters more.
cards.a: Coordination presents ideas as equal and subordination as unequal, so the writer's choice ranks ideas for the reader; in an argument, putting the objection in a dependent clause and the position in the main clause tells the audience which idea should decide the question.
cards.h: → coordination = balance, subordination = imbalance → grammar ranks ideas → the ranking is a claim
cards.n: 'Subordination adds variety' is the trap; variety is a side effect, the ranking is the point.
o: Two writers can report the same facts, one with 'and' and one with 'although,' and argue different positions.
The idea in the main clause is the one readers remember as the sentence's point, so choosing it is choosing the claim.

w.a: Coordination and subordination are just ways to make sentences longer.
w.why: ignores what each does to the ideas

w.a: Subordination is more sophisticated, so it is always better.
w.why: coordination is right when ideas are equal

w.a: Grammar choices are separate from the writer's argument.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the link to the claim

cards.q: Explain why a mismatched transition damages an argument's line of reasoning even when every sentence is true.
cards.a: Transitional elements tell readers how ideas relate; a wrong one ('furthermore' where the relationship is conflict) states a false relationship, so readers misread how the evidence supports the claim and the line of reasoning breaks, though every fact is accurate.
cards.h: → transitions assert relationships → a wrong one asserts a false one → readers misconnect evidence → reasoning breaks
cards.n: 'The transition is just awkward' is the trap; a transition is a small claim about how two ideas connect.
o: Coherence depends on each idea linking logically to the next, and a transition is the visible statement of that link.
Readers use transitions to predict what comes next, so a false signal sends them the wrong way.

w.a: A transition only makes writing flow better; it does not affect the argument.
w.why: transitions state relationships between ideas

w.a: If all the facts are true, the argument is sound.
w.why: true facts wrongly connected do not support the claim

w.a: Any transition is better than none.
w.why: a false relationship is worse than an unstated one

cards.q: Explain why a colon can do the work of a transitional phrase such as 'that is' or 'namely.'
cards.a: Punctuation shows relationships among ideas: a colon tells readers that what follows explains, specifies, or proves what came before, so it signals the same relationship as 'that is' or 'namely' without the extra words, keeping the emphasis on the ideas.
cards.h: → punctuation signals relationships → a colon means what follows explains → same job as the phrase, lighter
cards.n: 'A colon introduces a list' is the one-unit answer; the credited point is the relationship it signals.
o: The CED lists clarifying and organizing among punctuation's purposes, and a colon clarifies by signaling that what follows explains what came before, which is transition work done inside a sentence.
Replacing a transitional phrase with a colon can sharpen emphasis because nothing stands between the claim and its support, and the colon alone already signals that support follows.

w.a: A colon is only used before a list.
w.why: misses its use before an explanation or proof

w.a: Punctuation is about correctness, not meaning.
w.why: the CED says punctuation shows relationships among ideas

w.a: A colon and a comma do the same thing.
w.why: a comma does not signal that what follows explains what came before

cards.q: Explain why repeating a key word across paragraphs can build coherence rather than seem repetitive.
cards.a: Repetition shows that a later paragraph continues an earlier one's idea, so readers see the link without a transition; when the repeated word is the argument's key term, it also keeps that idea in focus, which makes the line of reasoning easy to trace.
cards.h: → a repeated key term is a visible link → readers connect paragraphs → the key idea stays in focus
cards.n: 'Never repeat words' is the trap: the CED names repetition as a way to develop relationships between parts of a text.
o: Swapping a key term for loose synonyms can make readers wonder whether the writer means a new idea.
Deliberate repetition emphasizes the idea the writer wants readers to carry through the argument.

w.a: Good writers always use synonyms to avoid repetition.
w.why: synonyms can blur a key term

w.a: Repetition is a device for speeches, not written arguments.
w.why: it also creates coherence on the page

w.a: Coherence comes only from transition words like 'however.'
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores repetition and reference

cards.q: Explain why the end of a sentence and the end of a paragraph are strong places for a writer's main point.
cards.a: Arrangement can emphasize ideas: readers give the final position the most weight because it is what they carry into the next sentence or paragraph, so a claim placed last becomes the idea that frames what follows.
cards.h: → readers weigh what comes last → it carries into what follows → the claim placed last frames the next step
cards.n: 'Save the best for last' is a slogan; the reason is that the final position carries forward into the reader's next step.
o: A periodic sentence delays the main clause to the end, so the point arrives with the weight of everything before it, and a paragraph's final sentence works the same way for the paragraph.
A paragraph that ends on commentary leaves readers with the explanation rather than with raw evidence, just as a sentence's final clause is the part readers carry forward.

w.a: The main point should always come first so readers see it.
w.why: ignores the emphasis of the final position

w.a: Position in a sentence does not affect meaning.
w.why: the CED says arrangement can emphasize ideas

w.a: Ending a paragraph with a quotation is strongest because it is evidence.
w.why: leaves the reader with evidence instead of the point

cards.q: Contrast bias in a writer's word choice (Rhetorical Situation) and bias in how a source treats other positions (Claims and Evidence).
cards.a: Word-choice bias shows in loaded diction, such as calling a plan a 'scheme,' which reflects the writer's leanings and can cost credibility with readers who do not share them. Source bias is measured by how far a source considers other positions: one that never mentions opposing evidence is more biased, whatever its vocabulary. A calmly worded source can be one-sided, and a heated one can still weigh the other side.
cards.h: → each kind of bias + why the two can come apart
cards.n: Judging a source's bias by its tone alone is the trap; the CED measures source bias by whether other positions are considered.

cards.q: Contrast the position and the tone of these two invented letters to a parks board, and explain which is likelier to persuade undecided readers. Letter 1: 'The skate park will bring noise and litter; the skateboard crowd has never respected this neighborhood.' Letter 2: 'I worry that a skate park beside the library would be loud during study hours, and I ask the board to consider the lot on Fourth Street instead.'
cards.a: Both take the same position, against a skate park at this site; their tones differ. Letter 1 is contemptuous: 'the skateboard crowd' dismisses a whole group and suggests prejudice, which undecided readers may hold against the writer. Letter 2 is concerned and constructive: it names one specific cost and offers an alternative. Letter 2 is likelier to persuade, because its word choice makes the writer seem fair.
cards.h: → shared position + each tone + which persuades and why
cards.n: Deciding the letters 'disagree' is the trap: same position, different tones, and the tone decides whom each can persuade.

cards.q: Identify how the descriptive words in this invented source reveal its perspective, and say how a synthesis essay should use it: 'The reckless, budget-busting light-rail scheme would bulldoze a quiet neighborhood to serve a handful of downtown commuters.'
cards.a: 'Reckless,' 'budget-busting,' 'scheme,' 'bulldoze,' 'quiet,' and 'a handful' all convey the writer's opposition: the descriptive words judge the project while seeming to describe it. A synthesis essay can still use the source for its concerns about cost or displacement, but should acknowledge its slant and check its claims (how many commuters, exactly?) against a more neutral source.
cards.h: → the loaded words + the perspective + how to use it
cards.n: Discarding the source as 'biased' is the trap; the CED says strong arguments use sources while accounting for their limits.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence from a synthesis essay and correct it: 'Source D was written by the bus manufacturer, so it is biased and cannot be used.'
cards.a: Error: bias does not disqualify a source; the strongest arguments acknowledge a source's biases and limitations and account for them. Corrected: 'Source D, from the manufacturer, naturally favors electric buses, so I rely on its fuel figures only where Source B's independent audit confirms them.' The writer uses the evidence while showing readers how much weight it can bear.
cards.h: → the error + a sentence using the source with its limits
cards.n: Tempting because avoiding 'biased' sources feels careful; dropping them discards evidence and skips the reasoning the CED rewards.

cards.q: Identify the error in this student's analysis of an invented sentence and correct it. Sentence: 'The proposal is ambitious, untested, and costly.' Analysis: 'The writer calls the proposal "ambitious," which shows she supports it.'
cards.a: Error: it gives 'ambitious' a fixed positive connotation without reading its context; the word can praise or warn. Corrected: 'Listed beside "untested" and "costly," "ambitious" suggests overreach, so the writer doubts the proposal.' Tone is inferred from connotation in context, and the company a word keeps is part of that context.
cards.h: → the error + a reading that uses the surrounding words
cards.n: Tempting because 'ambitious' is praise in most contexts; connotation depends on the words around it.

cards.q: Decide which word better fits an invented nurses' union letter to hospital administrators the union must keep negotiating with, and explain: 'The proposed staffing plan is (A) reckless (B) unworkable.'
cards.a: (B). 'Unworkable' criticizes the plan precisely, as something that will not function, without accusing the administrators of carelessness, so the union keeps its credibility and the working relationship it needs at the table. 'Reckless' judges the people behind the plan; its connotation may satisfy members but makes the audience defensive.
cards.h: → letter + what each word judges + effect on this audience
cards.n: (A) is tempting because it is stronger; strength aimed at the people you must persuade usually costs more than it gains.

cards.q: Write a revision of this invented sentence that keeps its position but removes the loaded words that would cost credibility with undecided readers: 'The greedy developers want to bulldoze our beloved park for their ugly luxury condos.'
cards.a: Model: 'The developer's plan would replace the park, the only playground within walking distance for most families here, with 140 condominiums priced beyond what most current residents could pay.' It keeps the opposition but trades judgments ('greedy,' 'ugly') for specifics that let readers reach the judgment themselves, which undecided readers trust more than name-calling.
cards.h: → one sentence: same position, specifics for insults
cards.n: Deleting the adjectives and stopping is the trap: the revision still needs specifics that carry the writer's point.

cards.q: Identify the irony in this invented op-ed passage and the perspective it signals: 'Congratulations to the district on its new $3 million stadium scoreboard. Students will now see the score in perfect clarity, even if their history textbooks still end in 1998.'
cards.a: The writer praises ('Congratulations,' 'perfect clarity') what the argument actually condemns; the gap between the celebratory words and the outdated textbooks exposes the district's priorities. The irony relies on readers valuing textbooks over scoreboards, and the perspective is critical and sardonic: a complaint about spending delivered as mock praise.
cards.h: → what is said vs meant + the value it relies on
cards.n: Taking 'Congratulations' at face value is the trap; irony emerges from the gap between the words and the argument.

cards.q: Describe how the style of this invented opening (short declaratives, plain words, one number) shapes the audience's perception of the writer: 'I drive the 6 a.m. bus. Twelve kids ride it. Three of them fall asleep before the first stop.'
cards.a: The style is plain and spare: three short declarative sentences, everyday words, one concrete count. It presents the writer as a firsthand witness who reports rather than argues, so readers trust the observation, and the sleeping children carry the point (the start time is too early) without the writer stating it. The style builds credibility before any claim is made.
cards.h: → the style's features + the writer it presents + effect
cards.n: 'The sentences are short' is description only; the credited answer says what the plainness makes the audience believe about the writer.

cards.q: Decide which invented source is more reliable for the claim 'the new crosswalk reduced accidents,' and whether tone is the reason. Source A, a neighborhood blog post in a calm, reasonable voice, says 'everyone agrees the corner feels safer now.' Source B, a city traffic engineer's dry report, gives crash counts for the two years before and after the crosswalk.
cards.a: Source B. It offers data from a qualified source that bears directly on the claim, while Source A offers a feeling ('feels safer') and an unsupported generalization ('everyone agrees'). Tone is not the reason: a measured voice can make a weak source sound reliable, and a dry one can hide a strong source. Reliability comes from expertise and evidence, not from how agreeable the writing sounds.
cards.h: → the source + what makes it reliable + tone's role
cards.n: Source A's calm tone is the trap: it makes the writer sound reasonable, but sounding reasonable is not evidence.

cards.q: Decide which invented version better emphasizes the key point of a letter to a school board, and explain: (A) 'The board must act now, before another student is hurt,' with 'must,' 'now,' and 'another' set in boldface. (B) 'The board must act before the first snow, not after the first accident.'
cards.a: (B). It creates emphasis through arrangement: the contrast sets 'first snow' against 'first accident' and ends on the stakes, so the point lands without typographic help. In (A), three boldface words compete; emphasis from design features works only when used sparingly, and heavy boldface reads as shouting, which costs credibility with a board the writer needs to persuade.
cards.h: → letter + how each creates emphasis + effect on the board
cards.n: (A) is tempting because boldface looks forceful; three bolded words cancel one another, and the board hears volume instead of a reason.

cards.q: Explain why a loaded word can weaken an argument with the very audience the writer most needs to persuade.
cards.a: Loaded diction reveals bias; readers who already agree accept it, but undecided or opposed readers, the ones an argument must move, see the writer as unfair, so the word costs credibility exactly where persuasion is needed.
cards.h: → a loaded word signals bias → allies accept it → undecided readers distrust the writer → persuasion fails
cards.n: 'Loaded words are unprofessional' is a rule, not a reason; the point is which audience they alienate.
o: Loaded language asks readers to adopt a judgment before seeing the evidence, which undecided readers resist.
A neutral word lets evidence persuade; a loaded one makes undecided readers notice the writer's feelings instead.

w.a: Loaded words make writing more powerful, so they always help.
w.why: ignores the undecided audience

w.a: Loaded words are wrong because they are inaccurate.
w.why: a loaded word can be accurate and still cost credibility

w.a: Word choice is a matter of style and does not affect whether an argument persuades.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses audience and credibility

cards.q: Explain why a measured tone is not proof that a source is reliable.
cards.a: Tone is the writer's attitude; reliability depends on the source's expertise, its evidence, and whether it considers other positions. A calm voice can make an unsupported claim sound reasonable, so a reader who judges by tone mistakes style for credibility.
cards.h: → tone = attitude → reliability = expertise + evidence + fairness → a calm style can dress up weak claims
cards.n: 'Calm sources are unbiased' is the trap: a measured tone can be one-sided if it ignores other positions.
o: A source's bias is measured by how far it considers other positions, which tone alone cannot show.
A heated source with sound data can be more reliable on a factual question than a calm source with none.

w.a: A calm source is reliable because it is not emotional.
w.why: confuses tone with evidence

w.a: An angry source is always unreliable.
w.why: anger does not erase evidence

w.a: Tone and reliability are the same thing in a synthesis essay.
w.why: the one-unit answer that merges style and credibility

cards.q: Explain why noticing a source's descriptive words helps you judge how far it considers other positions.
cards.a: Descriptive words convey a perspective as well as describe; a source that labels every opponent 'extreme' or every cost 'trivial' signals that it has not weighed other views, which is how the CED measures bias, so its adjectives are evidence of its limits.
cards.h: → adjectives carry perspective → one-sided labels signal unweighed views → bias = how far others are considered
cards.n: Reading adjectives as neutral description is the trap; they often show whether a source has considered the other side.
o: A source that describes the opposing view in its own best terms shows it has considered that position.
Loaded description of opponents shows a source has judged rather than weighed them, which tells the essay writer to check its claims against a more neutral source.

w.a: Adjectives are only description, so they say nothing about bias.
w.why: the CED says descriptive words convey a perspective

w.a: A source with no adjectives cannot be biased.
w.why: bias can lie in what a source leaves out

w.a: Descriptive words matter in rhetorical analysis, not in synthesis.
w.why: the one-unit answer that keeps style out of source evaluation

cards.q: Explain why irony depends on what the audience already values.
cards.a: Irony emerges from the gap between what a writer says and what readers expect or value; mock praise of a scoreboard works only if readers already rank textbooks higher, so readers who do not share the value may take the praise literally or feel mocked themselves.
cards.h: → irony = gap between words and expectations → the gap needs a shared value → without it readers miss or resent it
cards.n: 'Irony means saying the opposite' is the one-unit answer; it misses that the audience's values make the gap visible.
o: An ironic writer counts on the audience to supply the real judgment, which makes the audience a partner in the criticism.
The same ironic line can persuade one audience and offend another, because it relies on shared expectations.

w.a: Irony works on any audience because it is clever.
w.why: ignores the shared values it relies on

w.a: Irony just means saying the opposite of what you mean.
w.why: the definition leaves out the audience

w.a: Irony is a style device, so the audience does not affect it.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the audience

cards.q: Explain why precise word choice supports a writer's credibility, not only clarity.
cards.a: Precise words reduce confusion and let the audience see the writer's exact perspective; readers take precision as a sign that the writer knows the subject, so an argument that says 'unworkable' rather than 'bad' earns trust as well as understanding.
cards.h: → precise word = exact meaning → readers see the exact perspective → precision signals knowledge → trust
cards.n: 'Precise words are clearer' is only half the answer; the CED also ties diction to how the audience perceives the writer.
o: Vague words force readers to guess, and a writer who makes readers guess seems either unsure or evasive.
A precise word limits the claim to what the writer can defend, which avoids the overstatement that costs a writer trust.

w.a: Precise words just make writing sound more sophisticated.
w.why: confuses precision with vocabulary

w.a: Credibility comes from evidence, not from word choice.
w.why: the CED says diction influences how the writer is perceived

w.a: Longer, more formal words make a writer more credible.
w.why: precision, not length or formality, carries the effect

cards.q: Contrast an anecdote as a type of evidence (Claims and Evidence) and narration as a method of development (Reasoning and Organization).
cards.a: An anecdote is a brief story offered as support for a claim, one piece of evidence among others. Narration is a way to develop and organize reasoning: the writer recounts real experience in detail and reflects on its significance, so the story carries the argument's structure. An anecdote can sit inside any method of development; narration makes the experience and its meaning the argument's spine.
cards.h: → anecdote's role + narration's role + the difference
cards.n: Treating them as synonyms is the trap: one is a piece of evidence, the other a way of organizing reasoning around experience.

cards.q: Contrast an analogy as evidence (Claims and Evidence), a comparison that relates to an audience (Rhetorical Situation), and comparison-contrast as a method of development (Reasoning and Organization).
cards.a: An analogy as evidence supports a claim by reasoning from a familiar case to a new one. A comparison meant to relate to an audience works only if the audience shares and understands what it compares to. Comparison-contrast as a method organizes reasoning by examining similarities or differences within like categories. One comparison can do all three jobs, but each job has its own test: apt reasoning, shared understanding, like categories.
cards.h: → three roles + the test each must pass
cards.n: Answering 'they all compare things' is the trap; each Big Idea asks a different question of the same comparison.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented comparison and correct it: 'Riverton's schools assign less homework than Lakeview's, while Lakeview's schools field more sports teams, so Riverton's students are better rested.'
cards.a: Error: the comparison switches categories, homework for one town and sports teams for the other, so the conclusion about rest does not follow. Corrected: 'Riverton's high schools assign about an hour less homework a night than Lakeview's, and Riverton's students report about forty minutes more sleep, so less homework may leave them better rested.' Comparison-contrast needs like categories.
cards.h: → the error + a like-for-like comparison
cards.n: Tempting because both facts may be accurate and both concern students; a comparison proves nothing unless it compares the same thing.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented argument and correct it: 'Since the town installed security cameras downtown, shoplifting reports have doubled. The cameras are encouraging theft.'
cards.a: Error: it assumes that because reports rose after the cameras went in, the cameras caused more theft, ignoring the likelier explanation that cameras catch thefts that once went unreported. Corrected: 'Shoplifting reports doubled after the cameras went in, most likely because more thefts are now detected; the figure measures reporting, not theft.' A cause-effect claim must rule out other causes.
cards.h: → the flawed inference + a corrected reading
cards.n: Tempting because the sequence (cameras, then more reports) looks like cause; a flawed line of reasoning can rest on accurate numbers.

cards.q: Decide which method of development (narration, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, definition, or description) best serves each invented purpose, and why: 1. show residents what the county means by a 'food desert' 2. argue that ending the late bus lowered grades 3. persuade the board to choose bid A over bid B 4. make legislators feel a night-shift nurse's twelve hours 5. help readers picture the flood-damaged gym 6. show that 'affordable' in the new ordinance excludes most teachers 7. argue that the town's two libraries should merge
cards.a:
1 → definition (establish the term before arguing about it)
2 → cause-effect (a cause and its consequences)
3 → comparison-contrast (like categories: cost, time, quality)
4 → narration (real experience with reflection on it)
5 → description (sensory detail makes the damage concrete)
6 → definition (the argument turns on what the word covers)
7 → comparison-contrast (the two libraries set side by side), or cause-effect if the case rests on what a merger would bring about
cards.h: → one method + why, per line
cards.n: Line 7 is the trap: methods combine, and the credited answer names the one that carries the reasoning, with a reason.

cards.q: Explain how defining 'affordable housing' at the start of an invented argument to a city council both develops the reasoning and limits the claim.
cards.a: A definition (for instance, rent and utilities no higher than 30 percent of a median household's income, a common benchmark) develops the reasoning by giving the council a test every later piece of evidence can be measured against. It also qualifies the claim: the writer argues about housing that meets this standard, not all cheap housing, so the argument's scope is set before any dispute begins.
cards.h: → what the definition does for reasoning + for scope
cards.n: Calling the definition 'background' misses that whoever defines the term sets the terms of the debate.

cards.q: Identify whether the comparison in this invented sentence works as reasoning that supports the claim or only as a vivid figure, and say what it depends on: 'Cutting the school nurse to save money is like removing a smoke detector to save on batteries.'
cards.a: It works as an analogy that supports the claim: it maps a small saving against a rare but catastrophic risk, the structure the writer sees in the nurse cut. It depends on the audience's shared understanding of smoke detectors, which almost everyone has, and on the likeness holding; an opponent could answer that a nurse costs far more than batteries, the analogy's weak point.
cards.h: → reasoning or figure + what it maps + its weak point
cards.n: Calling it 'just a simile' is the trap: an analogy that maps a structure is evidence, and it can be attacked where the likeness breaks.

cards.q: Write a two-sentence opening for an invented argument that the town should keep its bookmobile: one sentence of narration and one of reflection that points toward the claim.
cards.a: Model: 'Every other Thursday when I was nine, the bookmobile parked outside the laundromat on Route 6, and I read a borrowed adventure novel while my mother folded towels. I did not know then that it was the only library within twenty miles of our trailer park; I know now that for some children in this county, it still is.' Narration gives real detail; reflection draws out its significance and turns it toward the claim.
cards.h: → one narrated moment + one reflective turn
cards.n: A story with no reflection is the trap: the CED's narration includes insight into significance, which turns a memory into a reason.

cards.q: Identify what the description in this invented passage does as evidence and as a method of development: 'The clinic's waiting room has eleven chairs for a morning line of forty. Patients stand in the stairwell. The one fan points at the receptionist.'
cards.a: As evidence, the details illustrate the claim that the clinic is overwhelmed, and the count (eleven chairs, forty patients) amplifies it into a measurable shortage. As a method of development, description relates the features of a place so readers can picture it; the arrangement ends on the fan, a small detail that implies whose comfort the building serves first. The details persuade without the writer stating the claim.
cards.h: → evidence purpose + method + what the last detail does
cards.n: 'The writer uses imagery' names a device and stops; the credited answer says what the details prove and how.

cards.q: Evaluate this invented analogy from a letter opposing a later school start: 'Starting school later is like letting employees come to work whenever they feel like it.'
cards.a: The analogy fails at its key point: a later start is a fixed time set for everyone, not a choice left to each student, so it misrepresents the proposal. It may still persuade readers who know workplaces, since comparisons work when the audience shares them, but the flawed likeness makes the line of reasoning specious, and a rebuttal need only name the difference.
cards.h: → where the likeness breaks + why it may still persuade
cards.n: Rejecting the analogy because 'school is not a job' misses the real flaw: the proposal sets a schedule; it does not remove one.

cards.q: Explain why an analogy persuades only when the audience already understands the thing it compares to.
cards.a: An analogy reasons from a familiar case to an unfamiliar one; if readers do not know the familiar case, nothing transfers, so the comparison neither clarifies the claim nor relates to the audience, and it fails as evidence.
cards.h: → an analogy transfers understanding from known to unknown → unknown source case → nothing transfers → no support
cards.n: 'Analogies make writing vivid' is the one-unit answer; the CED's test is whether the audience shares the comparison.
o: A comparison to a sport or technology the audience does not know makes readers work to decode it, which distracts from the claim.
Choosing a comparison from the audience's own experience lets readers check the likeness for themselves, and signals that the writer understands them.

w.a: Any analogy helps because comparisons make ideas clearer.
w.why: an unfamiliar comparison clarifies nothing

w.a: Analogies are decoration and do not need to be understood to work.
w.why: the CED says effective comparisons must be shared and understood

w.a: The audience only needs to understand the claim, not the comparison.
w.why: the comparison carries the reasoning

cards.q: Explain why a comparison-contrast argument fails when its categories of comparison are unlike, even if every fact is accurate.
cards.a: Comparison-contrast reasons that a difference within one category supports a conclusion; if the categories are unlike (homework here, sports teams there), there is no difference in any one category to reason from, so accurate facts give the argument no apt support.
cards.h: → comparison needs like categories → unlike ones measure different things → nothing to reason from → no support
cards.n: 'The facts are true, so the argument works' is the trap: accuracy does not make a comparison apt.
o: Unlike categories hide the real question, since readers cannot tell whether the two things differ where it matters.
An opponent can refute such an argument without disputing a single fact, simply by pointing out the mismatch.

w.a: If every fact is accurate, the comparison proves the point.
w.why: accuracy is not relevance

w.a: Comparisons only need to be interesting to work.
w.why: the CED requires like categories

w.a: The only problem is that the paragraph is confusing to read.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses the missing support

cards.q: Explain why narration needs reflection to count as reasoning in an argument, not just a story.
cards.a: Narration offers details of real experience, but the reasoning lies in the writer's reflection on its significance, which connects the story to the claim; without reflection the experience is evidence with no commentary, and readers must guess what it proves.
cards.h: → story = evidence → reflection = commentary → without it no link to the claim → readers guess
cards.n: 'Stories are persuasive on their own' is the trap; the CED builds reflection into what narration is.
o: Reflection does for a narrative what commentary does for a statistic: it explains its relevance to the line of reasoning.
A reflective turn tells readers which detail of the story matters, so they do not draw a different lesson.

w.a: A good story persuades by itself, so reflection is unnecessary.
w.why: a story can support many conclusions without commentary

w.a: Reflection is only for personal essays, not arguments.
w.why: the CED includes it in narration as a method of development

w.a: Narration is just a way to start an essay.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores its role as reasoning

cards.q: Explain why a cause-effect argument built on one sequence of events is open to the charge of oversimplification.
cards.a: Cause-effect asserts that one thing produced another, but a single sequence ('after the cameras went in, reports doubled') cannot rule out other causes; claiming one cause for a complex outcome oversimplifies it, and readers who see another explanation reject the reasoning.
cards.h: → one sequence is not proof of cause → other causes unruled out → a single-cause claim oversimplifies
cards.n: 'Correlation is not causation' is a slogan, not an explanation; say which other cause the argument ignores.
o: One sequence leaves other causes standing, which is why a writer protects a causal claim by qualifying it ('one likely cause') and naming the alternatives she has considered.
One sequence cannot separate a cause from a coincidence, so several sequences pointing the same way, or a case where the cause was absent, make a causal claim better supported.

w.a: If one event came right after another, the first caused the second.
w.why: timing alone does not establish cause

w.a: Cause-effect arguments are always weak, so writers should avoid them.
w.why: the CED lists cause-effect as a method; it needs support

w.a: The argument just needs more description of the events.
w.why: more detail does not rule out other causes

cards.q: Explain why the way a writer defines a key term can decide an argument before the evidence arrives.
cards.a: A definition sets the characteristics a thing must have, and later evidence is measured against it; if 'affordable' is defined by a standard most teachers cannot meet, evidence about teachers then proves the claim almost automatically, so the definition frames what counts as proof.
cards.h: → the definition sets the test → evidence is judged by that test → whoever sets the test frames the verdict
cards.n: 'Definitions just explain words' is the trap; in an argument, a definition is often the first and most contested claim.
o: An opponent who accepts the writer's definition has already conceded much of the argument, because the definition fixes what the evidence must show.
A definition limits the scope of the claim, a form of qualification readers may not notice.

w.a: Definitions are neutral, so they cannot affect the argument.
w.why: a definition chooses which features count

w.a: A writer should skip definitions and go straight to evidence.
w.why: evidence needs a standard to be measured against

w.a: Definitions matter in dictionaries, not in arguments.
w.why: the one-unit answer that misses a definition as a claim

cards.q: Explain how the context of an invented source, a 2011 district report on student computer use written before the district gave every student a laptop, should affect how you use its evidence in a synthesis essay about school laptops today.
cards.a: The report's time and occasion limit what it can show: its findings describe a school before laptops were universal, so they cannot directly prove how students use them now. Use it for what holds across time, such as a baseline or a before-and-after contrast, and say so in the commentary; the strongest arguments acknowledge a source's limitations and account for them.
cards.h: → what the date limits + how to use it anyway
cards.n: Treating an older source as simply wrong is the trap; its context limits what it proves, and the commentary should name that limit.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented synthesis paragraph and correct it: 'Source A says community gardens reclaim vacant lots. Source C says some neighbors worry about rats. Source E says one garden supplied a food pantry all summer.'
cards.a: Error: the paragraph summarizes sources one by one with no claim of the writer's own, so there is no synthesis and no line of reasoning. Corrected: 'A garden earns its lot when it feeds people: Source E's pantry harvest shows what Source A's reclaimed lots can become, and Source C's worry about pests can be met with enclosed compost bins.' The writer's claim now organizes the sources.
cards.h: → the error + a claim-led rewrite
cards.n: Tempting because it cites three sources, the minimum; citing is not synthesizing until the sources serve the writer's own claim.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented sentence from a synthesis essay and correct it: 'Children who read over the summer lose less of their reading progress, so the library's summer program deserves funding.' (The finding comes from Source B, a study by a university education department.)
cards.a: Error: evidence from Source B is presented as common knowledge, with no attribution; writers must acknowledge others' ideas, and the exam asks that sources be clearly indicated. Corrected: 'A university study of summer reading (Source B) found that children who read over the summer lose less of their reading progress, so the library's program protects gains the school year paid for.' Naming the study also lends its credibility to the claim.
cards.h: → the missing element + an attributed version
cards.n: Tempting because the finding sounds like common knowledge; it came from a source, and naming the study also borrows its authority.

cards.q: Contrast a source that complements your thesis and one that contradicts it (Claims and Evidence), and say where each belongs in your line of reasoning (Reasoning and Organization).
cards.a: A complementing source adds support from another angle, so it belongs inside the body paragraph whose evidence it extends, often right after the main evidence. A contradicting source challenges the thesis, so it belongs where the essay concedes or rebuts, usually before the final reasons, so the argument ends on the writer's strongest ground. Leaving the contradiction out makes the argument less credible.
cards.h: → each relationship + where it goes + why
cards.n: Leaving contradicting sources out is the trap; the CED says evidence may support, complement, or contradict, and credible writers use all three.

cards.q: Decide whether to quote, paraphrase, or summarize in each invented case, and why: 1. a source calls the plan 'warehousing children,' and you will analyze that phrase 2. a twelve-page study's overall finding 3. a sentence dense with technical terms your readers will not know 4. a statistic 5. an expert's exact words that you will dispute 6. three sources that make the same point
cards.a:
1 → quote: the connotation of the exact words is the evidence
2 → summarize: readers need the conclusion, not the pages
3 → paraphrase: plain words serve an audience that lacks the terms
4 → paraphrase with attribution: a number needs a source, not quotation marks
5 → quote: disputing someone's words fairly means giving them exactly
6 → summarize with all three attributions: the agreement is the point
cards.h: → one method + why, per line
cards.n: Quoting everything is the trap: a quotation earns its place only when the exact wording matters, as in lines 1 and 5.

cards.q: Write a sentence that introduces this invented source with a signal phrase conveying its perspective and its relation to your claim (that the school should serve breakfast after first period): Source E, a middle-school nurse, reports that most students who visit her before 10 a.m. with headaches have not eaten.
cards.a: Model: 'The students' hunger shows up first in the nurse's office: Source E, a middle-school nurse who sees them daily, reports that most of her before-10 a.m. headache visits come from students who have not eaten, exactly the window a second-period breakfast would cover.' The signal phrase names her perspective (daily firsthand observation), and the final clause ties the evidence to the claim.
cards.h: → signal phrase with perspective + evidence + link
cards.n: 'Source E says' is the trap: it attributes but conveys neither the source's perspective nor why the evidence matters.

cards.q: Identify one claim this invented bar chart supports and one it cannot, and explain why. Title: 'Average weeknight sleep by grade, district survey of 1,600 students.' Bars: 9th grade 7.6 hours · 10th grade 7.3 · 11th grade 7.0 · 12th grade 6.8.
cards.a: Supports: in this district, reported weeknight sleep falls with each grade, by 0.8 hours (48 minutes) from 9th to 12th grade. Cannot support: that early start times cause the decline or that it lowers grades, since the chart shows neither start times nor achievement. Commentary should claim what the evidence shows and name what it does not, which also answers an objection before an opponent can raise it.
cards.h: → one supported claim + one unsupported + the reason
cards.n: Reading the chart as proof of a cause is the trap: it shows a pattern by grade, not what produces it.

cards.q: Decide which invented source a student writing to a skeptical school board should lead with, and which to hold for the rebuttal paragraph: Source A, the district's own attendance data showing a rise after a pilot program; Source B, a student petition with 900 signatures; Source C, a national study the board has publicly questioned.
cards.a: Lead with Source A: evidence the board produced and trusts starts the argument on shared ground. Hold Source C for the rebuttal, where the student can answer the board's doubts about it directly instead of letting them undercut the opening. Source B shows student support but not results, so it suits the conclusion's call to act. The audience decides the order as much as each source's strength does.
cards.h: → lead source + rebuttal source + the audience's reason
cards.n: Leading with the national study because it is the largest is the trap: this audience has already said it doubts it.

cards.q: Identify the error in this invented synthesis thesis and correct it: 'Sources A, C, and E all show that school gardens are good.'
cards.a: Error: the thesis reports what sources say instead of stating the writer's own position, and 'good' is too vague to defend. Corrected: 'School gardens deserve a line in the budget, because they teach science through work students can see and supply fresh food the cafeteria cannot afford.' Synthesis integrates others' arguments into the writer's own; the sources then support that claim.
cards.h: → the error + a position the sources can support
cards.n: Tempting because it names three sources up front; a thesis about the sources is a summary, not a position.

cards.q: Explain how noticing that two invented sources share a position but not a perspective can strengthen a synthesis paragraph: Source B, a pediatrician, and Source D, a school bus company's safety director, both support a later school start.
cards.a: Two sources reaching the same position from different perspectives, medical and transportation safety, show that the claim holds across fields, which is stronger than two sources with the same background. Commentary can say so explicitly, turning the agreement itself into evidence. Naming each perspective also lets the writer weigh any interest, such as the bus company's own scheduling costs.
cards.h: → why differing perspectives help + how commentary uses it
cards.n: Listing them as 'two more sources that agree' wastes the point: the difference in perspective is what makes the agreement meaningful.

cards.q: Explain why a synthesis essay should be organized by the writer's claims rather than by source.
cards.a: Synthesis integrates others' arguments into the writer's own, and the sequence of paragraphs reveals the line of reasoning; paragraphs built around sources reveal only the order the sources were read, while paragraphs built around claims show how several sources together support each step.
cards.h: → synthesis = sources inside the writer's argument → paragraph order shows reasoning → source order shows reading order
cards.n: 'Covering each source in turn is thorough' is the trap; it produces summary, and the paragraph order argues nothing.
o: When one paragraph combines two sources, the commentary can show how they complement or complicate each other, which a source-by-source essay never does.
Claims organize the essay around the prompt's question; sources are the evidence each claim draws on.

w.a: Organizing by source is clearer because each source gets its own paragraph.
w.why: clear summary is not a line of reasoning

w.a: It does not matter how the essay is organized as long as three sources are cited.
w.why: citing three sources is the minimum, not synthesis

w.a: The sources are the argument, so they should lead.
w.why: the one-unit answer that puts sources over the writer's claims

cards.q: Explain why naming a source's perspective, not just its position, can strengthen commentary in a synthesis essay.
cards.a: Position is where a source stands; perspective is why it stands there, from its background, interests, and expertise. Naming the perspective lets commentary weigh the evidence (a manufacturer's interest, a nurse's firsthand view) and show when different perspectives converge, which is stronger than counting agreements.
cards.h: → position = stance, perspective = why → naming why lets commentary weigh it → converging perspectives add force
cards.n: 'Source B agrees with me' is the trap; agreement says little until the commentary says from where.
o: Perspective explains a source's biases, which the strongest arguments acknowledge and account for.
Two sources with the same position but different perspectives answer different objections an audience might raise.

w.a: Only the position matters, since that is what supports the thesis.
w.why: misses what perspective adds to weighing evidence

w.a: Perspective and position mean the same thing.
w.why: the CED says they are different

w.a: Mentioning a source's background is just extra detail.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores how it shapes commentary

cards.q: Explain why a source's date and occasion can limit what its evidence proves.
cards.a: Every text is written in a context of time, place, and occasion; findings from another year or setting describe that context, so using them as proof about today stretches them, and a writer who ignores the gap oversteps the evidence while one who names it stays credible.
cards.h: → texts belong to a context → findings describe it → using them beyond it overstates → naming the gap keeps trust
cards.n: 'Old sources are unreliable' is the trap; the point is not age but the gap between the source's context and the claim's.
o: A source written for a particular occasion, such as a campaign, may emphasize what that occasion rewarded, just as a finding from another year describes conditions that may since have changed.
Because a finding describes its own year and setting, acknowledging that context in the commentary answers the objection before an opponent can raise it.

w.a: Older sources are always wrong, so they should not be used.
w.why: age does not make evidence false

w.a: A source's context does not matter if it comes from an expert.
w.why: expertise does not close the gap in time or setting

w.a: Context only matters in rhetorical analysis.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores sources' contexts

cards.q: Explain why including a source that contradicts your thesis can make a synthesis essay more persuasive.
cards.a: Writers enhance credibility when they concede or rebut contradictory evidence; readers who can see all six sources know the contradiction exists, so answering it shows the writer weighed the whole conversation, while ignoring it looks like evasion.
cards.h: → readers know the counterevidence → answering it shows fairness → credibility rises → ignoring it looks evasive
cards.n: 'Only use sources that agree' is the trap; readers of a synthesis essay know which sources you skipped.
o: A contradicting source, once rebutted or conceded in part, narrows the claim to what survives, which makes it harder to attack.
Engaging positions already argued is how a writer enters an ongoing conversation instead of talking past it.

w.a: A contradicting source weakens the essay, so it should be left out.
w.why: the CED ties rebuttal and concession to credibility

w.a: Every source must be used, including the ones that disagree.
w.why: the prompt requires three sources, not all six; the reason is credibility

w.a: Contradicting sources only confuse readers.
w.why: the one-unit answer that ignores what the audience already knows

cards.q: Explain why quoting a source's exact word can be better evidence than paraphrasing it.
cards.a: When the evidence is the source's word choice, its connotation, a paraphrase replaces the very thing being analyzed; quoting keeps the word so commentary can explain what it reveals about the source's perspective, which a paraphrase would erase.
cards.h: → some evidence is the wording itself → a paraphrase swaps it out → a quote keeps it → commentary can analyze it
cards.n: 'Quotations are more accurate' is the one-unit answer; the credited point is that connotation lives only in the exact word.
o: A quotation also shows fairness when the writer will dispute it, because readers see the source's own words.
Paraphrase suits information; quotation suits language, when how something is said is part of what it means.

w.a: Quotations are always better than paraphrases because they are exact.
w.why: a quotation of plain information adds nothing

w.a: Paraphrasing is always better because it shows understanding.
w.why: it erases wording the analysis needs

w.a: It does not matter which one you use as long as you cite it.
w.why: the choice decides what evidence remains

cards.q: State the overall format of the AP English Language and Composition exam.
cards.a: Section I: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, worth 45% of the score. Section II: three free-response essays in 2 hours 15 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period), worth 55%.
cards.h: → two sections with times and weights
cards.n: Total testing time is 3 hours 15 minutes; the FRQs are worth more than the entire MC section.

cards.q: State what Section I of the AP Lang exam contains.
cards.a: 45 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes in five sets (two reading sets of 11-14 questions, three writing sets of 4-9), split between reading questions (rhetorical analysis of nonfiction passages) and writing questions (revising a draft passage for argument, evidence, and style).
cards.h: → count, time, two question types
cards.n: Roughly 23-25 reading-analysis questions and 20-22 writing/revision questions - budget about 80 seconds per question.

cards.q: Contrast the two kinds of multiple-choice questions on the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Reading questions ask what a published passage does - the writer's choices, purpose, audience, and reasoning. Writing questions present a student draft and ask which revision best achieves a stated goal, such as adding evidence or improving a transition.
cards.h: → two types + what each asks
cards.n: Writing questions always name a goal; the right answer is the one that serves that goal, not the prettiest sentence.

cards.q: State the structure of Section II of the AP Lang exam.
cards.a: Three essays in 2 hours 15 minutes: Q1 Synthesis, Q2 Rhetorical Analysis, Q3 Argument. The first 15 minutes are a suggested reading period for the synthesis source packet; each essay is then given about 40 minutes.
cards.h: → three essays + timing
cards.n: The essays are equally weighted, so never let one essay eat another's time.

cards.q: Explain how to use the 15-minute reading period.
cards.a: Read the Q1 prompt first, decide a tentative position, then skim all sources marking each one's stance and one usable quotation. Sketch a three-part line of reasoning. You may begin writing before the 15 minutes end.
cards.h: → ordered plan
cards.n: Reading sources without a position first is the main way students burn the reading period.

cards.q: Identify what the synthesis question (Q1) demands.
cards.a: Take a defensible position on the issue and develop an argument that incorporates and cites at least three of the six provided sources as support. The sources are evidence for your claim, not the subject of the essay.
cards.h: → task + source requirement
cards.n: The prompt's phrasing is usually 'develop a position' - a summary of the debate with no position cannot earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the rhetorical analysis question (Q2) demands.
cards.a: Read a nonfiction passage with a given rhetorical situation, then analyze the rhetorical choices the writer makes to achieve their purpose - explaining how and why the choices work on that audience, not merely which devices appear.
cards.h: → task + emphasis
cards.n: The thesis must name the writer's message or purpose; a list of devices alone does not earn Row A.

cards.q: Identify what the argument question (Q3) demands.
cards.a: Respond to a short prompt or quotation by taking your own defensible position and supporting it with evidence you supply - personal experience, observation, reading, history, current events - developed with commentary.
cards.h: → task + evidence source
cards.n: No passage is provided, so evidence quality is entirely on you; specific named examples beat general assertions.

cards.q: State the three rows of the AP Lang essay rubric and their point values.
cards.a: Row A: Thesis, 0-1 point. Row B: Evidence and Commentary, 0-4 points. Row C: Sophistication, 0-1 point. Total 6 points per essay.
cards.h: → three rows with values
cards.n: The same 6-point rubric applies to all three essays; Row B alone is two-thirds of the score.

cards.q: Explain exactly what earns the Row A thesis point.
cards.a: One point for a defensible thesis that responds to the prompt with a position, and that may preview the line of reasoning but need not. It may sit anywhere in the essay (several sentences if they are close together) and must be more than a restatement of the prompt.
cards.h: → criteria for the point
cards.n: It is all-or-nothing: a partially defensible thesis earns zero, not a half point.

cards.q: Identify the most common reasons students lose the Row A point.
cards.a: Restating the prompt; describing the passage or sources instead of claiming; listing devices with no message ('the author uses ethos, pathos, and logos'); an obvious, undebatable statement; or a position so vague it must be inferred.
cards.h: → list of causes
cards.n: Write the thesis last in paragraph one, in one sentence, and make sure a reasonable person could disagree with it.

cards.q: Explain the Row B scale from 0 to 4.
cards.a: 0: no relevant evidence, or the response only restates the thesis. 1: mostly general evidence, and/or evidence summarized rather than explained. 2: some specific relevant evidence, with explanation of how some of it relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or the line of reasoning is faulty. 3: specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning, with explanation of how some of the evidence supports that line of reasoning. 4: specific evidence for all claims in a line of reasoning, with commentary that consistently explains how the evidence supports it.
cards.h: → five-level scale
cards.n: The jump from 1 to 2 is the jump from summarizing evidence to explaining it; the jump from 2 to 3 is establishing a real line of reasoning.

cards.q: Contrast a Row B score of 3 and a Row B score of 4.
cards.a: A 3 supports all claims in a line of reasoning with specific evidence but explains only some of it. A 4 sustains it: every claim has specific, well-chosen evidence and the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports a coherent line of reasoning.
cards.h: → what changes at 4
cards.n: Consistency and a visible line of reasoning are the difference; one brilliant paragraph among three thin ones is a 3.

cards.q: Explain what the Row C sophistication point rewards.
cards.a: One point for a response that demonstrates sophistication of thought or a complex understanding of the rhetorical situation, as part of the argument, not merely a phrase or reference.
cards.h: → criterion + scope
cards.n: Only a small share of essays earns it, and never through grand-sounding closing lines or complex language that does not enhance the argument.

cards.q: Identify the recognized routes to earning the sophistication point.
cards.a: Synthesis and argument: consistently exploring complexities or tensions; articulating implications or limitations by situating the argument in a broader context; rhetorical choices that consistently strengthen the argument; a consistently vivid, persuasive style. Rhetorical analysis: explaining the significance of the writer's choices given the situation, the purpose of the passage's tensions, or the same style route.
cards.h: → four routes (three on Q2)
cards.n: Choose one route and sustain it; attempting all four superficially reads as unfocused.

cards.q: Identify what does NOT earn the sophistication point.
cards.a: Sweeping generalizations ('humans have always struggled with this'), a single fancy sentence, unsupported claims about society, dense vocabulary without substance, and hedged both-sides commentary that never commits.
cards.h: → list of non-qualifiers
cards.n: Readers are told to reward sustained complexity, not isolated flourishes.

cards.q: State a workable timing plan for the AP Lang free-response section.
cards.a: 15 minutes reading and planning Q1; 40 minutes writing Q1; 5 minutes planning and 35 minutes writing Q2; 5 minutes planning and 30 minutes writing Q3; 5 minutes final check. Wear a watch and switch essays on schedule even if unfinished.
cards.h: → minute-by-minute plan
cards.n: Three complete decent essays outscore two excellent ones plus a fragment, because each is scored independently out of 6.

cards.q: Explain how to read a synthesis source set quickly.
cards.a: Read the prompt and take a position first. Then, for each source, read the header, the first and last paragraph, and skim the middle, jotting a two-word stance label and starring one usable line. Note which sources conflict - that tension is where sophistication lives.
cards.h: → procedure per source
cards.n: Charts and images count as sources and are underused; they often supply the cleanest data point.

cards.q: Explain how to write a rhetorical analysis body paragraph.
cards.a: Name the rhetorical choice; quote the specific evidence briefly; explain the effect on the intended audience; then link that effect to the writer's overall purpose. Choice, evidence, effect, purpose - in that order, every paragraph.
cards.h: → four-step chain
cards.n: The 'effect' and 'purpose' steps are the ones students skip, and they are exactly where Row B points live.

cards.q: Explain how to organize a rhetorical analysis essay other than device by device.
cards.a: Organize by the argument's movement: how the writer shifts from establishing credibility, to intensifying urgency, to demanding action - analyzing choices as they serve each stage. This foregrounds purpose instead of cataloguing techniques.
cards.h: → organizing principle
cards.n: Chunking the passage by rhetorical purpose is the surest structural route away from device-hunting.

cards.q: Identify why 'device-hunting' lowers a rhetorical analysis score.
cards.a: Naming devices without explaining their effect produces evidence with no commentary, capping Row B at 1 or 2. A correct label ('this is anaphora') proves nothing about how the passage works on its audience.
cards.h: → problem + rubric consequence
cards.n: You may earn a 6 without naming a single device by name, as long as you explain the choices.

cards.q: Identify why summarizing the passage or sources lowers a score.
cards.a: Summary reports content; the rubric rewards analysis of how content works. A summary-driven essay usually has no defensible thesis (Row A zero) and evidence without commentary (Row B 1-2).
cards.h: → problem + rubric consequence
cards.n: If your paragraph could be written by someone who agreed with nothing you believe, it is summary.

cards.q: Explain why five-paragraph autopilot hurts on AP Lang.
cards.a: The formula forces exactly three body paragraphs whether the argument needs two or five, encourages one-source-per-paragraph listing, and spends space on formulaic intros and restating conclusions instead of commentary. Let the line of reasoning set the paragraph count.
cards.h: → named problems + alternative
cards.n: There is no required number of paragraphs; readers score reasoning, not shape.

cards.q: Explain how to handle the argument essay's requirement to take a position.
cards.a: State one clear position in the thesis and hold it. You may qualify - agree with limits or under conditions - but you must be committed enough that a reader could argue against you; balanced 'both sides have points' essays fail Row A.
cards.h: → requirement + allowed nuance
cards.n: Qualifying is not fence-sitting: 'X is justified only when Y' is a strong, defensible position.

cards.q: Define what an AP prompt means by 'evaluate.'
cards.a: To evaluate is to judge the merit, validity, or effectiveness of something against criteria and to argue for that judgment - not to describe or summarize it.
cards.h: → definition + what it excludes
cards.n: Evaluate is not an AP Lang essay task verb (those are analyze, argue your position, synthesize); judging whether the Q2 writer succeeded earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain the 'defend, challenge, or qualify' instruction on an AP Lang prompt.
cards.a: Defend means argue the claim is right; challenge means argue it is wrong; qualify means agree in part while specifying the conditions or limits under which it holds. You must choose one and sustain it - all three are equally scoreable.
cards.h: → three options + rule
cards.n: Current prompts say 'argues your position on...', not 'defend, challenge, or qualify'; the three stances still work, but wavering between them fails Row A.

cards.q: Explain how to write a strong qualified position.
cards.a: Name what you accept in the claim, name the conditions or cases where it fails, and state the principle that separates them. 'Civil disobedience is justified when legal channels have been exhausted, but not when the cause has not yet been argued publicly.'
cards.h: → three moves + model sentence
cards.n: A qualified thesis must still be one sentence with one governing position, not two claims joined by 'but.'

cards.q: Explain how to use the context paragraph that precedes an FRQ passage.
cards.a: It supplies the rhetorical situation - writer, audience, occasion, exigence, and purpose - which the analysis must use. Mining it for audience and occasion is the fastest way to make commentary specific rather than generic.
cards.h: → what it gives + how to use
cards.n: Ignoring the framing paragraph is a common cause of vague, audience-free commentary on Q2.

cards.q: Explain what a Q2 rhetorical analysis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state the writer's purpose or message and indicate the kinds of choices used to achieve it, in a way that can be developed - not a list of devices and not a summary of the passage's topic.
cards.h: → required components
cards.n: 'Uses ethos, pathos, and logos to persuade the audience' is the classic Row A zero.

cards.q: Explain what a Q1 synthesis thesis must contain.
cards.a: It must state your own defensible position on the prompt's issue, specific enough to be argued with the sources, and it should suggest the reasoning that will organize the essay. It should not simply report what the sources collectively say.
cards.h: → required components
cards.n: A thesis that only reports the debate cannot be argued with, and reporting is the most common way Row A gets lost on Q1.

cards.q: Explain what counts as acceptable evidence on the Q3 argument essay.
cards.a: Anything specific and accurate: history, current events, literature, film, science, personal experience, or observation. Readers do not privilege one domain; they reward specificity, accuracy, and the commentary that connects it to the claim.
cards.h: → range + criterion
cards.n: Two developed examples with real commentary beat five name-dropped ones.

cards.q: Explain the ratio of evidence to commentary you should aim for.
cards.a: Roughly one sentence of evidence to two of commentary. If a paragraph is mostly quotation or mostly source summary, it is under-analyzed no matter how apt the evidence is.
cards.h: → ratio + diagnostic
cards.n: Highlight your quotations: if more than a third of a body paragraph is highlighted, cut evidence and add commentary.

cards.q: State a 5-minute end-of-essay checklist.
cards.a: Does the thesis take a defensible position? Does each topic sentence make a claim? Is every quotation followed by explanation? Are at least three sources cited (Q1)? Does the last sentence of each paragraph tie back to the thesis?
cards.h: → five checks
cards.n: Most of these are cheaper to handle while drafting than at the end, so treat the list as habits rather than a final sweep.

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice reading questions.
cards.a: Read the question stem before rereading the lines, return to the cited lines and their surrounding context, predict an answer in your own words, then find the choice closest to it. Eliminate choices that are true of the passage but do not answer the stem.
cards.h: → ordered strategy
cards.n: The most common wrong answer is accurate about the passage but irrelevant to what the question asked.

cards.q: Explain the best strategy for AP Lang multiple-choice writing/revision questions.
cards.a: Identify the stated goal in the stem (add evidence, sharpen the claim, improve the transition), then judge each option only against that goal. Read the sentences before and after the insertion point, since the answer usually depends on that link.
cards.h: → goal-first strategy
cards.n: Grammatically fine but goal-irrelevant options are the standard distractors here.

cards.q: State the guessing policy and pacing target for the multiple-choice section.
cards.a: There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. With 45 questions in 60 minutes, the pace is about 80 seconds per question, so about 15-19 minutes for an 11-14-question reading set and 5-12 for a 4-9-question writing set.
cards.h: → policy + pace
cards.n: Never leave a blank; mark and return rather than stalling on one hard question.

cards.q: Explain how to annotate a passage efficiently during the exam.
cards.a: The exam is fully digital in Bluebook, so annotate with the app's highlight and note tools rather than a pen: highlight the shifts (but, yet, however), the audience and occasion clues, and one or two places where tone changes, and drop a short note where each purpose-driven chunk of the passage begins. Do not highlight every device you recognize.
cards.h: → what to mark + what to skip
cards.n: Annotation should produce a structure you can write from, not a decorated page.

cards.q: State how AP Lang exam scores are reported and composed.
cards.a: The final AP score is a 1-5 scale. It combines the multiple-choice section (45%) with the three free-response essays (55%), each essay scored 0-6 on the same rubric and weighted equally.
cards.h: → scale + weighting
cards.n: A composite around half the available points typically reaches a 3; exact cut scores shift each year.

cards.q: Explain how AP readers score the essays.
cards.a: Each essay is scored row by row against the 6-point analytic rubric by a trained reader, independently of your other essays, and readers are instructed to reward what the response does well rather than deduct for what is missing.
cards.h: → process + guiding principle
cards.n: There is no penalty carried across essays: a weak Q1 does not lower your Q2 score.

cards.q: Explain how grammar and mechanics affect an AP Lang essay score.
cards.a: There is no separate grammar row. Errors matter only when they interfere with the reader's understanding of the argument; a well-reasoned essay with imperfect surface polish can still earn 6.
cards.h: → rule + limit
cards.n: This is not license to ignore clarity: errors that interfere with communication bar the fourth Row B point.

cards.q: Explain what happens if an essay does not respond to the prompt.
cards.a: Responses that are off-topic, that only repeat the prompt, or that are written in a language other than English receive a score of 0. A blank or completely blank-page response receives no score at all.
cards.h: → conditions for zero
cards.n: These outcomes are rare but absolute, and the most common route to one is answering a prompt that was skimmed rather than read.

cards.q: Decide what to do when you have 10 minutes left and no essay started on Q3.
cards.a: Write a one-sentence defensible thesis immediately, then two body paragraphs with one specific example each and two sentences of commentary each. Skip the introduction beyond the thesis and skip the conclusion. Thesis plus real commentary can still earn 3-4 points.
cards.h: → triage plan
cards.n: A thesis with two developed paragraphs scores far above a polished intro with nothing after it.

cards.q: Explain how to plan an essay in five minutes.
cards.a: Write the thesis in one sentence, then list two to four subclaims in the order they build, and note the single piece of evidence attached to each. That list is your topic sentences; if the subclaims do not build, reorder before writing.
cards.h: → three-step plan
cards.n: Reordering costs seconds on a list and minutes once paragraphs exist, which is the whole reason to write the list first.

cards.q: Identify habits that make commentary generic.
